PART II - PLAYER ROLE, COMPLEXITY & DISCOVERABILITY

2.1 High Action Visibility, Low Mandatory Interruption
New hard design doctrine:
The player should almost always be able to discover meaningful actions, but available actions should not become mandatory
interruption spam.
At a business, project, property or institution, the player should be able to understand:
  • what can be done;
  • why the action might matter;
  • what it requires;
  • what it may accomplish;
  • what uncertainty remains;
  • what happens if it is ignored;
  • whether it can be self-managed, delegated or subcontracted.

2.2 Feature breadth doctrine
Revision XIX supersedes any interpretation that feature count itself is a design problem. Large feature breadth is acceptable and
desirable when features are:
  • causal;
  • interconnected;
  • economically meaningful;
  • reusable across systems;
  • visible enough to learn through play;
  • compatible with the scale-transformation and delegation doctrines.
Reject isolated novelty mechanics that do not affect the wider simulation. Do not reject a deep mechanic merely because the
project already contains many systems.

2.3 Discoverability requirement
The game should not require an external wiki to reveal basic possibilities such as subcontracting a railway survey, using public-
land right-of-way, arranging a freight contract, checking an operating bottleneck, hiring a manager or examining a business for
sale. UI, reports, world evidence, NPC advice, manager proposals and workflow surfaces should reveal legitimate options when
the player has enough information to know they exist.

2.4 Text-playtest option count is not Canon
The repeated use of exactly nine strategic options was a text-playtest format. It is not a final-game rule.





                                                   3

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 128/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART III - TASKS, WORK & FAILURE

3.1 Meaningful task granularity
Business execution should not collapse a whole production chain into one abstract task when intermediate work has real labor,
equipment, timing, quality or failure consequences.
A bakery may generate meaningful tasks such as retrieve ingredients, measure, mix, knead, proof, shape, prepare oven, bake,
unload, cool, package, stage, load and deliver. Other industries should follow the same principle.
The target is meaningful granularity, not animation granularity. Do not turn every hand motion into a simulation object.

3.2 Continuous time and parallel work
Tasks use the authoritative continuous clock. A 37-minute task finishes 37 minutes later, not at the next arbitrary hourly or daily
tick. Independent workers, equipment and work areas can proceed in parallel when prerequisites and resources permit.

3.3 Task failure inputs
Task outcome can depend on relevant:
  • capability and experience;
  • difficulty;
  • fatigue;
  • supervision;
  • equipment and material condition;
  • environment and weather;
  • time pressure;
  • information quality;
  • other domain-specific causes.

3.4 Failure creates consequences, not generic penalties
Task failures should produce domain-specific results such as rework, delay, material loss, batch loss, weak quality, injury,
property damage or fire where causally justified. Do not resolve every failure through a generic percentage debuff.
A failure can create actual follow-up work. A repairable mistake should create the corrective task rather than merely reducing
Efficiency.





                                                   4

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 129/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART IV - MANAGEMENT, DELEGATION & AUTONOMY

4.1 Manager titles do not impose hierarchy
Manager and General Manager are descriptive authority roles, not RPG tiers.
A reasonable naming convention is:
  • Manager: routine authority over one business, site or operating unit.
  • General Manager: routine authority across several businesses or substantial operating units.
This does not require a General Manager to have subordinate managers. One capable manager can cover several units when
workload, geography, expertise and decision volume allow it.

4.2 Management remains real labor
Management consumes finite attention. More businesses, locations, workers, contracts, exceptions and travel create real
administrative burden. The player can personally manage when workload permits and can avoid management payroll until the
economics justify delegation.

4.3 Manager optimization
Capable managers may improve schedules and operating practice by changing actual decisions such as start times, recurring
task timing, delivery windows, assignment order, equipment sequencing, stock timing and customer service windows. The benefit
comes from better execution, not a Management Efficiency multiplier.

4.4 Transferability audit
When preparing a business for disposition, ask:
If the current owner disappeared tomorrow, what consequential decisions would stop being made?
The answer identifies genuine authority gaps. Fix them through policy, staffing, governance or other real continuity measures
rather than forcing a manager checkbox.

4.5 Autonomy testing
A business may prove transferability through a period in which the owner takes no routine operating decisions. The exact
duration is scenario calibration. The test succeeds only if routine decisions continue, obligations are met and the enterprise
remains stable without hidden owner intervention.

4.6 Manager Activity
Add a player-visible Manager Activity concept separate from the financial ledger. It answers:
What did delegated people decide or handle so the owner did not have to?
Useful information can include date/time, manager, business/site, decision, trigger, standing policy or authority, outcome,
whether an escalation occurred and directly measurable financial impact where that impact is defensible.
Do not fabricate counterfactual dollar savings for every decision. When value cannot be measured honestly, report the activity
without an invented number.

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 130/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART V - BUILDING DEFECTS, INSPECTION & KNOWLEDGE

5.1 Ordinary defects can be discovered through use
Workers using a building can notice observable problems such as leaks, damaged floors, sticking doors, obvious chimney
trouble, visible deterioration or other symptoms. Ordinary property should not require a generic monthly Building Inspection
simply to reveal what normal occupants would notice.

5.2 Specialist inspection remains valid
Hidden or high-risk systems can require specialists, including boilers, electrical systems, water systems, mines, structural
questions, rail infrastructure and other technically difficult domains.
Inspection changes knowledge. Repair changes physical state.

5.3 Poor records reduce information, not reality
Bad bookkeeping should produce missing, stale, incomplete or unreconciled information. It should not randomly fuzz facts that
were actually known. Better records improve Recorded State and decision support; they do not change Actual State by magic.

PART VI - ANIMALS & BIOLOGICAL WORK ASSETS

6.1 Preventive animal care
Working animals require real feed, water, rest and ordinary observation. Depending on species and use, recurring work can
include grooming, hoof observation, harness checks, condition observation and other practical care.

6.2 Specialist care
Farriers and veterinarians may operate on-map or off-map. Travel, call-out burden and group visits can matter. A standing
service agreement does not magically service every animal; actual animal-level or cohort-level work still occurs.

6.3 Persistent animal state and imperfect information
Animals retain biological health, fatigue, injury, feed/nutrition, disease exposure, age and relevant temperament/behavior.
Inspection improves knowledge rather than revealing perfect hidden truth. Seller descriptions can be truthful, mistaken or
dishonest.
Player-facing descriptions can map internal continuous values into understandable bands, but exact band boundaries remain
calibration.

6.4 Working cats and dogs
Where historically and practically supported, cats can reduce actual rodent pressure and dogs can contribute to guarding,
herding or ranch work. Their value must arise from real tasks and conditions, not passive magical bonuses.





                                                   7

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 132/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART VII - B2B, SUPPLIERS & PRODUCT ECONOMICS

7.1 B2B relationship workflow
Preserve a full business-to-business commercial loop:
identify -> approach -> learn need -> propose -> negotiate quantity/price/cadence/credit/delivery -> accept/refuse/counter ->
perform -> renew/end.
The player-facing UI should explain B2B rather than assume the acronym is universally understood.

7.2 Item-level sourcing
Different merchandise can legitimately use different suppliers. Supplier evaluation can consider invoice price, landed cost,
quality, minimum order, credit terms, lead time, freight responsibility, reliability, seasonal capacity and origin.

7.3 Consolidated freight economics
A supplier with a higher invoice price can still be economically superior when consolidated freight lowers landed cost. Freight
burden must be allocated using real transport/storage/handling burden rather than arbitrary equal division.

7.4 Capital turnover
Margin percentage alone is not enough. Faster payment, shorter inventory holding periods and better capital turnover can make
a lower-spread relationship more profitable than a slower high-margin buyer.
Product and buying reports may therefore distinguish invoice cost, landed cost, current selling price, target/minimum margin,
financing cost, inventory age and sales velocity.

7.5 Pricing changes customer behavior
Higher prices can cause customers to buy from local rivals, travel, source off-map, substitute, postpone or stop buying.
Sustainable profit is the objective; maximizing margin percentage is not.





                                                   8

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 133/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART VIII - LIQUIDITY, LINE OF CREDIT & TREASURY

8.1 Dynamic liquidity requirement
Revision XIX deepens the Operating Reserve doctrine. Do not treat reserve policy as a universal fixed cash floor.
A business should protect the cash actually needed for foreseeable near-term obligations and risk, including payroll, supplier
bills, debt service, committed purchases, transport/animal needs, project draws, seasonal requirements and a justified
contingency.
A reserve can rise before harvest or a major payment and fall afterward. Protected liquidity is a policy/read model derived from
real commitments, not a separate money pool.

8.2 Line of Credit
Line of Credit becomes a first-class credit facility where historically appropriate.
A Line of Credit should conceptually track:
  • lender;
  • authorized limit;
  • outstanding amount;
  • undrawn availability;
  • rate or discount terms;
  • purpose;
  • collateral/security;
  • draw and repayment history;
  • maturity or renewal;
  • covenants or lender discretion.
Unused availability is neither cash nor debt. Financing cost should reflect actual time outstanding rather than treating an annual
rate as a cost on every inventory turn.

8.3 Owner-capital backstop
A standing policy may allow owner capital to support an owned business if projected liquidity becomes unsafe. Material capital
calls should still escalate rather than silently emptying the owner's personal funds.

8.4 Debt repayment policy
Highest-effective-rate debt repayment was successful in the playtest and is a valid player policy. It is not a universal Canon
mandate. Other strategies can be rational depending on liquidity, covenants, maturity, collateral, opportunity cost and risk.





                                                   9

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 134/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART IX - BUSINESS SALES & CONTINUITY

9.1 Cash inclusion is an explicit transaction term
Sale of a business does not silently transfer all business cash. The agreement must state what cash, working capital,
receivables, payables, inventory and other assets or obligations are included.
A buyer must have sufficient working capital to operate after closing, whether that capital comes from included cash, the buyer's
own funds, financing or another explicit arrangement.

9.2 Continuing contractual rights after sale
A seller may retain a limited contractual right or service arrangement after disposition where legally and commercially valid. Such
a right must be explicit, bounded and distinct from retained operating control. The bakery employee-meal arrangement from the
playtest is an example of the structure, not a universal clause.

9.3 Employees after sale
Employees remain independent Persons. The buyer may offer continued employment; workers may accept, negotiate, refuse,
leave or retire. Business ownership does not transfer ownership of people.

PART X - RAILWAY CAPITAL LADDER

10.1 Low-entry railway path
Railway ownership should not require the player to begin with a giant trunk-line construction project. Historically plausible entry
can include:
lease/access -> operate -> retain earnings -> selectively own rolling stock -> buy track/facilities -> improve terminals -> build
short extensions -> build larger regional corridor.
This is a possibility set, not a mandatory linear technology tree.

10.2 Leasing is strategic
Track access, terminals, locomotives, cars and backup equipment can be leased or contracted where historically supported.
Ownership is justified by economics and strategic control, not by an abstract progression reward.
Emergency equipment access can be superior to owning an underutilized backup asset.





                                                  11

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 136/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XI - RAILWAY PROJECT DEVELOPMENT

11.1 Railway development chain
A serious railway corridor can involve:
corridor selection -> reconnaissance/traffic study -> route alternatives -> engineering/survey -> alignment/gauge decisions ->
anchor customers/traffic commitments -> connection/interchange arrangements -> finance -> right-of-way/control -> construction
-> facilities/equipment -> opening service -> operating history -> later extension.
The exact sequence can overlap where reality allows it.

11.2 Specialist work
Small railways can hire outside engineering, traffic, land, legal and financial specialists rather than permanently employing every
function. Prime contractors may coordinate several specialist tasks when the contract scope genuinely covers them.

11.3 Financeability and Economic Viability
New hard Canon lock:
Financeability asks whether enough capital can be assembled to build the project.
Economic Viability asks whether the completed railway can generate enough value to support operation, maintenance, financing
and continued reinvestment.
A project can pass one gate and fail the other. Both must remain visible.

11.4 Commitments are not track
Surveys, options, rights, traffic commitments and financing intentions are valuable development state but do not become
operational railway until the physical and legal work is completed.





                                                  12

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 137/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XII - STAGED RAILWAY CONSTRUCTION & ECONOMIC NODES

12.1 Build in economic stages
A railway corridor can be constructed and opened in sequential segments. The company does not have to complete the final
intended destination before earning revenue from an already useful section.

12.2 Intermediate Service Nodes
A stage can terminate at a real economic node such as:
  • town or settlement;
  • major farm cluster;
  • stock-loading point;
  • grain concentration;
  • mill or mine;
  • timber camp;
  • wagon-road junction;
  • industrial site;
  • other traffic-generating location.

12.3 No artificial profitable checkpoint rule
The game must not manufacture a profitable station every few miles merely to support staged gameplay. Some intermediate
nodes will fail the economic test. The correct stage length comes from geography, traffic and cost.

12.4 Segment economics
Each stage should be evaluated on its own capital requirement, traffic, revenue, operating burden, equipment need, financing
burden and strategic value. A completed stage can generate cash and information that help finance or justify the next stage.





                                                  13

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 138/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XIII - RAILWAY RIGHTS, PARALLEL TRACK & INTERCHANGE

13.1 Same-company additional track
A railway may add passing sidings, yard tracks, partial double track or full double track as traffic and geography warrant.

13.2 Competing parallel construction
A different railway may build a parallel line where it can lawfully obtain its own right-of-way and construction authority. The
existence of another railway does not give a competitor free use of that railway's land.

13.3 Physical proximity does not grant legal authority
Track touching another track, crossing it or running beside it does not automatically grant operating rights.
Keep distinct:
  • crossing right;
  • connection;
  • interchange;
  • terminal access;
  • joint use;
  • trackage rights;
  • lease;
  • ownership.
Dakota-specific 1880s crossing/connection law remains a dated legal implementation/research matter where exact procedural
detail is needed.





                                                  14

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 139/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XIV - RAILWAY CONSTRUCTION TIME & PHYSICAL EXECUTION

14.1 Historical-speed baseline
For projects rather than biology, planning duration should begin from the fastest reasonably achievable historical baseline under
competent execution and the actual site/technology conditions. Variance then comes from weather, material delivery, labor,
engineering, ground conditions, financing, defects and contractor performance.
Do not make every major project slow simply because it is large. Do not make every project fast merely because exceptional
historical construction speeds existed.

14.2 Winter is task-specific
Winter can make some work impractical while allowing other tasks to continue, such as material preparation, shop fabrication,
structures, administrative work or selected construction. No universal winter shutdown rule.





                                                  15

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 140/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XV - RAILWAY OPERATING CAPACITY

15.1 Diagnose the real bottleneck
High locomotive utilization does not automatically mean the company needs another locomotive. Scheduling, staging, yard
geometry, interchange timing, car availability, crew coverage or customer windows may be the true constraint.

15.2 Peak versus average utilization
Reports should distinguish peak-period strain from full-day or full-period utilization.

15.3 Capital evidence
Expansion decisions can consider:
  • queue duration;
  • late movements;
  • profitable traffic lost or deferred;
  • maintenance downtime;
  • utilization;
  • service reliability;
  • expected future committed traffic.
The company should not buy an asset merely because it is the most obvious object associated with the bottleneck.

15.4 Yard geometry as infrastructure
Leads, crossovers, sidings, staging tracks and customer layout can materially affect throughput. Small physical improvements
can outperform expensive equipment purchases.

15.5 Freight-car availability is its own capacity problem
Locomotive availability and freight-car availability are separate constraints. Connecting-road equipment, leases and owned cars
can coexist. A railway does not need to own every car that touches its network.

15.6 Minimal station design
A new freight node can open with the minimum facilities needed to perform the traffic safely and reliably. Do not require an
elaborate passenger depot when the business case only supports siding, freight shelter, loading platform or livestock facilities.





                                                  16

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 141/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XVI - GOVERNMENT, LAND, MAIL & RAILWAY TAXATION

16.1 Government is not a generic railway subsidy button
Public support must follow actual dated law, program, contract or land authority. The major congressional land-grant/bond
programs for specific railroads do not create a universal subsidy available to every small railway.

16.2 Federal public-land right-of-way
The General Railroad Right-of-Way Act of 1875 is a canonical candidate for route economics where the route crosses qualifying
federal public domain and the company satisfies the dated legal requirements. The route must distinguish land status rather than
treating every mile as ordinary private purchase.
Useful land-status concepts include:
  • private property;
  • federal public domain;
  • railroad grant land;
  • reservation/trust/restricted land;
  • existing transportation right-of-way;
  • other legally distinct land.

16.3 July 30, 1886 corporate-aid restriction
A dated legal event should reflect the federal restriction on territorial/local-government stock subscriptions, credit lending or
borrowing for corporate benefit after July 30, 1886. Do not casually offer Dakota Gateway a county stock subscription in 1888.

16.4 Postal contracts
The Post Office can be a paying transportation customer. Mail service uses real schedules, handoff, reliability and contract
terms. It is not free subsidy income.

16.5 Railway-specific taxation
Dakota railway taxation should use dated railway-specific authority where validated. The 1883 territorial gross-earnings tax
framework identified in playtest research should be represented after reconciling the applicable line/company start date. Exact
applicability and rates remain a legal-data issue rather than a generic system constant.





                                                  17

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 142/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XVII - CORPORATE FINANCE, EQUITY & CONTROL

17.1 Corporate treasury
Corporate cash belongs to the corporation, not to the player's personal wallet. A minority shareholder cannot use company cash
for a personal purchase or unrelated enterprise without a lawful corporate transaction.

17.2 Cap table and dilution
New share issuance changes every holder's economic percentage. Before issuance, the player should be shown current
ownership, post-issue ownership if they do not participate and the amount required to preserve the current percentage where a
pro-rata opportunity exists.

17.3 Distinct corporate concepts
Keep separate:
  • contributed capital;
  • economic ownership;
  • voting rights;
  • board control;
  • officer/manager authority;
  • creditor claims.
Do not infer 51% control merely from being founder or President. Do not invent modern super-voting founder shares without
historical/legal support.

17.4 Bond finance
Bond face amount, coupon, maturity, security and outstanding debt are distinct from net cash proceeds. Issuance discount and
costs can make net proceeds lower than face debt.





                                                  18

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 143/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XVIII - RAILWAY DIVERSIFICATION & TOWNSITE DEVELOPMENT

18.1 Corporate-purpose constraint
Railway cash should not casually buy unrelated businesses. An investment must be permitted by the company's legal/charter
authority and governance and should have a defensible corporate purpose.

18.2 Rail-adjacent ventures
Historically and economically plausible ventures can include:
  • freight warehouses;
  • team tracks/public loading facilities;
  • stockyards;
  • station/freight property;
  • townsite/land development;
  • selected hotels/eating houses where demand supports them;
  • communications or utility relationships;
  • other traffic-supporting infrastructure.

18.3 Own versus enable
The railway should compare direct ownership with letting an independent entrepreneur invest. Providing a site, siding and service
to an independent elevator can outperform tying up railway capital in the elevator itself.

18.4 Double benefit must be causal
A townsite, warehouse or other adjacent investment may earn direct profit and create railway traffic, but neither benefit is
automatic. The actual town or business must succeed.

18.5 Strategic land options
The railway can use legitimate options or conditional control to preserve strategically important land without purchasing every
future parcel immediately.

18.6 Unrelated businesses
A saloon, bakery, General Store or other unrelated enterprise should ordinarily use the player's personal capital or a separate
company rather than silently consuming railway treasury.





                                                  19

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 144/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XIX - CORPORATE SALE, MERGER & FINAL TRANSFER

19.1 Minority owner cannot sell the company alone
A player owning a small percentage of a railway may support a whole-company sale but cannot personally convey every share or
asset without the appropriate corporate authority.

19.2 Whole-company transaction
A serious corporate sale or merger can require:
  • buyer diligence;
  • board approval;
  • shareholder approval where applicable;
  • creditor/bond treatment;
  • contract assignment or consent;
  • treatment of subsidiaries/property;
  • employee transition;
  • transfer of officer/management authority.

19.3 Enterprise value versus equity value
Headline enterprise value and shareholder consideration are not the same when debt is assumed or retained. Player proceeds
come from the economic claim actually owned.

19.4 Pre-close distributions
A pre-closing shareholder distribution is a separate transaction from the purchase consideration.

19.5 Transfer ends control
A qualifying sale or merger must actually transfer control. No hidden continued owner authority is allowed after closing unless a
separate new employment, board or contractual relationship explicitly grants it.





                                                  20

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 145/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XX - GENERAL STORE RETAIL LABOR

20.1 Clerk-mediated retail
The 1880s General Store should generally be modeled as clerk-mediated rather than as a modern self-service shop. Customers
may browse visible goods, but ordinary purchases can require the proprietor or clerk to retrieve merchandise, weigh or measure
bulk goods, cut or grind where applicable, wrap/package purchases, record credit/barter and settle payment.

20.2 Staffing emerges from workload
Do not hard-code two employees. A low-traffic store can operate with one person. Customer service consumes real time and
competes with receiving, stocking, ordering, bookkeeping, cleaning, deliveries, post-office/telephone work and other tasks. As
traffic rises, queues and deferred back-room work make additional clerks economically valuable.

20.3 Family-run stores
General Stores were often family businesses, but the whole family is not universally required. Valid configurations include one
proprietor, proprietor plus spouse, wider family operation, proprietor plus outside clerks or a much larger mercantile staff.
Family members are real Persons. Their work consumes time, creates fatigue, competes with household duties and may
substitute for outside paid labor without becoming invisible free labor.





                                                  21

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 146/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XXI - BARTER, STORE CREDIT & IN-KIND VALUE

21.1 Barter is a valid transaction form
Rural commerce may use cash, store credit and barter simultaneously. A customer can exchange eggs, butter, honey, produce,
game, labor or other accepted goods for merchandise where historically and economically appropriate.

21.2 Bartered goods remain real goods
Goods received in trade become real owned inventory or another real asset. They can be resold, shipped, consumed, spoiled,
rejected for quality or otherwise handled physically. Do not convert barter directly into invisible cash.

21.3 Mixed payment
A transaction may combine goods-in-kind, cash and customer account credit.

21.4 Valuation
Barter value is market/relationship/quality-dependent and can be negotiated. The transaction record should preserve both the
physical goods and the agreed economic valuation.

21.5 Historical change
Barter may decline as cash and financial systems deepen, but it does not disappear through one global technology unlock.

21.6 In-kind compensation
Meals, lodging, goods or other in-kind consideration can be components of employment or service compensation where
historically appropriate. They remain distinct from cash wages.





                                                  22

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 147/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XXII - TELEPHONE, TELEGRAPH & GENERAL STORE COMMUNICATIONS

22.1 Telephone versus telegraph
Telegraph is already a mature long-distance written communications system at the 1880 start. Telephone is a newer spoken
communications network beginning to spread unevenly through business subscribers and exchanges.
They remain parallel systems rather than one replacing the other.

22.2 General Store as early telephone hub
A General Store can plausibly be the first or one of the first local telephone subscribers when telephone service reaches a
settlement. Other early candidates can include hotels, post offices, railway offices, banks and major merchants.

22.3 Public-access/message role
Where most households lack telephones, a connected business can become a place for public calls or message receipt. This
can increase foot traffic and change ordering/market-information speed while also consuming clerk labor.

22.4 Network-dependent adoption
No global TELEPHONE UNLOCKED event gives every building service. Use:
invention/existence -> regional network/exchange -> local availability -> business subscription/connection -> household or rural-
network diffusion.
Rural/farmer mutual telephone systems become increasingly important later in the campaign as historically supported; exact
adoption timing remains regional data.





                                                  23

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 148/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XXIII - DATED HISTORICAL WORLD EVENTS

23.1 Historical events should change systems
Major historical, technological, institutional or legal developments should appear as dated world events when they materially alter
gameplay. They are not trivia cards.
A useful event notice tells the player:
  • what changed;
  • when it changed;
  • where it applies;
  • which mechanics are affected.

23.2 Railroad Standard Time
North American railroad standard time adoption on November 18, 1883 is a canonical candidate major event.
Before adoption, railway/local time conventions can differ where gameplay requires the distinction. After adoption, relevant
railway timetables, connections and time references use the standardized railway-time regime. Civil/local adoption may still vary
where historically appropriate.
The event matters even if the player does not own a railway. A merchant depending on rail schedules can experience the
change.





                                                  24

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 149/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XXIV - SALOONS, GAMBLING, DRINK SOLICITATION & PROSTITUTION

24.1 Historical occurrence governs eligibility
Revision XIX supersedes the Revision XVII production-scope interpretation to the extent it could be read as excluding historically
documented player-facing vice businesses solely because they were illegal.
New hard principle:
If an economic activity is historically documented in the relevant place/time, illegality alone does not exclude it from the simulated
economy or eventual player ownership. Legality and enforcement instead determine risk, consequences and available
arrangements.
This does not make every historically occurring activity a near-term implementation priority.

24.2 Legal Status versus Enforcement Posture remains authoritative
An activity can be illegal and widely known or locally tolerated at the same time. Tolerance does not legalize the activity or create
permanent immunity. Enforcement can change with police/prosecutor practice, politics, complaints, reform pressure, serious
incidents and other grounded causes.

24.3 Saloon gambling
Where supported by local/date-specific history, a saloon or related establishment may operate gambling through real
tables/games, equipment, dealers, bankroll/stakes, customers, wins/losses, theft/fraud exposure and legal/enforcement risk.
The exact game catalogue, house edge, legality and enforcement remain research/data rather than universal constants.

24.4 Female drink solicitation / entertainment labor
Historically supported establishments may employ women whose primary job includes socializing with patrons and encouraging
drink purchases rather than ordinary bartending. Compensation can include wages, commission or a combination.
Drink solicitation and prostitution are not automatically the same occupation. They can coexist or overlap in some historical
establishments, but one must not imply the other by default.
Workers remain Persons with agency. They can negotiate compensation, refuse terms, leave, change jobs or work part-time
where circumstances allow.

24.5 Prostitution and brothel ownership
Historically supported prostitution/house-of-ill-fame activity becomes in-scope for future player business design rather than
permanently excluded. The earlier legal research remains authoritative: such operation is not an ordinary licensed lawful
business in the normal campaign, no generic Brothel License is authorized and fines do not transform illegality into lawful
operation.
Coercive recruitment is not authorized as a normal player-facing economic mechanic. Adult participants remain people with
agency.
Implementation priority remains separate from Canon eligibility. A dedicated brothel management system may remain later-
phase work until it receives a full design/research pass.

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 150/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XXV - SALOON SCENARIO FAMILY

25.1 Saloon Circuit
Add a scenario concept built around progressively larger saloon markets. The player begins in a very small settlement and
expands or opens additional saloons in larger towns, with each location exposing different limiting problems rather than repeating
the same business at higher numbers.
Possible progression themes include:
  • very small town: inventory, supply, getting enough customers;
  • small town: competition, staffing, evening traffic;
  • growing town: entertainment, higher-volume purchasing, customer segmentation;
  • large town: management, internal controls, theft, multiple shifts and reputation;
  • regional center: large operation, managers, complex suppliers, ancillary businesses and institutional pressures.
The exact number of towns/saloons remains scenario calibration.

25.2 Saloon Enterprise Ladder
A separate variant can use build/improve/sell progression through increasingly large saloon enterprises.

25.3 Vertical integration
Supporting businesses such as bakery, butcher, freight, lodging or other historically plausible services can supply a saloon
network when the logistics and economics actually make sense.
Do not canonize the playtest's placeholder $1,000-per-quarter target or any placeholder drink/commission figures.

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 151/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XXVI - REWARD / PRIVATE DETECTIVE AGENCY

26.1 Candidate business archetype
Add Reward / Private Detective Agency as a researched candidate business family for the 1880-1905 setting.
A possible commercial loop is:
reward or private case becomes known -> agency accepts/solicits case -> choose agent(s) -> fund travel/expenses ->
investigation/pursuit -> capture/recovery/failure -> reward or client payment -> agent compensation -> agency margin.

26.2 Agent differentiation
Agents can differ through actual capabilities such as tracking, investigation, riding, firearms, negotiation, local knowledge,
languages or other case-relevant skills.

26.3 On-map and off-map cases
The same persistent agent/case identity can support locally manifested pursuit and longer off-map work.

26.4 Historical/legal distinctions
Do not collapse:
  • posted criminal rewards;
  • private detective work;
  • bail/surety fugitive recovery;
  • law-enforcement rewards;
  • company-sponsored pursuit.
Exact arrest authority, jurisdiction, reward entitlement and ordinary compensation structures remain research holds before full
business lock.

PART XXIX - EXPLICITLY REJECTED OR SUPERSEDED INTERPRETATIONS

The following are not Canon requirements:
  • Manager required for every business sale.
  • General Manager automatically requires subordinate managers.
  • Fixed universal $200 or other static business cash reserve.
  • Railway must reach Dry Willow to complete Enterprise Ladder.
  • Entire 43-mile or 17-mile corridor must be built before any railway revenue.
  • Every few miles of railway must contain a profitable stopping point.
  • Ownership is always better than leasing.
  • A second locomotive should be purchased solely because peak utilization is high.
  • The railway should own every station business.
  • Railway treasury can casually buy unrelated businesses.
  • Business cash automatically transfers in a sale.
  • Corporate treasury is personal owner cash.
  • Board control is the same as economic ownership.
  • Every General Store requires two employees.
  • The 1880s General Store is modern self-service retail.
  • The whole family is required to run every General Store.
  • Universal monthly building inspection.
  • Inspection automatically repairs condition.
  • One giant Make Bread task is sufficient for all bakery labor.
  • Failures should resolve as generic percentage penalties.
  • One-click subcontracting may magically complete an underlying project.
  • Feature count should be minimized merely to avoid feature creep.
  • Exactly nine strategic options is a game rule.
  • Historical events should be decorative trivia popups.
  • Telephone is a global technology unlock.
  • Telephone is a replacement for telegraph.
  • Drink solicitation automatically implies prostitution.
  • Illegality alone excludes a mechanic from the game.
  • Every saloon should have gambling or prostitution.
  • The bakery-oven household-rental idea remains parked unless stronger evidence/design need emerges.

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 156/346 ====================

                           LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIX / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

PART XXXI - REVISION XIX LOCK SUMMARY

Revision XIX hard locks:
  • Complexity should be interconnected and discoverable, not artificially minimized.
  • Action visibility and interruption are separate design problems.
  • Meaningful task granularity and causal rework are authoritative.
  • Dynamic liquidity supersedes fixed universal reserve assumptions.
  • Line of Credit is a distinct facility; undrawn capacity is not cash or debt.
  • Manager titles do not impose mandatory organizational hierarchy.
  • Manager Activity is distinct from the Ledger.
  • Railway Financeability and Economic Viability are separate gates.
  • Railway corridors may open in economically valid stages.
  • Intermediate nodes are not guaranteed to be profitable.
  • Track proximity does not grant land or operating rights.
  • Corporate cash, economic ownership, voting control, board control and managerial authority remain distinct.
  • Railway diversification must have lawful corporate purpose and causal economics.
  • General Store retail is predominantly clerk-mediated; staffing follows workload.
  • Barter is a real transaction that transfers real goods.
  • Telephone availability is local/network-dependent and can make a General Store an early communications hub.
  • Historical events should change simulation state; Railroad Standard Time is a major 1883 candidate event.
  • Historically documented illegal activity can exist in simulation; illegality creates legal/enforcement risk rather than automatic
    exclusion.
  • Drink solicitation and prostitution are distinct activities.
  • Saloon scenario variants and a reward/private-detective agency are preserved as new scenario/business directions.
END OF REVISION XIX INTEGRATION

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


LAND & LEDGERS

Canonical Project Bible - Revision XVIII
System Audit Integration - August 30, 2026
Authority and preservation rule
Revision XVIII preserves Revision XVII in full except where this new integration section explicitly adds, deepens or changes
a prior rule. Nothing from Revision XVII is removed, condensed, simplified or silently replaced. The seven completed system
audits below are now Canon. Where an audit says KEEP, the prior rule remains authoritative. Where an audit says DEEPEN,
the new material adds authority without deleting the prior rule. Where an audit says SIMPLIFY, the simplification applies to
player-facing presentation or implementation burden only unless the text explicitly changes simulation behavior. Where an
audit states a new lock, doctrine or distinction, that rule supersedes any older wording that would otherwise conflict.

These audits are intended to consolidate existing Canon rules into shared cross-system grammars so that future business,
AI, UI and implementation work does not invent incompatible local interpretations.


SYSTEM AUDIT 01 - ECONOMY & TRANSACTION CORE
Final verdict: KEEP + DEEPEN.
The economic foundation is already unusually strong. The Canon distinguishes owner cash from business cash, cash from
Net Worth, physical stock from recorded stock, credit sales from cash receipts, internal transfers from genuine consolidated
portfolio profit, landed cost from invoice price, and capital contribution from intercompany advance and bank borrowing. The
weakness is not lack of economics; it is the absence of one authoritative transaction grammar tying those rules together
across every business.

1. System purpose
The Economy & Transaction Core answers:
When something economically meaningful happens, what changed, who owns it, who owes whom, when was value earned
or consumed, when did cash actually move, and what does each party legitimately know about it?
The same economic truth must support a one-store owner and a mature portfolio with dozens of businesses, properties,
obligations, contracts, internal supply chains, banks and investments.

2. Universal economic loop
Need / Demand -> Offer / Price / Terms -> Order / Agreement -> Commitment / Reservation -> Physical Fulfillment ->
Economic Transaction -> Cash / Receivable / Payable / Inventory / Asset changes -> Bookkeeping -> Settlement ->
Reconciliation -> Historical Memory.
The steps are not interchangeable.

An order is not revenue.
A shipment leaving the supplier is not automatically inventory at the destination.
An invoice is not cash.
Collection of an old account is not a second sale.
Borrowing is not revenue.
Buying a wagon is not the same economic event as paying wages.
Moving value between controlled businesses does not create new consolidated wealth.

4. Cash architecture
The following economic concepts remain distinct:
Liquid Owner Cash: immediately spendable owner-side money.
Business Cash: cash belonging to a particular business ledger.
Bank Cash: cash belonging to the banking institution, not to the owner personally.
Restricted/Committed Funds: cash constrained by a real obligation or arrangement where applicable.
Operating Reserve: a standing management policy protecting desired liquidity.
Capital Authorization: permission for a particular capital expenditure or project.
Net Worth: grounded assets less liabilities.
Book/Ledger Equity: accounting carrying-value concept, not synonymous with Net Worth.
Derived Discretionary Cash report
Add Discretionary Cash as a derived management report, never as a new money pool.
Example:

Business Cash: $340
Known obligations due soon: $120
Operating Reserve target: $100
Approximate discretionary cash: $120
This report may be uncertain when future collections, expenses or records are uncertain.

5. Profit, cash flow and wealth are separate
New explicit Canon lock:
Profit, cash flow and change in Net Worth are three different measurements.
A business can be profitable and short of cash. It can receive cash while losing money. A player can exchange cash for
property without immediately reducing wealth by the full purchase price. Borrowing increases liquidity without creating
equivalent wealth. Credit sales can create earnings before collection and therefore produce apparent success alongside cash
strain.
Every serious business report should conceptually support three perspectives:

Performance: did operations create or destroy economic earnings during the period?
Cash Flow: where did actual money come from and where did it go?
Position: what does the entity own and owe now?

7. Revenue recognition
New common principle:
Revenue is recognized when the business has actually earned the consideration under the relevant transaction or
contract, not merely because an order exists or cash happened to move.
Examples:
Ordinary retail: goods physically transferred and sale completed.
Services: qualifying service performed.
Construction: contractually earned work or milestone according to the agreed structure.
Freight: qualifying transport service completed or agreed billable milestone reached.
Customer deposits/prepayments can create cash before all revenue is earned. Credit sales can create revenue before cash
is collected. Backlog is not revenue.

8. Accounts Payable / supplier trade credit
Accounts Payable becomes a first-class working-capital system equal in importance to customer credit.
Possible supplier terms include:

cash before shipment
cash on delivery
partial deposit
supplier account
scheduled settlement
overdue account with relationship consequences
A business can be well stocked while owing substantial money. Supplier credit therefore changes working capital without
creating free inventory.

9. Working Capital as a named foundation
Opening commercial gameplay should explicitly teach and report the cycle:
Cash -> Inventory -> Sale -> Receivable -> Cash

while supplier credit can create:

Supplier Delivery -> Inventory -> Payable -> Later Cash Payment.

Working Capital Health should be explained through components rather than one magic score:

cash
inventory
receivables
receivable aging
payables
upcoming payroll
debt payments


                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 6

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 163/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


committed contracts
operating reserve
stock replacement needs
Managers may produce explanations such as:
sales are strong but too much money is tied up in customer accounts;
cash looks healthy because replacement inventory has been delayed;
business is profitable but bills due exceed expected collections.

10. Inventory ownership and availability
New general doctrine:
Physical possession is not necessarily ownership, and physical presence does not mean inventory is freely
available.
A location may contain:
owned available inventory
owned inventory reserved for customers or agreements
owned project stock
owned stock unavailable because of condition/spoilage
customer-owned property in storage or service
goods in transit
The economic question is always: what is here, who owns it, and what is it available for?

11. Historical cost vs replacement cost
Reports may distinguish:
Acquisition/carrying cost: what existing stock actually cost the business.
Current replacement cost: what comparable stock would cost now.
Selling price: current asking or realized price.
Realized margin: what was actually earned on sold inventory.
Replacement margin: whether current selling economics can replace stock at current sourcing cost.
A business can therefore report a positive realized margin while replacement economics are poor after a supply shock.

12. Pricing
KEEP the existing causal pricing system. Price information may include, when legitimately known:
current selling price
recent realized prices
acquisition cost of current stock
current replacement quote
observed competitor/local range
recent sales velocity
stockout frequency
estimated demand response and confidence
Never expose a magical Optimal Price answer.

13. Demand is not a sale
New lock:
There is no free-floating quantity called Demand that automatically becomes sales.
A need becomes a sale only when buyer need exists, buyer can act, seller is known/reachable, terms are acceptable,
stock/service capacity exists and physical execution occurs.

14. Internal transfers and carrying value
A free or low-cash internal transfer does not make the input economically free.
If a sawmill transfers lumber that cost $60 to produce to an owned construction business for $0 cash, the construction
business does not receive economically costless lumber. The physical inventory carries relevant cost/history and the portfolio
has created no new wealth.


                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 7

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 164/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


Cash transfer price, accounting treatment and economic opportunity value may differ, but all must remain truthful.

15. Portfolio consolidation
New hard Canon lock:
Controlled-business transactions must not be double-counted as consolidated external revenue, profit, receivables
or liabilities.
Reports distinguish:
External Revenue: value earned from outside the controlled economic group.
Internal Transfer Activity: transactions among controlled ledgers.
Consolidated Portfolio Revenue: external revenue after elimination of internal duplication.
Intercompany receivables and liabilities are likewise eliminated in consolidated portfolio position while remaining real at the
individual-ledger level.

16. Capital purchases
Explicit distinction:
Operating expenditure consumes ordinary operating resources.
Capital acquisition exchanges cash/obligation for a durable asset.
Financing cash flow changes debt/capital structure.
Owner/portfolio capital movement transfers value among owners and controlled ledgers.
Buying an asset is not automatically an operating loss on the purchase date. The asset can later wear, lose value, require
repair, be damaged, become obsolete, be sold or be salvaged.
Detailed historical depreciation schedules remain unneeded unless later research/design requires them.

17. Losses
Common loss treatment:
spoilage reduces inventory and creates loss;
theft reduces actual cash/inventory and may first appear as a discrepancy;
bad debt reduces receivables and creates credit loss;
destroyed asset reduces asset value;
fire can destroy several asset/inventory states at once.
Actual State and Recorded State may temporarily disagree until discovery and reconciliation.

18. Bookkeeping
KEEP existing doctrine. Known transaction facts remain exact. Poor bookkeeping can cause missing, stale or unreconciled
information; it does not make a known twelve-cent transaction become an approximate number.
Bookkeeping improves knowledge and control, not real sales or production by magic.

19. NPC parity
KEEP. NPCs can overstock, understock, price badly, misjudge supplier terms, extend excessive credit, hold too little cash,
delay capital spending or allocate capital poorly under the same economic rules as the player.

20. Scale transformation
Early game: Can I afford this reorder? Can I extend this tab? Can I make payroll?
Growing business: What reserve should management protect? Which supplier terms are best? How seasonal should
inventory be?
Portfolio: Which business receives scarce capital? Equity, advance or bank borrowing? Which business is profitable but
illiquid?
Capital command: Which divisions retain cash, distribute cash, borrow, reinvest or restructure?

21. Historical transformation
Underlying economic truth remains stable from 1880-1905. The environment changes through rail, telegraph, telephone,
banking, larger firms, improved market reach, deeper specialization and higher organizational complexity.

22. Canon locks from Audit 01
Commitment is not fulfillment.
Revenue is not cash.
