projected reliability benefit of replacement

59. Preventive maintenance is not perfect
Good maintenance reduces avoidable exposure but cannot eliminate age, accidents, latent defects or unusual stress.
Neglected assets can sometimes continue longer than expected.

60. Maintenance is not a designer money sink
Hard philosophy lock:
Every maintenance cost must correspond to real work, material, downtime, risk reduction or physical restoration.

61. Canon locks from Audit 06
Condition is not Defect.
Condition is not Operating State.
Symptom is not Diagnosis.
Inspection is information.
Maintenance is work.
Routine service should normally be automated.
Maintenance preserves capability; capital improvement changes capability.
Repair scope persists.
Temporary repair is not full restoration.
Failure requires causal exposure.
Secondary damage is possible.
Criticality is contextual.
Downtime is an economic cost.
Spare parts and redundant assets are different resilience strategies.
Failed assets persist.
Animals are not machine assets.
Audit 06 Canon status: LOCKED.

SYSTEM AUDIT 07 - MARKETS / OPPORTUNITY & PRESSURE / RIVAL AI
Final verdict: KEEP + DEEPEN.
This system determines whether the world is a living economy or merely a player-facing simulation. Existing Canon already
uses bounded choice, localized markets, real alternatives, equal-rule NPC competition and discoverable rival intent. The
critical new rule is that Opportunity & Pressure is an analytical/synthesis layer; it observes and interprets economic reality but
does not create it.

1. System purpose
The combined system answers:
Where is economic value being left on the table, where is strain accumulating, who can perceive it, who can realistically act
on it, what competing responses are underway, and how does the opportunity change as actors commit resources?
Three distinct jobs remain:
Markets: counterparties actually choose and transact.
Opportunity & Pressure: synthesize persistent evidence.
Rival AI: economic actors perceive some evidence and act using real resources.

2. Fundamental market loop
Need / Supply / Opportunity exists -> Actor has reason to reconsider -> Actor becomes aware of alternatives ->
Feasible alternatives identified -> Shortlist evaluated -> Choice/negotiation -> Physical/economic execution ->
Transaction succeeds/partially succeeds/fails -> Evidence accumulates ->
Prices/availability/relationships/profitability change -> Businesses and entrepreneurs reconsider.

3. Opportunity & Pressure is non-causal synthesis
New foundational lock:




                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 36

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 193/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


Opportunity & Pressure never manufactures demand, supply, labor, customers, money, property, capacity or rival
resources. It analyzes evidence produced by authoritative systems.
A shortage exists because customers cannot obtain what they need. The analytical layer can identify and report that
shortage; it does not create it.

4. Market specificity
KEEP competition specific to:
good/service + customer group + reachable geography.

There is no one empire-wide Market Share score.

A store can simultaneously lead workwear, trail grocery staples and barely participate in remote-camp supply.

5. Market share is derived
Market share describes completed transactions and estimated relevant market activity. It does not directly buff pricing power
or determine the next customer choice.

6. Outside option
KEEP. Customers can substitute, postpone, repair, produce at home, travel, buy from another settlement or let demand leak
off-map. Improved rail/transport can expose local firms to outside competition as well as create sourcing opportunities.

7. Market power = alternatives
Elevate to foundational doctrine:
Bargaining power arises primarily from the quality of credible alternatives, not a Monopoly/Influence stat.
This applies to sellers, buyers, lenders, borrowers, employers, workers, carriers and property owners.

8. Opportunity / Pressure lifecycle
Formalize persistent states:
Background Condition
Emerging Signal
Confirmed Opportunity / Pressure
Intensifying
Contested / Responding
Easing
Resolved
Reversed
Former shortages can become oversupply.

9. Opportunities can disappear without completion
An opportunity can fade because demand disappears, a route changes, an existing firm expands, outside supply arrives or
another structural condition changes. It does not require a quest-completion flag.

10. Opportunity evidence dimensions
Internal synthesis may consider:
unmet demand
urgency
prices
observed margins
lost sales
refused jobs
leakage/distance
missed recurring commitments
capacity utilization
expected persistence
entry cost
labor availability



                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 37

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 194/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


site availability
supply access
financing access
Player-facing reports should explain causes rather than show a raw Opportunity Score.

11. Pressure evidence
Housing, labor, freight and other pressures should be explained through actual symptoms such as crowding, vacancies,
wages, overtime, missed loads, premium prices, leakage, failed hiring and delay.

12. Confidence and evidence quality
The simulation can know more than the player. Opportunity reports should be limited by legitimate information and can use
confidence language/ranges when evidence is incomplete.

13. Player and rival information differ
Different actors know their own books, customers, suppliers, property discussions and relationships. Two entrepreneurs can
see the same settlement and reach different conclusions without either cheating.

14. Rival economic decision loop
Formalize:
Trigger -> Actor notices possible problem/opportunity -> Gathers/recalls information -> Feasible consideration set ->
Estimates economics -> Compares alternatives -> Forms Intent -> Seeks resources -> Makes commitments ->
Execution -> Observes results -> Adjusts/continues/abandons.

15. Rival Intent is persistent
Rival plans can progress through states such as:
Considering
Investigating land
Seeking finance
Negotiating parcel
Project authorized
Construction underway
Opening preparation
Operating
No hidden countdown is required.

16. Rival plans can fail
Intent does not guarantee entry. Plans can fail because of seller refusal, finance denial, labor shortage, cost, supplier failure,
better alternatives, liquidity or market change.

17. Rivals can be wrong
NPCs can overestimate demand, underestimate construction cost, overexpand, price badly, overstock, choose poor property,
take too much debt, misread temporary demand, lose employees or overpay for acquisitions. These are decisions under
shared rules, not hidden inefficiency penalties.

18. Rivals can also be highly competent
Some NPCs can identify opportunities early, have strong supplier knowledge, deep capital, trade expertise, good hiring,
strong acquisitions or strategic patience. Advantages arise from actual resources, skill, knowledge, relationships and policy,
not difficulty modifiers.

19. Owner preference shapes strategy
NPC decisions can respond to reserves, obligations, expected return, uncertainty, risk tolerance, commitments, relationships,
expertise, time horizon and feasible alternatives.
Avoid giant personality-bonus systems. Preferences should bias real choices.

20. Opportunity cost applies to rivals
NPCs have finite capital, management time and property. Choosing one opportunity can prevent another. Rival strategy
therefore changes when the player acquires critical resources first.




                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 38

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 195/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

21. Entry requires assembled capabilities
KEEP. New firms require real combinations of skill, knowledge, capital/finance, property, suppliers, labor and confidence.
Strong demand alone does not spawn a business.

22. Local opportunity does not require local startup
Unmet demand can resolve through local expansion, outside supply, regional entrant, substitution, demand destruction or
customer migration.

23. Existing firms can respond before new entrants
New doctrine:
Opportunity response must consider expansion or adjacent capability growth by existing businesses as well as
startup formation.
Examples: General Store expands assortment; carrier buys another team; livery adds drayage; mill adds flour/feed sales.

24. Adjacent expansion
Capability-based business architecture should let historically/economically adjacent services grow organically where existing
assets, labor and knowledge support them.

25. Market saturation / oversupply
Add explicit pressure detection for:
falling utilization
persistent vacancy
growing unsold inventory
discounting
declining margins
idle equipment
closures
Oversupply is not simply Shortage Resolved.

26. Saturation does not automatically close firms
Firm survival depends on cash reserves, debt, property ownership, owner labor, other profitable lines, expectations and
creditor tolerance. Do not despawn the weakest firm mechanically.

27. Price wars
KEEP as real competition using cash, inventory, margins and reserves. Deep-reserve rivals can survive longer. Customers
can benefit. No generic Price War modifier is necessary.

28. Competition is multidimensional
Businesses compete through:
price
availability
assortment
reliability
credit
location
hours
delivery
service quality
specialization
relationships
speed
capacity
reputation





                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 39

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 196/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

29. Labor competition
Rivals can recruit, poach, raise wages and seek managers or specialists. Hiring activity can itself become evidence of rival
intent.

30. Supplier competition
Rivals can reserve supplier output, sign agreements, buy scarce stock or secure transport capacity. Competitive harm
emerges through actual allocation rather than sabotage events.

31. Property competition
Rivals can pursue frontage, depot sites, industrial land, rental development and strategic adjacent parcels under the same
acquisition rules as the player.

32. Distressed acquisitions and recombination
KEEP. Business closure/failure releases property, machinery, wagons, inventory, employees, managers, customer
relationships and supplier capacity. Rivals, creditors, employees or the player can acquire/recombine them.

33. Rival exit decision
NPC owners can choose to continue, shrink, change service mix, sell assets, seek partners, sell the business, refinance,
close or liquidate based on actual recovery capacity and alternatives rather than Profit < 0 for N months.

34. Closure changes the market
When a business closes, customers seek alternatives, workers move, property/equipment becomes available, competitor
backlogs change and new opportunities can emerge automatically.

35. Employees/managers can become entrepreneurs
New deepening:
Experienced employees/managers with sufficient savings/finance, skill, knowledge, property access and willingness can
become business owners. Entrepreneurship is not limited to a hidden investor pool.

36. Off-map entrepreneurs
Regional/outside investors remain valid but must obey Information Distance, migration/travel, property, finance and setup
requirements. They do not materialize because a town has a need slot.

37. Entry lead time
Even after deciding to enter, actors must obtain property, finance, construction, staffing, inventory/equipment and other
required capabilities. Competition therefore develops through real lead time.

38. Contested opportunities
An opportunity can remain active while rival response is already underway. Player may learn that another actor is seeking
land, finance, employees or suppliers and decide whether to act, differentiate, wait or abandon.

39. Rival intent confidence
Player-visible rival information can be:
confirmed fact
strong evidence
rumor/weak evidence
Do not present all intent equally.

40. Rivals can conceal plans
Sophisticated actors do not need to publicly declare strategy. Intent becomes visible through credible traces such as property
inquiries, lender conversations, recruitment, supplier activity, construction and public records where appropriate.
No espionage minigame is required.

41. Opportunity & Pressure does not reveal hidden intent automatically
Hard lock:
The simulation’s knowledge of a rival plan does not make that plan player-known.

42. Forecast uncertainty
Market/opportunity reports should show assumptions and risks.
Example:


                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 40

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 197/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


Current evidence: 95% boarding occupancy; recent families unable to secure rooms.

Forecast assumption: mine expansion proceeds.

Known risk: two housing projects already under construction.

43. Pipeline response awareness
New core rule:
Opportunity analysis should account for known committed response already in the pipeline.
Housing under construction, freight fleets ordered, recruiting underway and supplier expansions can change the future
outlook even before current shortage fully resolves.
This prevents analysis from pretending nobody is reacting, while still allowing overbuilding because information and forecasts
are imperfect.

44. Speculative boom/bust
Opportunity, delayed projects and forecast error can naturally create cycles such as housing shortage -> simultaneous
projects -> demand weakens -> vacancy -> distress -> acquisitions.
No scripted crash event is required.

45. Available capacity vs nominal capacity
Known business assets do not equal market availability. Existing wagons may be committed; contractor crews may have full
backlog; lodging may be unsuitable. Opportunity analysis should use actual available capacity where information permits.

46. Service gaps
KEEP service opportunities such as finance, printing/news, medicine/pharmacy, barber/bath, fuel and repair, not only
commodity shortages.

47. Institutional pressure
Some pressures involve civic/public institutions that private owners cannot directly build/own. Player opportunities may
instead involve contracts, land, financing or indirect support.

48. No Town Needs checklist
Avoid UI such as Doctor 0/1 or Blacksmith 0/1. Report actual economic symptoms:
Repair backlog has doubled. Several jobs were sent to another node.

49. Opportunity categories
Analytical categories may include:
trade/inventory
labor
housing
services
land/frontage
freight/infrastructure
credit/capital
production inputs
regional-node viability
These are synthesis categories, not separate economic universes.

50. Persistent trend evidence
Use rolling evidence and periodic synthesis rather than full rescan/notification spam. Stockouts, failed purchases, missed
orders, failed hires, vacancy changes, boarding saturation, route delays and closures update trend state.
One ordinary stockout does not automatically create a business opportunity.

51. Structural events can matter immediately
Extreme discrete changes such as bridge collapse, bank failure or major mine closure may instantly create large pressure
without needing weeks of rolling evidence.

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 198/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

52. Rival response changes the signal
When competitors order capacity, hire, build or secure property, the opportunity forecast should change. Once new capacity
operates, underlying evidence changes and pressure can ease or reverse.

53. Competitive Response / Market Movement memory
Add an analytical view of material responses already underway, such as:
rival acquiring land
housing under construction
carrier expanding fleet
bank tightening lending
merchant exiting
This helps explain where opportunities/pressures are heading.

54. Rivals do not react perfectly to every signal
Even strong opportunities may persist because actors lack savings, property, credit, willingness, family flexibility, confidence
or compatible skill.

55. Entrepreneur confidence
Interpret confidence as willingness to commit under evidence, uncertainty, reserves, experience, risk tolerance and
circumstances. Do not create an arbitrary 0-100 entrepreneur meter as the primary authority.

56. Entry friction is real requirements
Some businesses are easier to enter than others because they need different combinations of site, capital, equipment, labor
and institutional form. Do not represent this only as a generic Entry Difficulty stat.

57. High profit attracts attention only if observable
Exact private profits are not automatically public knowledge. Rivals may infer success from traffic, hiring, deliveries,
expansion, supplier volume, reputation or other observable consequences.

58. Commercial Standing and opportunity access
A well-known/trusted owner may hear about deals, partnerships, supplier arrangements, financing or private property earlier
because counterparties know them. Do not convert this into artificial opportunity tiers.

59. Rival reputation
NPC businesses build localized reputation through actual quality, reliability, promises, credit behavior and service. Reputation
affects future choices through memory and evidence.

60. No mandatory named nemesis
Important rivals may emerge naturally and can change over the campaign. Do not require a permanent designated Rival
character.

61. Competition and cooperation can coexist
New lock:
Economic actors can compete in one relationship and cooperate in another.
Rivals can subcontract, share suppliers, syndicate, lend, buy/sell assets, refer overflow work, partner or merge while
competing elsewhere.

62. Consolidation after market failure
Overcapacity can lead to closure, asset sales, contract transfers, worker movement and acquisition rather than simple
deletion.

63. Regional competition
Local firms compete with nearby nodes and later rail-connected outside suppliers. Improved infrastructure is a two-way door:
it can reduce sourcing costs while increasing outside competition.

64. Regional specialization
Different nodes can become stronger in livestock, lumber, mining, finance, distribution, lodging, agricultural supply or repair
because of actual geography, investment and history, not fixed Town Type labels.





                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 42

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 199/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

65. Market reach is product/service-specific
No universal market radius. Reach depends on product/service, urgency, transport, information, delivery capability and
customer willingness.

66. No scripted anti-player rival spawn
Player dominance does not trigger a rival merely because market share crosses a threshold. Rival entry requires genuine
attractive opportunity plus a feasible actor.

67. Monopoly is a strategic condition, not a policy
Sole suppliers can choose high price, moderate price, good service, rationing or other strategies. Entry pressure responds to
actual conditions and alternatives.

68. Predatory/very-low pricing carries real cost
If permitted by applicable law, a wealthy business can price aggressively, but cash burns, inventory still costs money and the
rival may outlast the player. No rival hit points.

69. Distress opportunities
Rivals can notice weak businesses, debt, valuable property or strong customer relationships and attempt acquisition under
the same diligence/finance rules as the player.

70. Opportunities can be lost causally
The player can lose an opportunity because another actor buys the lot, secures the contract, hires the worker, acquires the
business or signs the supplier. Do not use magical expiration timers.

71. Player-facing Opportunity / Pressure / Movements
A useful high-level presentation can separate:
Opportunities: attractive openings.
Pressures: current strain.
Movements: material known responses underway.
Do not turn every minor NPC action into an alert.

72. Persistent history
Opportunity state, pressure state and rival intent persist across saves. Major market events can feed the Lifetime Ledger
selectively, while granular transactions remain in underlying ledgers/history.

73. Canon locks from Audit 07
Opportunity is evidence, not causation.
Pressure is persistent strain, not a random debuff.
Market share is derived.
Markets are specific by good/service, segment and geography.
Alternatives create market power.
Choice is bounded.
NPCs obey equal economic physics.
Rival information is bounded.
Rival intent is not execution.
Player knowledge of rivals requires evidence.
Existing firms can respond through expansion.
Opportunities can reverse.
Pipeline response matters.
Forecasts remain uncertain.
Economic actors can compete and cooperate simultaneously.
Failure recombines economic assets.
Audit 07 Canon status: LOCKED.

REVISION XVIII - CROSS-SYSTEM CONSOLIDATION LOCKS
The seven audits above create several shared authorities that now apply across all future business and system design unless
a later Canon revision explicitly supersedes them.

A. Shared execution-object pattern
Several systems now have authoritative persistent execution objects:
Project for construction/development work.
Shipment for physical cargo movement.
Work Order for maintenance/repair/service work.
Employment relationship + Work Demand/Assignment for human labor.
Commercial Agreement/Commitment for standing economic promises.
These objects are not interchangeable. Agreements create commitments; execution objects carry out actual
physical/economic work.

B. Shared separation of reality, relationship and information
Across all systems:
ownership is separate from possession/custody/control;
physical location is separate from legal ownership;
actual state is separate from recorded/known state;
forecast is separate from fact;
authority is separate from capability;
commitment is separate from fulfillment.

C. Shared anti-teleportation / exclusivity doctrine
People, assets, goods, animals, projects, property rights and transport capacity cannot be used simultaneously in physically
incompatible ways merely because separate UI screens request them.
Time, location, ownership, custody, assignment and capacity remain authoritative.

D. Shared portfolio-accounting doctrine
Controlled businesses remain separate economic ledgers even when labor, goods, transport, maintenance or capital move
among them. Internal activity may be reported locally but is eliminated or appropriately consolidated when calculating
portfolio-wide external revenue, receivables, liabilities and profit.
Vertical integration transforms dependencies into internal responsibilities. It does not make labor, logistics, materials,
maintenance, property or capital free.

E. Shared information doctrine
The simulation may know exact underlying reality. Player/NPC knowledge depends on legitimate evidence.
Reports may distinguish:

Known Fact
Recorded State
Evidence
Inference
Forecast
Unknown
Unknown is preferable to invented precision.

F. Shared automation doctrine
Routine execution should usually follow:
Player Decision -> Standing Policy -> Manager/Routine Execution -> Exception Escalation.

The player should make strategically meaningful decisions, not repeatedly click routine continuation, dispatch, maintenance,
household purchases or ordinary staffing actions.

G. Shared causal-failure doctrine
Adversity should normally arise from real shortages, defects, financial structures, market changes, competing commitments,
information gaps, bad decisions or physical disruption.


                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 44

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 201/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


Avoid global random debuffs when the simulation can express the underlying cause directly.

H. Shared scale-transformation doctrine
Every mature system should change the nature of player decisions from owner-operator detail toward policy, capital
allocation, management selection and exception handling as the portfolio grows.
The game should not simply multiply early-game clicks by fifty.

I. Shared historical-transformation doctrine
Core economic physics remain coherent from 1880-1905. Historical change should alter infrastructure, information speed,
available institutions, technology, asset complexity, market reach, regional connectivity and organizational scale rather than
arbitrarily unlocking stronger numeric tiers.

J. Revision XVIII preservation rule restated
No prior Revision XVII rule is deleted by this integration unless an Audit explicitly says a prior interpretation is changed.
Where the audits add a distinction that prior sections lacked, both bodies remain authoritative, with Revision XVIII controlling
the new distinction. Where an audit says KEEP, the existing Revision XVII text remains part of the active Canon unchanged.
Revision XVIII System Audit Integration status: COMPLETE THROUGH SYSTEM AUDIT 07.

REVISION XVII PURPOSE
Revision XVII closes the final two historical research holds created by the first full playtest reconciliation. It resolves the
business-form boundaries around feed, grain, livery, freight, drayage and related services, and it establishes the historically
supportable legal/institutional treatment of prostitution and houses of ill fame without promoting that subject into active
production scope. All unrelated Revision XVI mechanics remain authoritative, including human capability, construction,
private lending, banking, taxation, acquisition, portfolio management, Double Houses and the Lifetime Ledger.
This revision follows the same evidence hierarchy used in Revision XVI: historical/legal locks govern behavior where the
sources are sufficiently strong; design locks define the intended mechanic; calibration remains tunable; and parked material
is preserved without authorizing implementation.

CANON LOCK - RESEARCH CLOSURE DOES NOT AUTHORIZE FEATURE BLOAT
   Feed, grain, livery and freight are resolved by capability and economic function rather than by multiplying shallow
    business classes.
    Brothel/prostitution research establishes legal and world-simulation truth, but player ownership and dedicated
   management remain parked.
   The 1880-1905 campaign remains governed by causal physical and accounting truth. Historical labels never substitute
     for real assets, services, custody, contracts, labor and legal exposure.
  No tuning number discovered in playtest or research becomes a historical constant merely because the underlying
    business form is now confirmed.

1. RESEARCH ITEM 6 - FEED, GRAIN & RELATED MERCHANT FORMS

1.1 No universal Feed & Grain archetype
Revision XVI Section 15.1 is superseded. Period Dakota evidence distinguishes flour-and-feed merchants, grain
dealers/buyers, general merchants, agricultural-implement dealers, mills and grain-storage/elevator operations while also
showing that individual proprietors could combine several of those lines. The game should therefore treat feed retail, grain
buying, storage, milling and adjacent agricultural merchandise as related but separable commercial capabilities rather than
one atomic Feed & Grain business class. [R6-1] [R6-2]

CANON LOCK - BUSINESS FORM FOLLOWS ACTUAL FUNCTION
  A standalone Feed or Flour-and-Feed Merchant is valid.
  A General Merchant may carry feed, flour, grain or adjacent farm-facing merchandise if its real stock policy, storage and
    suppliers support those lines.
  A mill may sell flour/feed through an attached or remote commercial outlet.
  A Grain Dealer/Buyer is distinct from a feed retailer because the core relationship is producer-to-market aggregation and
    resale/shipment.
  A Grain Warehouse/Elevator is a storage and handling capability that may coexist with dealing but is not synonymous
     with it.
    Agricultural implements and broader farm merchandise may overlap with feed/grain commerce, but the game must not
     force a modern one-stop farm-supply-store model backward into the period.

1.2 Feed / Flour-and-Feed Merchant
Feed commerce is a valid independent business role in Dakota and Black Hills settlements. It can serve households, farms,
ranches, livery operators, freight carriers, construction operations using draft animals and other commercial customers. The
exact stock mix is location- and period-dependent; common supported lines can include hay, oats, bran, mill feed, flour and
other historically justified merchandise. A dedicated feed merchant should compete with broader merchants and direct
producer relationships rather than receiving artificial exclusivity.

1.3 Grain Dealer / Grain Buyer
Grain dealing is producer-facing commercial aggregation. A dealer buys or otherwise arranges acquisition of grain, bears
working-capital and market exposure, and then sells or ships into a larger market. The activity depends on actual farm
surplus, quality/grade knowledge where represented, storage/handling access, prices, transport and outside relationships.
The same proprietor may also sell feed, but the two revenue loops remain distinguishable. Rapid City evidence in the 1890s
explicitly described grain business and hay/feed business separately. [R6-3]

1.4 Grain Warehouse / Elevator and custody truth
Grain storage requires an ownership distinction that ordinary retail inventory does not always require. Dakota warehouse law
recognized grain delivered to a warehouse/elevator under receipt arrangements as a bailment rather than automatically a
sale to the operator. Land & Ledgers must therefore be able to represent grain physically present at a facility while owned by
another party. [R6-4]

CANON LOCK - PHYSICAL POSSESSION IS NOT AUTOMATIC OWNERSHIP
   Operator-owned commodity inventory and customer-owned/stored commodity must remain separate property states.
   Warehouse/elevator receipts or equivalent claims represent a delivery/custody obligation rather than magically
    converting customer grain into merchant stock.


                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 2

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 204/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


  A warehouse/elevator may also conduct dealing where its actual business configuration supports it.
1.5 Settlement scale, rail and elevator development
No date alone unlocks a grain elevator. The appropriate economic preconditions are substantial local or feeder-area
production, storage/aggregation demand, working capital, market access and a transport connection capable of moving
enough bulk grain. A wagon-era gateway can have hay/feed commerce and open-lot storage without possessing a mature
rail elevator. Rail can make elevator investment much more attractive, but local service, traffic and crop structure still matter.
This is a world-economy condition, not a technology-tree step.

1.6 Feed as a transport-industry input
Feed is an important business-to-business input for the horse economy. Period livery evidence records substantial stocks of
hay, oats and bran. Feed shortages and price movements should therefore propagate into livery and freight costs through
actual consumption: weather or crop trouble can reduce feed supply; operating costs rise; carriers respond through margins,
rates, route choices, reduced capacity or failure. Conversely, freight and livery expansion create real demand for feed. [R6-2]

1.7 Commission and terminal relationships
Commission merchants and larger outside grain-market intermediaries are historically valid, but this research does not
require them to become an immediate standalone player storefront. Their strongest current role is as counterparties and
market-access relationships through which local dealers, elevators and producers reach larger markets. Direct ownership
may be promoted later only if it passes the project depth-before-width test.

2. RESEARCH ITEM 6 - LIVERY, FREIGHT, DRAYAGE & EXPRESS

2.1 Livery and professional hauling are distinct functions
Revision XVI Section 15.2 and the classification wording inherited from Revision XV Section 9.5 are superseded to the extent
they imply that Livery / Freight is one inherent business form. Federal Census instructions explicitly distinguished livery stable
keepers from hostlers and separately distinguished expressmen, teamsters, draymen and carriage/hack drivers. Period
South Dakota advertising shows both separate livery and dray businesses and combined livery establishments with a dray
line in connection. [R6-5] [R6-6] [R6-7]

2.2 Livery Stable
A Livery Stable is primarily an animal-care and mobility-service business. Historically grounded services may include
transient/feed stabling, longer boarding, hire of horses or teams, hire of rigs, supplied drivers where offered, horse/stock
sales and passenger/hack/bus service where supported. A livery needs actual stable capacity, feed, water, animal care,
equipment and labor. It does not need to haul customer freight merely because it owns teams and wagons.

2.3 Freight / Hauling Carrier
A Freight / Hauling Carrier sells transportation capacity for customer cargo. The existing Canon mechanics governing cargo
class, distance, route difficulty, road condition, wagon fit, team requirements, driver labor, loading/unloading, feed,
water/stopping access, upkeep and lead time remain authoritative. The correction is classification: those mechanics belong to
professional hauling rather than automatically to every livery. A carrier may operate its own private stable without selling
public livery services.

2.4 Drayage / Cartage / Transfer
Drayage/cartage is a valid short-haul specialization within the professional hauling family. Typical work includes depot-to-
merchant, depot-to-warehouse, warehouse transfer, local commercial delivery, baggage and other short-distance
movements. It becomes particularly important after rail arrives because rail can reduce some long-haul wagon traffic while
increasing feeder and final-mile movement around the depot.

2.5 Express and baggage
Express/baggage service is a distinct service profile where historically appropriate. The Census distinguished expressmen
from teamsters and draymen, while period businesses could combine express, baggage and dray service. The current Canon
should support this as a specialization or contract/service type without automatically promoting Express Company into a
separate shallow business archetype.

2.6 Combined enterprises are fully valid

CANON LOCK - COMBINATION IS ALLOWED, CAPACITY IS NOT DUPLICATED
   Dedicated Livery, dedicated Freight/Hauling, dedicated Dray/Transfer and combined Livery + Hauling configurations are
      all historically valid.
  A combined establishment can share stable space, teams, wagons, feed stocks, hostlers, drivers and repair
     relationships.
   Shared ownership does not create a synergy modifier. The same horse, team, wagon or worker cannot perform two jobs
     at once.



                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 3

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 205/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


  A livery hire can displace a freight job and a freight commitment can make rigs unavailable to livery customers.
    Opportunity cost is real.

2.7 Rail transforms route demand rather than deleting hauling
The existing rail-transition doctrine is reaffirmed. A new rail connection can destroy or weaken specific long-haul wagon
routes while creating depot drayage, feeder routes, local delivery, farm/ranch collection and secondary-node connection
work. Do not apply a generic Railroad -50% Freight Revenue modifier. The contracts, routes, cost structure and competitive
alternatives change first; profitability follows.

3. CROSS-SYSTEM BUSINESS CAPABILITY DOCTRINE
Research Item 6 reinforces a broader design rule already implicit in Revision XVI: an economically meaningful business
should be defined by the capabilities and relationships it actually possesses, not by an immutable RPG-style business class.
A single legal/business ledger can legitimately combine several compatible lines, while a shared physical facility can serve
several ledgers or activities without erasing ownership.

CANON LOCK - LABELS DESCRIBE, SYSTEMS EXPLAIN
   Business names and historical categories are player-facing descriptions of real capabilities.
   Adding a service requires the assets, labor, storage, market access, authority and working capital that service actually
    needs.
  A General Store carrying feed does not become a different legal entity merely because its merchandise mix changed.
  A freight carrier adding a public livery line must actually add public stabling/hire capacity; the new label alone grants
    nothing.
  NPC businesses use the same capability logic and may broaden, narrow, combine or exit lines when their resources and
    market conditions support it.

4. RESEARCH ITEM 7 - PROSTITUTION / HOUSES OF ILL FAME

4.1 Historical/legal status through the normal campaign
Revision XVI Section 20 is superseded: the legal/institutional research hold is now complete. Dakota Territorial law prohibited
keeping bawdy houses, houses of ill fame, houses of assignation or prostitution, and the prohibition was enforceable in
territorial courts. South Dakota municipalities received express power in 1890 to suppress bawdy/disorderly houses and
houses of ill fame, and South Dakota continued prosecution through the end of the normal campaign horizon, including State
v. Cambron in 1905. [R7-1] [R7-2] [R7-3]

HISTORICAL/LEGAL LOCK - NOT AN ORDINARY LICENSED BUSINESS
   During the normal 1880-1905 campaign, a house of prostitution / house of ill fame is not treated as an ordinary lawful
    licensed business.
  No generic Brothel License may be created from Western-game convention.
  A locally tolerated establishment remains legally exposed unless a specific dated authority actually changes its legal
     status.
   The 1913 South Dakota nuisance-abatement/closure regime is outside the normal campaign and must not be imported
    backward.

4.2 Deadwood: tolerance is an enforcement condition, not legalization
Deadwood demonstrates that unlawful premises could nevertheless be widely known, durable and openly tolerated for long
periods. The correct simulation distinction is therefore Legal Status versus Enforcement Posture. An establishment can be
unlawful, commonly known and currently tolerated at the same time. Tolerance may change with police/prosecutor practice,
political leadership, complaints, reform pressure, serious incidents or other local causes. Prior tolerance does not create a
property right or permanent immunity. [R7-4]

4.3 Property owner and premises-use exposure
Territorial law could reach an owner or other person who knowingly let or permitted premises to be used for prohibited
purposes. Property ownership, occupancy/lease, operating control, actual premises use and owner knowledge must therefore
remain separate facts. A mixed-use building can contain a prohibited upstairs use without the entire parcel becoming a
special Brothel Property class. [R7-1]

4.4 Fines are not licenses
This research did not establish a sufficiently authoritative, universal 1880-1905 Deadwood system in which payment of a
recurring prescribed fee legally authorized prostitution. Period or local fines may be represented when town-specific evidence
supports them, but payment of a fine does not itself change the underlying legal status. Do not implement Pay Fine -> Legal
for 30 Days.





                                           REVISION XVII INTEGRATION 4

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 206/346 ====================

                         LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVII / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE

4.5 Selective tolerance is not general immunity
A town can tolerate the existence of a prohibited establishment while still enforcing assault, theft, disorder, coercion or other
crimes, and it can later prosecute the establishment itself. No Vice District blanket immunity is permitted. The legal and
enforcement systems should remain capable of selective or changing priorities.

4.6 Worker agency and prohibited recruitment
The period law also addressed forms of coercive or deceptive recruitment into prostitution. Historical recognition of that
exploitation does not create a desirable player management lever. If prostitution is ever represented beyond
background/world context, adult participants must remain persons with agency rather than purchasable production inputs.
Coercive recruitment is not an authorized player-facing economic mechanic in this Canon pass.

4.7 Production status remains parked

PARKED - WORLD TRUTH WITHOUT PLAYER-OWNED BROTHEL MANAGEMENT
    Historically appropriate settlements may represent prostitution premises as part of the local world/economy if future
    scope justifies it.
   The game does not currently require a Brothel construction menu, prostitution staffing screen, vice skill tree or dedicated
    player business archetype.
   Research closure authorizes accurate treatment if encountered; it does not create production priority.
   Any future promotion into active ownership must receive a separate design/scope review against the project depth-
    before-width standard.

5. REMAINING RESEARCH STATUS
The playtest historical/legal research sequence identified in Revision XVI is now complete. Research Items 1-5 remain
incorporated through Revision XVI; Research Items 6-7 are incorporated here. There are no remaining historical research
holds from this particular playtest reconciliation docket. Future questions may still require research as new systems are
proposed, but they are not unresolved carryovers from Revision XVI.

6. CALIBRATION HOLDS - DO NOT CONVERT INTO HISTORICAL LOCKS
Revision XVI Section 21 remains authoritative and is extended by the following Research Item 6/7 calibration holds:
   Exact prevalence of standalone feed merchants, grain dealers, elevators and combined merchant forms by
     settlement/year.
   Exact grain-elevator capacity, storage charges, dealer margins, feed margins, grade discounts and shrink/spoilage
    assumptions.
   Exact hay/oat/bran consumption by animal class, work intensity and season.
   Exact livery boarding rates, rig-hire rates, freight/dray charges and utilization targets.
   Exact number of teams, stalls, wagons and staff required for profitable livery or freight operations.
   Exact prevalence of dedicated versus combined livery/dray/freight enterprises.
   Any town-specific prostitution fine amount, cadence, enforcement probability or tolerated-establishment frequency.
   Any prostitution revenue, pricing, rent or customer-volume assumptions if the parked content is ever simulated.
7. SUPERSESSION & INTEGRATION MAP
Revision XVII is intentionally narrow. It supersedes only the unresolved business-form and prostitution/legal-treatment holds
while preserving Revision XVI in full elsewhere.
   Revision XVI 15.1 Feed & Grain research hold -> superseded by Revision XVII Sections 1 and 3.
   Revision XVI 15.2 Livery versus Freight research hold -> superseded by Revision XVII Sections 2 and 3.

   Revision XVI statements parking brothel/prostitution content -> deepened with a researched illegal/tolerated/enforcement

    above conflicts.

REVISION XVI PURPOSE

Revision XVI formalizes the strongest design discoveries from the first full text-based playtest and the historical/legal research
conducted immediately afterward. It does not replace the systemic spine established by Revision XV. It adds connective tissue
that the playtest proved was necessary: people as transferable human capability rather than occupation bundles; continuous
learning and mentorship; project work as physical staged execution; Construction & Contracting as a real business role; fallible
manager-originated capital proposals; a cleaner separation of owner equity, intercompany finance and bank debt; deeper
acquisition economics; historically grounded private banking progression; taxation; and a persistent Lifetime Ledger capable of
remembering the player's actual commercial career.

The common rule remains causal simulation over abstract game bonuses. A skilled worker matters because the person can
perform or understand real work. A contractor succeeds because the estimate, crew, materials, schedule and execution were
good. A manager becomes valuable because good judgment reduces unresolved exceptions and improves decisions. A bank
becomes powerful because it controls real capital under real balance-sheet constraints. A large portfolio becomes manageable
because the player has built an organization, not because an empire level grants free efficiency.

Research interpretation rule

Revision XVI distinguishes four levels of authority. Historical/legal locks are supported strongly enough to govern simulation
behavior. Design locks describe the intended game mechanic even where numerical values remain tunable. Calibration holds
remain deliberately data-driven and should not be mistaken for historical claims. Parked concepts are preserved without
authorizing implementation. When a playtest assumption conflicted with stronger period evidence, the researched interpretation
controls.

CANON LOCK - PHYSICAL AND ACCOUNTING TRUTH REMAIN THE COMMON TEST

   People, money, materials, vehicles, authority, information and obligations must remain attributable to actual entities and
     relationships.
    Internal ownership may improve control and coordination, but it never makes labor, materials, capital, transport or risk free.
  A forecast or professional opinion remains an estimate even when it comes from a highly competent manager.
   Ordinary convenience automation may remove repetitive clicks, but it must preserve the underlying ledger transaction and
    consequences.
   The same meaningful economic rules apply to NPCs and the player unless a legal or informational difference genuinely
    explains an exception.

1. OPENING CALIBRATION & EARLY COMMERCIAL PRESSURE

1.1 Day-One starter doctrine

The normal introductory owner-operator experience should feel like the beginning of a career, not a small established empire.
The strongest default remains one meaningful starter business, normally the General Store, paired with limited Liquid Owner
Cash and enough business working capital to operate without making the first year trivial. The opening should not routinely
include the cash, inventory, transport fleet, debt structure and managerial depth of an already mature merchant.

Exact dollar amounts remain balance values. The Canon locks the relationship rather than a universal number: the player
should have enough to make decisions immediately, but not enough to neutralize inventory pressure, supplier reliability, labor,
credit exposure and early expansion tradeoffs.

CANON LOCK - EARLY PRESSURE COMES FROM OPERATING REALITY, NOT ARTIFICIAL POVERTY

   Low liquidity should interact with real commitments rather than merely forcing the player to wait for money.
   Early opportunity should arrive alongside scarcity: a recurring account can improve demand certainty while reserving stock
    and exposing the business to fulfillment risk.
   The introductory economy should teach working capital, supplier reliability, stock discipline, customer commitments and
    opportunity cost before it teaches empire administration.
   Exceptional starts or later scenarios may begin wealthier; this is a default introductory calibration doctrine, not a universal
    scenario restriction.

2. UNIVERSAL HUMAN CAPABILITY ARCHITECTURE

2.1 Occupation is context, not character class

Every meaningful person should be capable of carrying a broad profile of human abilities. Occupation describes what that
person currently does and where much of their experience was accumulated. It must not function as a hard class that
determines which skills the person is allowed to possess.
                                            REVISION XVI INTEGRATION 2

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 211/346 ====================

                          LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVI / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE
The period record itself supports this granularity: census instructions distinguished actual professions, trades and kinds of work
rather than accepting vague labels, and differentiated bank clerks from officers, salesmen from clerks, hostlers from livery
keepers, foremen from helpers and different transport occupations. Land & Ledgers should therefore model people from task
capability upward rather than from a small set of game-job archetypes downward.

2.2 Aptitude, Skill, Experience and Knowledge

Revision XVI separates four authorities that may correlate but must not collapse into one rating.
   Aptitude - the person's tendency to learn or perform related capabilities well. Aptitude can accelerate development or make
      difficult learning easier; it does not create fictional prior training.
    Skill - the person's present capability at a real class of task.
   Experience - the relevant work, problems, seasons, responsibilities and unusual situations the person has actually
    encountered.
   Knowledge / Domain Familiarity - what the person understands about a particular industry, place, customer base, market,
    procedure, organization or technical domain.
A naturally numerate employee can be promising for bank work without already knowing banking. A strong negotiator can still
be a poor lumber buyer if they do not understand grades, suppliers, seasonality or freight. An experienced carpenter can have
useful adjacent competence without becoming a mason simply because both work on buildings.

2.3 Transferable skills and task-derived catalogue

Skills should be derived from economically meaningful tasks and allowed to transfer wherever the same capability truly matters.
The eventual master catalogue should be broad enough to express real differences without duplicating the same human ability
under every industry.
   Commercial/social examples: selling, customer service, negotiation, interviewing, correspondence, relationship
    maintenance.
    Clerical/financial examples: literacy, numeracy, bookkeeping, reconciliation, cash handling, documentation, estimating,
    record organization.
   Management examples: supervision, scheduling, delegation, conflict handling, quality judgment, planning and task
     coordination.
    Physical/trade examples: measuring/layout, framing, finish carpentry, painting, roofing, masonry, blacksmithing,
    mechanical diagnosis, repair, loading and safe material handling.
   Transport/animal examples: driving, route judgment, animal handling, stable work, loading, dispatch and freight
    documentation.
    Industry familiarity remains separate so a person can have transferable competence without magically understanding every
     industry that uses it.

2.4 Attempt rule - competence shapes consequences, not arbitrary permission

Low skill should not normally make a physically and legally possible task unavailable. A weak painter can paint a shed. A
novice can assist a skilled mason. The economic consequence emerges through time, finish quality, material waste, rework,
supervision burden, customer response, durability and safety. Hard prohibitions should come from genuine legal authority,
physical impossibility, equipment requirements or specialist knowledge where the task truly cannot be performed competently
without them.

The simulation should also avoid bizarre adjacent zeroes. A person with years of general construction work is likely to have at
least some measuring, material handling, basic finishing and adjacent task familiarity even when one trade remains their
strongest capability. Generation and learning should reflect plausible exposure rather than isolated RPG skill silos.

2.5 Mastery scarcity and UI restraint

Extremely high mastery should be rare. Internal systems may use detailed numerical values for tuning and simulation, but
ordinary competent workers should occupy the broad middle rather than constantly appearing as ninety-plus-point masters.
Exact scale bands remain calibration. The player-facing experience should favor qualifications, work history, observed
performance, references, traits and informed estimates over a wall of exposed numbers.

3. CONTINUOUS LEARNING, MENTORSHIP & PROFESSIONAL
DEVELOPMENT

3.1 Learning by doing

Employees improve from actual relevant work. Calendar time alone does not create competence. The learning authority should
consider task relevance, difficulty, novelty, repetition, feedback and whether the person was genuinely involved. The first
months of meaningful exposure can teach more than the thousandth repetition of a simple mastered task.

Failure can teach without undoing the loss. A worker who makes and corrects an estimating error may improve future judgment.
A clerk who reconciles a difficult discrepancy gains more useful experience than one who simply copies routine figures.
Adjacent work can build limited adjacent capability when the employee actually participates.

3.2 Continuous rather than binary training

Training is not a completion switch. If an employee spends three weeks of a planned four-week instruction period working with
a competent mentor, the learning that occurred during those three weeks remains. Completion can matter for a credential, a
recognized status, confidence, authority or social standing where historically appropriate, but it does not suddenly manufacture
the underlying competence on the final day.

3.3 Instructor quality and teaching ability

Learning can depend on instructor competence, the instructor's ability to teach, learner aptitude, learner prior knowledge, task
variety, real time together, opportunities to perform the work, quality of feedback and difficulty of the material. A brilliant
practitioner who communicates poorly may be a weaker teacher than a somewhat less exceptional practitioner who can
explain, supervise and correct effectively.

3.4 Mentorship and outside professional services

Employers may use internal mentorship or purchase outside instruction, assessment or temporary specialist support when
historically plausible. Formal apprenticeship is a valid period institution but must not become the only path to learning. Informal
shop training, supervised work, temporary specialists and professional consultation can all improve capability through real time
and exposure.

CANON LOCK - NO TRAINING BUFF

    Training changes what the person knows or can do because instruction and practice occurred.
      It does not create an unexplained percentage productivity modifier.
  A competent assessment can improve the organization's knowledge of the worker without revealing perfect hidden truth.
   Promotion may follow training and demonstrated capability, but training never forces promotion and promotion never
    creates competence.

4. TASK QUALITY, MISTAKES & CAPABILITY-SPECIFIC REPUTATION

4.1 Quality is broader than mistake severity

Revision XV already permits hidden minor, moderate and major mistakes. Revision XVI adds ordinary quality variation. A job
can be completed without a discrete mistake and still be excellent, acceptable, visibly mediocre, defective or prone to early
failure. Relevant causes include task difficulty, skill, experience, supervision, equipment, material quality, fatigue, weather and
other task-specific conditions.

Severity must be domain-specific. Weak ordinary painting may cause uneven finish, slow work, excess paint use and mild
customer dissatisfaction. Weak structural masonry can create cracking, costly reconstruction or safety risk. The simulation must
never resolve every low-skill outcome through the same generic penalty table.

4.2 Reputation remembers what actually happened

Service and contractor reputation may preserve evidence by capability rather than collapsing every outcome into one universal
trust number. A construction company can be known for strong carpentry, weak painting, excellent reliability and fair dealing.
These dimensions should emerge from job history, customer experience and observed failures rather than from purchased
reputation upgrades.



                                            REVISION XVI INTEGRATION 4

Reputation remains localized. A failed roof should damage the relevant contractor/site/capability reputation. It does not
automatically cause customers to distrust an unrelated bakery owned by the same principal. Broader Owner or Commercial
Standing transfers only where counterparties have a legitimate reason to treat the owner's wider history as evidence.

5. CREW LEADERSHIP, FOREMEN & ORGANIZATIONAL COVERAGE

5.1 No mandatory foreman slot

A crew does not require a formal Foreman position solely because it reaches an arbitrary employee count. Small capable crews
can coordinate informally. Practical leadership can shift to the person with the strongest relevant skill, experience, planning
judgment or communication ability for the work currently underway.

The strongest framer may direct framing while a mason directs masonry and an experienced smith handles specialized
hardware. This is not a free efficiency system. Informal or committee leadership can produce unclear accountability, conflicting
instructions, waiting, duplicated work and sequencing errors.

5.2 Formal foremen become valuable through real complexity

A dedicated foreman or project leader becomes increasingly valuable as crews grow, experience becomes uneven, work is
geographically distributed, several tasks must be sequenced or specialist coordination becomes difficult. A strong foreman
combines enough trade understanding with planning, communication, scheduling, delegation, conflict handling and quality
judgment to reduce actual organizational failure.

CANON LOCK - TITLE DOES NOT CREATE LEADERSHIP

   Appointing a weak leader can make the operation worse.
   An untitled experienced worker can still provide real coordination.
   Formal supervision changes authority and accountability; any performance benefit must arise from better decisions and
    execution.

6. PHYSICAL STAGED CONSTRUCTION & PROJECT EXECUTION

6.1 Projects have physical stage state

The existing project system is deepened from generic sequencing into a physical workflow. A project should know what
currently exists and what work remains. Depending on building type and period, stages can include site preparation, foundation
or masonry, framing, enclosure, roofing, windows and doors, applicable period systems, interior carpentry, finishing, fixtures
and final preparation. Not every project uses every stage, and exact sequencing remains data-driven by project type.

The player should be able to understand why a building is delayed without reading a generic progress percentage. The project
may be waiting for stonework, framing lumber, a roofer, a delivered fixture, better weather, financing or completion of a
prerequisite stage.

6.2 Stage consumption and stage funding

Labor and materials are consumed when the corresponding work occurs. Approving a $300 project does not necessarily
remove $300 immediately. The owner approves scope, budget and funding authority; actual cash leaves through purchases,
payroll, contractor invoices, delivered materials and progress payments as the work proceeds.

This makes construction financing structurally different from many lump-sum acquisitions. A project can begin with less than its
ultimate cost sitting idle in cash when future funding is credible. The risk is real: a project can later pause because money,
materials or labor fail to arrive.

6.3 Automatic continuation after authorization

Once a project is approved, routine continuation should not require repeated strategic clicks. Work proceeds while
authorization, labor, materials, prerequisite stages and site conditions permit it. Escalation is reserved for genuine exceptions:
cost overruns beyond policy, unexpected site condition, missing specialist, funding shortfall, major delay, scope change or other
owner-reserved decision.

6.4 Project Stockpile versus Operating Reserve

A Project Stockpile is physical inventory earmarked for a named project. It is distinct from the producing business's ordinary
operating reserve, target stock or sale inventory. Allocated project material is not simultaneously available for normal sale
unless the allocation is deliberately released.

                                            REVISION XVI INTEGRATION 5

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 214/346 ====================

                          LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVI / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE
Pre-buying materials can protect schedule but ties up capital and storage and can create theft, fire, deterioration, weather,
warping, handling and other material-specific risks. Project stockpiling is therefore a strategic hedge, not a dominant no-cost
tactic.

6.5 Direct-to-project sourcing and sourcing policy

The player should be able to instruct an owned producer to fulfill a project requirement directly. Lumber can leave the mill for
the building site without an unnecessary intermediate inventory-management click. Physical production, loading, travel,
unloading and ledger attribution still occur.

A project can source requirements from project stockpile, owned producers, direct-to-project production, external spot
purchase, standing supplier agreements, contractor-supplied materials, subcontractor-supplied components or customer-
supplied materials. Sourcing may differ by component.

6.6 Internal supply is not free

A vertically integrated project must preserve real cost and opportunity cost. Sawmill output consumed internally still required
logs, labor, equipment and yard capacity. Freight still consumed teams, drivers, feed, time and vehicle condition. Forge
hardware still consumed iron, fuel and smithing time. Internal transfer can reduce markup, delay or bargaining risk, but it
converts an external dependency into internal responsibility rather than eliminating scarcity.

7. CONSTRUCTION & CONTRACTING BUSINESS ARCHETYPE

7.1 Business identity

Construction & Contracting is promoted to a supported business archetype because it creates a distinct commercial
relationship: project capability can be bought and sold. A small contractor can exist with modest fixed property because much of
its productive value resides in people, tools, reputation, supplier relationships, subcontractors, scheduling and working capital.

Supported work can include new buildings, additions, repairs, structural work, painting, roofing, renovations, outbuildings,
property maintenance and project coordination where the firm has the capability. Individual trades can also remain independent
businesses or workers rather than every job passing through one general contractor.

7.2 Bidding and estimating

A contractor quote should be built from expected labor, materials, transport, subcontracting, tools/equipment burden, duration,
contingency and desired return. The estimate is a forecast informed by records and expertise. Underestimating can win work
and destroy margin. Overestimating can lose a profitable contract. Estimating expertise improves understanding of the work; it
does not directly add profit.

7.3 Backlog, work in progress and payment timing

Contract backlog is not revenue. Awarded work consumes calendar time, crews, materials, working capital, equipment and
supervision before it becomes completed work. Contracts may use deposits, delivered-material payments, milestone/progress
payments, completion balances or other historically appropriate terms. Exact percentages are contract/project data rather than
universal Canon values.

7.4 Subcontractors and temporary specialists

A firm does not need to keep every specialist permanently on payroll. Period practice supports prime contractors,
subcontractors, material suppliers and specialist installation work. Temporary specialists are therefore a normal response to
capability gaps. The commercial tradeoff is availability, price, coordination, quality control and dependence on outside capacity.

7.5 Organic scaling

A second crew, larger project or wider territory becomes possible only when real people, supervision, tools, cash, transport and
workload support it. There is no Contractor Level that grants another crew. Taking more work than the organization can execute
creates delays, cash strain, quality failures, breached commitments and reputation damage.

8. UTILIZATION, JOB ECONOMICS & BOTTLENECK DIAGNOSIS

8.1 Utilization is diagnostic, not victory

A highly utilized asset can be busy doing low-value work. A less utilized asset can become more profitable after weak jobs are
refused. Business reports should therefore distinguish utilization from contribution and expose the causal components where
records support them: revenue, direct cost, labor, maintenance, feed/team burden, empty positioning, idle time, margin,
rejected demand and opportunity cost.

8.2 Minimum service policies

Businesses may use economically grounded policies such as minimum job charges, call-out charges, minimum loads, service
zones, target margins and rush premiums. These are market-facing policies whose success depends on customers and
competitors, not designer-enforced restrictions.

8.3 Expansion follows persistent evidence

Managers should not recommend capital expansion merely because one month was busy. Evidence can include sustained
profitable utilization, repeated profitable work refused, recurring commitments, seasonality, route economics, driver/team
availability, empty mileage and credible future demand. Expansion should target the actual bottleneck rather than defaulting to
buying the next obvious asset.

9. DELEGATION, OWNER LOCKS, CAPITAL REQUESTS & DIVISIONS

9.1 Persistent owner policy modes

Delegated administration needs a practical distinction among one-time orders, ordinary manager discretion and persistent
owner locks.
  Do Once - execute a specific instruction once, then return to the standing policy.
   Manager Judgment - the manager retains ordinary discretion within authority.
  OWNER LOCKED - the strategic policy remains fixed until the owner changes it. A manager does not silently override it;
     conflict must surface as an actual authority/personnel problem.

9.2 Multidimensional authority

Delegation should not reduce every decision to one dollar threshold. Contracting, lending and treasury authority can consider
customer or borrower history, cargo or business type, route familiarity, price/margin policy, credit exposure, collateral,
connected-party status, whether new equipment is required and whether the choice displaces a materially better commitment.
Opportunity cost itself can create an escalation even when the nominal transaction is small.

9.3 Manager-originated Capital Requests

Managers can identify bottlenecks and propose investment without waiting for the player to inspect every business. A Capital
Request should state the amount, purpose, why now, evidence, expected result, alternative if rejected, preferred funding route
and urgency where relevant.

The manager's forecast remains a professional opinion. Competence, records, optimism, incentives and bias can all affect it.
Over time the owner can learn which managers are conservative, aggressive, accurate, cost-blind or unusually good at seeing
future demand.

9.4 Division / Operating Group layer

Large portfolios may introduce a Division or Operating Group between the owner and individual businesses. A division is an
administrative grouping under a senior manager; it is not a new legal super-ledger that erases the books of its member
businesses. Each business retains its cash, debt, assets, employees, contracts and operating history.

Division-level reporting can aggregate results and coordinate staff, purchasing, logistics or treasury only where actual authority
and resources exist. Senior managers can have distinct thresholds for intercompany transfers, borrowing, capital spending and
strategic commitments.

9.5 Zero personally managed businesses is a valid mature state

The ownership arc explicitly permits the player to reach a state in which no ordinary business is personally managed. The
player may act primarily as investor, capital allocator, governance authority, acquisition decision-maker and strategic principal.

The businesses continue to hire, buy, sell, maintain, contract, err, request capital and react to markets through real managers
and staff. Mature delegation is active simulation, not passive-income autoplay.

10. CAPITAL ARCHITECTURE, RESERVES & INTERNAL TREASURY

10.1 Three distinct internal funding relationships

Revision XVI separates three transactions that must not be collapsed into one generic fund transfer.
   Owner Capital Contribution - personal owner cash is permanently invested into the business. Business cash/equity rises;
    no artificial repayment date or interest obligation is created.
   Intercompany Advance - one controlled ledger temporarily finances another. The advancing ledger records a
    receivable/claim and the receiving ledger records an obligation. Repayment and terms remain visible.
   Bank Loan - a bank advances institutional funds to a borrower, creating a real bank asset and borrower liability subject to
     underwriting, liquidity, concentration and legal rules.

10.2 Funding route follows economic purpose

Permanent equipment or expansion may sensibly use retained business cash or owner capital. A temporary receivable or
seasonal mismatch may fit an intercompany advance or bank credit better. Debt may be attractive when preserving owner
liquidity or organizational independence matters. The player is not forced into one hierarchy, but managers should recognize
the structural differences among these funding routes.

10.3 Operating Reserve is not a Capital Budget

A standing operating reserve expresses ordinary resilience policy. A separately approved capital project or machine purchase is
a special authorization. The player does not need to permanently raise a $50 reserve to $190 merely because a $140 one-time
purchase was approved. After the purchase, ordinary reserve policy remains what it was unless deliberately changed.

10.4 Reserve floors, excess cash and owner sweeps

Treasury policy may distinguish a minimum/target operating reserve, protected obligations, an excess-cash threshold, owner
distribution rule and temporary capital authorization. Sweeps and transfers must remain real ledger entries. Managers do not
silently move major sums across controlled businesses without authority.

10.5 Automatic owner draws as a convenience layer

Owner cash and business cash remain separate. When the player makes a legitimate personal purchase and Liquid Owner
Cash is insufficient, the game may automatically execute the necessary owner distribution from an authorized owned business
if available distributable funds exist and the transfer would not materially endanger protected payroll, debt, supplier or other
obligations. The books still record Business Distribution -> Liquid Owner Cash -> Personal Purchase.

10.6 Routine debt-payment automation

Scheduled required payments may occur automatically by default when the paying ledger has authorized funds. The player can
disable this convenience policy. Extra principal repayment remains a strategic capital-allocation choice. If funds are insufficient,
the obligation becomes missed/delinquent according to its contract and dated legal regime; unrelated ledgers are not silently
raided without an explicit treasury policy.

11. PRIVATE LENDING, UNDERWRITING & CONTRACT-SPECIFIC DEFAULT

11.1 Personal/private lending

The owner may lend personal money directly where the dated legal regime permits, without owning a bank. This is distinct from
merchant account credit and from institutional bank lending. A private loan records borrower, principal, interest terms, payment
schedule, security, guarantors/sureties where used, payments, remaining balance, delinquency and enforcement state.

11.2 Flexible promissory-note structures

Period evidence supports multiple note structures rather than one universal loan template. Notes may be payable on or before
a maturity date, use installment or maturity structures, be renewed, carry security, include guarantors/sureties and contain
contractual acceleration after specified defaults. Historical law also permitted some agreed interest to be deducted in advance.

CANON LOCK - EARLY REPAYMENT IS CONTRACT-SPECIFIC
                                            REVISION XVI INTEGRATION 8

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 217/346 ====================

                          LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XVI / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE
  Do not create a generic rule that all future promised interest remains due after early repayment.
  Some notes permit payment on or before maturity with interest until paid; other lawful arrangements can price interest
     differently.
   The contract and dated interest/usury law determine the payoff economics.

11.3 Missed payment does not have one universal consequence

Some contracts can accelerate the entire balance after a missed installment; others can be renewed, tolerated, renegotiated or
worked out. The simulation should therefore resolve missed obligation -> contractual lender rights -> lender response/workout
-> enforcement where pursued. The existing Commercial Ruin doctrine remains unchanged.

Acceleration is contract-dependent rather than universal. Installment debt can sometimes be cured as to amounts then due; a
lender may have an optional acceleration right, an automatic clause or no acceleration mechanism for that default. Debt UI
should therefore distinguish delinquent installment, accelerated balance and enforcement rather than collapsing all three into
DEFAULTED.

Real-estate mortgages and chattel mortgages are security instruments rather than automatic title transfers. Foreclosure or
collateral sale follows the dated legal process; sale proceeds can first satisfy lawful costs and secured debt, with surplus
returning to the debtor where applicable, while a shortfall can leave a deficiency. Guarantors/sureties, renewals, consolidation,
refinancing and workouts are valid credit structures.

11.4 Underwriting is a negotiation over structure

A lender can approve less than requested, shorten maturity, request more collateral, require a guarantor, stage advances, alter
pricing or refuse. Borrower quality, collateral quality, title/information quality and lender liquidity are separate dimensions.
Borrower-reported information can be false, optimistic, incomplete or honestly mistaken. The player should see evidence and
professional judgment, not an omniscient default percentage.

12. ACQUISITION DILIGENCE, SELLER KNOWLEDGE & DEAL STRUCTURE

12.1 Normalize owner labor

Acquisition diligence must distinguish accounting profit from the economic burden of replacing a departing owner's labor. A
store earning $35 per month while the seller performs substantial skilled full-time work is not an absentee $35-profit investment.
Reports should identify owner labor contribution, replacement coverage and normalized earnings where evidence allows.

12.2 Seller misrepresentation and imperfect books

Sellers can exaggerate sales, omit costs, misstate inventory, conceal deferred maintenance, overvalue receivables, omit
obligations or present unpaid owner labor as profit. Deliberate fraud is possible but should be rarer than ordinary incomplete or
optimistic records. Diligence changes what the buyer knows; it does not rewrite the underlying business.

12.3 Transition assistance and person-specific knowledge

The seller or key employee may remain for a defined transition period to transfer customer relationships, supplier knowledge,
procedures, introductions, technical practice and unwritten routines. Knowledge can genuinely reside in individuals. Ownership
transfer does not automatically copy that knowledge into the new organization.

12.4 Partial acquisitions and retained ownership

Acquisition workflows may support purchases of inventory, equipment, wagons, land, particular assets or other transferable
rights without purchasing the whole business. Where appropriate, a seller may remain manager, retain a minority interest, enter
a partnership or agree to a staged buyout. Existing succession rules continue to support manager/employee buyouts.

12.5 Earn-outs and contingent seller obligations

An earn-out, profit share or other contingent seller payment is not ordinary bank debt. The agreement should define the
measured base closely enough to prevent meaningless manipulation: permitted operating expenses, manager compensation,
capital expenditure treatment, owner compensation, related-party transactions, reserve policy, access/audit rights and
termination conditions may matter. The obligation persists until satisfied, released or otherwise resolved by its contract.

12.6 Fraud suspicion can remain unresolved

Internal-control systems may generate genuine uncertainty. A discrepancy can result from error, shrinkage, poor records or
deliberate theft. A worker may become suspected without the simulation revealing a visible THIEF tag. Wrongful suspicion and

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 218/346 ====================
