PART IV


 Shared Business Simulation One operating architecture for businesses, cash, continuity, turnaround and portfolio
 control.

  READING RULE This part is the authoritative home for the systems listed here. Related appendices compress the same
   rules for

 routing and summary; they do not override the body.

 CORE IDENTITY

 6.1 Shared shell and operating role coverage

 Every business should inherit from one broad shared business model so the economy stays coherent. The shell
 distinguishes ownership, current managing authority, operating control, qualified-role coverage, task workload, labor
 terms, reputation and productive capacity rather than collapsing everything into one employee count. Identity includes
 business name, type, owner, parcel, status and founding story. Operations include workers, manager or foreman,
 operating hours, shift state, qualified-role coverage, task backlog and current throughput. Economy includes revenue,
 payroll, upkeep, input cost, output value, cash, debt exposure and policy settings. Asset state covers condition,
 presentation, display/storage/bulk capacity where relevant, overflow state, expansions, adjacent land, transport
 capacity and heating or fuel burden. Recurring commitments track buyer and seller obligations, due dates, priority and
 breach history. Operating roles remain a first-class hidden logic layer, but ordinary businesses should not require one
 full-time employee per narrow task. Compatible work can be covered by the same person when workload permits;
 specialization emerges when scale, skill or simultaneous demand makes it necessary.

6.1A Labor compensation and occupational markets

 Employment should be evaluated as a compensation package rather than cash wage alone. Historically plausible
 arrangements can include wages, meals, board, lodging, seasonal terms, work schedule, and job stability.
 Employer-provided board or bunk space can materially improve recruitment but creates its own food, housing,
 maintenance, and capacity burden. Exact wages remain occupation-, place-, and season-dependent rather than one
 universal town wage. Labor is not one interchangeable pool. NPCs carry skills and acceptable work paths that
 determine which roles they can cover competently. General labor can move across many low-skill tasks, while
 teamsters, clerks, smiths, sawyers, miners, foremen, bookkeepers, and other skilled roles create narrower labor
 markets. Seasonal demand can temporarily pull compatible workers into harvest, construction, freight, mining, or other
 surges, creating wage pressure in the overlapping occupations rather than an automatic townwide wage multiplier.

 6.1B Workload-based staffing, labor-hours, and task compatibility

 Long-term staffing should be driven by real work rather than rigid job slots. Businesses generate task demand from
 customer traffic, production, deliveries, receiving, stocking, bookkeeping, cleaning, maintenance, hauling, opening
 hours and other business-specific work. Employees contribute available labor-hours and can cover multiple compatible
 tasks. A quiet General Store may be run by one owner or clerk who serves customers, takes payment, restocks and
 handles ordinary upkeep; a booming store can require multiple people because several tasks must happen at once. A
 logger, mill hand, teamster, miner and clerk should not all be treated as interchangeable eight-hour work units. Job
 type, skill, physical conditions, travel, season, daylight, machinery and workload determine practical labor capacity.
 MVP hiring may remain simpler, but the design should avoid hard-coding permanent employee counts that prevent
 later workload-based staffing.

 6.1C Business Decision Authority and administrative work

 Every meaningful owner-operated business should expose administrative decisions capable of changing performance
 even when two businesses own similar physical assets. The current managing authority is whoever actually administers
 the business: the player when personally managing a player-owned business, an NPC owner for an NPC-run business, or
 a hired manager when the owner delegates. Ordinary employees execute assigned work - selling, stocking, cleaning,
 hauling, cooking, sawing, shoeing, operating machinery and similar tasks - but do not silently decide merchandise
 allocation, supplier strategy, staffing policy, pricing posture, credit posture or capital use. Owners and managers make
 those administrative decisions. NPC authorities use the same decision space as the player and can overstock slow
 goods, understock fast sellers, become too generous with credit, refuse profitable credit, hire badly, hold too little cash
 or fail to react to a changing market. Player advantage should come from judgment, attention and portfolio
 coordination, not exclusive mechanics.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 23

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 260/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


6.1D Operating schedules and temporal freedom

 Operating hours are a policy choice wherever the business can physically function. The managing authority should be
 free to set unusual or inefficient schedules, including overnight retail hours, rather than being forced into
 designer-approved opening times. The simulation then supplies consequences through customer schedules,
 lighting/fuel needs, employee availability, wages, fatigue or shift structure where implemented, safety and actual
 demand. Production and outdoor businesses remain constrained by their real processes: a forest crew

 cannot simply ignore visibility and weather, while an underground mine or adequately lit fixed industrial plant can be
 less dependent on daylight. The continuous 24-hour clock is authoritative; usable work time is job-specific.

 6.2 Owner cash versus business cash

 Owner cash and business operating cash remain separate authorities. Businesses should hold their own cash positions.
 The player can top up or withdraw from businesses, and automation rules can move cash at thresholds when a business
 is too full or too starved. A business should survive first and pay the owner later. This distinction becomes more
 important as the portfolio grows because it prevents every business from behaving like a personal pocket and allows
 the player to read which enterprises are truly healthy.

 6.3 Net worth and portfolio maturity

 Net worth remains the master success metric and should be treated as a real portfolio calculation rather than flavor
 text. Liquid Cash is immediately spendable owner cash. Net Worth is the grounded total economic position, including
 owner cash, business cash, owned asset value where supported, liabilities where supported, and later investment or
 debt exposure. This matters because the late game is not just richer versions of the early game. The player increasingly
 behaves like a portfolio owner directing capital across multiple operating entities, not a singlestore clerk who happens
 to own extra deeds.

 6.4 Delegation and executive maturity

 The business shell should support the project's long-arc delegation fantasy. Early in a business, the owner normally acts
 as the administrative authority. As the portfolio grows, a hired manager can take over routine administrative decisions
 such as ordinary hiring and replacement, merchandise-space allocation, reorder and supplier policy, routine pricing,
 customer-credit decisions within policy, scheduling and other day-to-day choices. The owner should be able to define
 authority bands and approval limits rather than surrendering the business completely. Capital projects, major debt,
 sale, acquisition, exceptional contracts or decisions outside delegated limits can still escalate. Managers themselves
 are real employees who can quit, be poached, relocate, become ill, retire or die; a management vacancy therefore
 creates a real administrative problem. Late ownership should mean bigger decisions at a higher level of abstraction, not
 passive autoplay or permanent micromanagement.

6.4A Organizational coverage, not Organizational Capacity points

 Do not expose one universal Organization or Capacity score. A growing portfolio can fail organizationally in different
 ways: execution coverage, decision coverage, information coverage, administrative coverage and specialist coverage.
 A business may have enough hands to perform the physical work but no manager authorized to resolve an unusual
 supplier decision. A remote mine may operate well locally while owner reports are stale. A profitable group may have
 strong managers but books that no longer reconcile. These conditions should create concrete symptoms - waiting
 approvals, stale records, unresolved exceptions, missed maintenance, weak hiring, repeated travel needs - and causal
 responses such as hiring, promotion, delegation, better records, communication, central staff, sale or slower expansion.

 6.4B Owner attention without action points

 The owner should not receive an arbitrary daily action allowance. Attention matters because the player character and
 their organization cannot be physically and informationally everywhere. If the owner leaves the store to inspect
 property, ordinary store work needs coverage. If a manager has authority, routine decisions can continue. If a remote
 exception can be resolved through correspondence, telegraph or telephone, physical travel may be unnecessary. The
 useful distinction is physical attention, decision attention and information attention. Delegation changes the player's
 relationship with time by making longer periods safe to advance when competent people and reporting systems can
 handle routine work.

 11.1 Diagnosis and transfer rule

 Buying a weak business should be fast access to an opportunity and its problems, not a magic profit button. Diagnosis
 buckets remain condition, pricing, supply, labor or management, demand fit, and reputation. Old Inherited relationship
 memory and commercial history remain a drag. Owner Reputation modifies recovery speed and seriousness but does





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 24

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 261/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 not erase structural problems. New management should generate only a small curiosity bump, not a miracle cure.

 11.2 Integration stance

 Possible integration stances remain stabilize first, re-stock aggressively, restore trust before growth, replace
 management quickly, refurbish first, keep the old name or rebrand, keep staff or clean house, and honor old credit later
 or tighten policy immediately. Integration stance should influence early cash burn, relationship-repair speed, employee
 retention, and how visible the ownership change feels to the town.

 11.3 Continuity logic

 Business continuity should resolve through three checks: legal control, financial continuity, and operating role
 coverage. The outcome is softer than a hard game-state ladder. A business may continue normally, continue in reduced
 form, or become dormant depending on business type and staffing structure. Retail and manager-led operations can
 often limp along under clerks, spouses, adult children, foremen, or acting managers. Skill-critical trades without
 qualified operators cannot. This same logic should govern NPC businesses and player businesses alike so the town feels
 internally consistent. A purchased, inherited, or defeated business keeps its baggage. Weak supplier ties, backlog,
 staffing problems, poor stock discipline, worn condition, bad books, and damaged trust should survive transfer until
 actively repaired. A change in owner can create curiosity and maybe some renewed trust, but it should not behave like
 a magical cleanse.

 11.4 Commercial succession and authority redistribution

 Death, retirement, incapacity, relocation, partner exit or career change should be treated first as a
 redistribution-of-authority problem, not as automatic business deletion or an automatic sale listing. Resolve three
 distinct questions: who legally owns or controls the relevant interest, who can actually operate or manage the
 enterprise and whether the enterprise can financially survive the transition. Possible outcomes include intact family
 continuation, spouse or heir ownership with hired management, existing-manager continuation, partner settlement,
 manager/employee buyout, outside acquisition, asset breakup, liquidation or dormancy. Exact probate and partnership
 procedure remains a legal research hold where not already validated. The core design lock is that legal identity,
 commercial identity and operating capability are related but not identical.

11.4A Business identity across ownership changes

 An acquired business should not become a historyless 'Player Store #4.' Preserve enough economically meaningful
 identity to recognize the firm across ownership changes: name, founder or founding story, founding date, premises,
 ownership history, major expansions/conversions, important long-lived relationships and serious failures where retained
 by the Campaign Record. The new owner can keep the name, modify it or rebrand, but acquisition does not erase the
 business's past.

 6.5 Asset Condition, Maintenance & Reliability

 Asset condition is a shared business system for buildings, wagons/carts, harness and transport equipment, farm
 machinery, sawmills, mine plant, utility equipment, railway assets and other maintainable property. Condition is a
 physical economic state, not merely a universal durability bar. Assets deteriorate according to their construction, use,
 load, environment, age, operating practice, storage/exposure and unresolved defects. Maintenance consumes
 appropriate labor, parts, tools/facilities, time and money. The owner or delegated manager chooses how aggressively to
 maintain; the simulation supplies the consequences.

6.5A Condition domains and readable state

 Condition should stop at economically meaningful component groups rather than every individual screw. A wagon
 might distinguish wheels/running gear, axle/bearing condition, frame/body and harness. A steam sawmill can
 distinguish boiler/pressure system, engine/mechanical state, drive system, saw/cutting system and building/support
 condition. A ranch windmill or water pump has different domains again. Player-facing presentation should normally use
 human-readable states such as Excellent, Good, Worn, Poor, Very Poor, Failed or specific known defects rather than
 pretending a nineteenth-century owner knows a component is exactly 67.4% healthy. Different asset classes must
 interpret condition differently; a worn roof and a worn boiler do not share one universal failure rule.

 6.5B Wear must come from work and exposure

  • Use wear derives from operating time, workload, load, route/terrain, heat, vibration, lubrication, material
    characteristics and the asset- specific stresses actually applied.

  • Environmental deterioration derives from storage, rain/snow, moisture, corrosion, sunlight/weathering and other
    supported exposures. Sheltered equipment lasts better because it is sheltered, not because a shed grants an abstract




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 25

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 262/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



    lifespan bonus.

  • Idle equipment can deteriorate more slowly through use while still suffering exposure, corrosion, decay or preservation
   problems where appropriate.

  • Boom conditions can create maintenance fragility because assets are run harder and maintenance windows disappear;
    recession can create time for maintenance while simultaneously reducing the cash available to pay for it.

 6.5C Service, inspection, repair, overhaul and replacement

 Maintenance work is divided conceptually into routine service, inspection, minor repair, major repair, overhaul/rebuild
 and replacement. Routine lubrication, cleaning, tightening and ordinary care should normally happen under standing
 policy without owner clicks. Inspection converts uncertainty into better information. Minor/major repairs address
 specific defects. Overhaul restores a heavily used asset through substantial work. Replacement is a capital decision and
 may also change capability if newer equipment differs materially from the old asset.

  • Maintenance keeps an asset doing what it already does. Capital improvement changes capability. Repairing a wagon
   wheel is not an upgrade; purchasing a larger or different freight asset is.

  • Repairs require actual compatible skill, material and facilities. A local operator can perform ordinary service; a
    blacksmith, wheelwright, machinist, engineer or specialist may be required for more demanding work.

  • Repair quality can distinguish proper, temporary and improvised work where economically meaningful. A field repair
   may restore a disabled wagon enough to return to town without making it equivalent to shop work.

6.5D Known defects and inspection confidence

 Known defects should matter more than a generic condition penalty. A loose wagon wheel, scored axle, leaking boiler
 tube, worn drive belt, damaged roof, failed fence section or pump problem creates consequences specific to the
 affected system. Defects can progress from developing to noticeable, serious, critical or failed according to the asset;
 sudden accident damage can bypass that progression. The simulation can know actual condition while the business
 knows only what employees and inspections have revealed. Ordinary workers notice obvious problems. Skilled
 operators can diagnose more. Specialist inspection increases confidence for expensive or safety-critical assets.
 Inspection knowledge becomes stale as the asset accumulates new use. This creates uncertainty without hiding facts
 that have already been properly measured or recorded.

 6.5E Maintenance policy and cash-reserve interaction

 Routine maintenance should be administered through standing policy in the same spirit as inventory replenishment.
 The managing authority can set automatic repair/maintenance spending limits, cash-reserve protection, approval
 thresholds, safety-critical shutdown rules, inspection cadence and spare-parts targets. If a routine job would drive
 business cash below the protected reserve, the manager can escalate it instead of silently spending the money. The
 player may deliberately defer maintenance. The game should usually allow this if the asset can still physically operate.
 Deferred work does not trigger a generic punishment; it allows wear, inefficiency, defects, hazard exposure and future
 repair cost to accumulate through the actual asset. Some neglect can remain lucky for a long time, which is why
 short-term operators and distressed businesses may rationally gamble on it.

 6.5F Efficiency, reliability and failure

 Avoid Maintenance Low = -15% Production. Gradual performance loss is valid only where physical deterioration really
 causes it: fouled boiler surfaces can increase fuel/steam burden, dull cutting equipment can reduce effective
 throughput, worn running gear can reduce practical travel reliability. Failure exposure is then calculated from
 asset/design characteristics, condition, unresolved defects, current load, environmental stress and operating practice.
 Probability should generally decide when a plausible stressed component fails, not whether a healthy new machine is
 randomly destroyed for drama. Catastrophic failure should normally require a credible causal chain such as serious
 defect plus continued operation, dangerous load, inadequate support, improper handling or extreme circumstances.
 Rare uncontrollable failures can exist but must remain rare enough that maintenance feels like risk management rather
 than tribute to RNG.

6.5G Spare parts, redundancy and downtime

  • Businesses may carry spare parts as real inventory. This ties up cash and storage but can turn a multi-week
    outside-order delay into an immediate repair.

  • Redundant installed capacity is different from parts inventory. A spare wagon, reserve pump, additional boiler or other
   backup asset may let production continue while the primary asset is down, at the cost of capital, maintenance and idle
    capacity.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 26

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 263/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



  • Maintenance consumes time as well as money. A good manager schedules work during low demand, overnight
   downtime, seasonal lull or weather shutdown where the real process permits it; poor scheduling can remove critical
    capacity during a peak period.

  • Seasonal maintenance is especially important for farm machinery and other assets whose failure during a narrow work
   window is much more costly than the same repair in the off-season.

6.5H Buildings, fire, safety and service businesses

 Buildings use the same system at a slower cadence: structure, roof/weatherproofing, chimney/heating, loading
 platforms and specialized systems can generate actual maintenance needs. Maintenance and presentation remain
 separate. A freshly painted building can have a neglected boiler; a weathered shop can be mechanically excellent.
 Maintenance feeds the existing causal fire and accident systems. Cracked stovepipes, damaged chimneys, overheating
 bearings, poorly maintained boilers, failed mine support, defective hoists or later electrical faults can create the
 relevant hazards. There is no universal Poor Maintenance fire/injury modifier. The defect produces the exposure.

 6.5I Asset history, used equipment, salvage and finance

 Maintainable assets should preserve meaningful history: purchase/install date, major repairs, overhauls, accident
 damage and replacement of major components. History affects diligence, resale, confidence and attachment.
 Used-equipment markets can therefore offer cheaper assets with uncertain condition; the player can inspect, refurbish,
 operate, resell or salvage them. Failed equipment can retain parts or scrap value instead of vanishing. Condition and
 maintenance backlog affect acquisition valuation and collateral value. Two sawmills with identical current annual profit
 should not be valued identically if one carries a major deferred overhaul. Banks, buyers, auditors and insurers where
 implemented can care about the real physical state of pledged property.

 6.6 Bookkeeping, Records, Reconciliation & Internal Controls

 Land & Ledgers should distinguish the business's physical/economic reality from the quality of its records without
 creating artificial uncertainty around known facts. The simulation knows actual stock, cash movement, receivables,
 shipments, wages and physical events. The business ledger records what was properly entered. Missing entries,
 counting errors, unrecorded damage, bad receiving, cash-handling mistakes or theft can create discrepancies, but a
 confirmed invoice or correctly recorded twelve-cent purchase remains exactly twelve cents.

6.6A Bookkeeping workload rather than mandatory job slots

 Bookkeeping generates administrative workload from transactions, customer accounts, supplier bills, payroll, inventory
 movements, leases, freight, debt and other business activity. A tiny owner-operated store may generate only modest
 evening record work that the owner or clerk can handle alongside other duties. A large merchant, mine, bank or
 portfolio can justify dedicated bookkeepers and later portfolio staff. Do not require one full-time bookkeeper merely
 because a business exists.

 6.6B Recorded state, physical counts and reconciliation

  • Known recorded transactions stay exact; the challenge is whether all relevant transactions and losses were recorded
    correctly.

  • Periodic cash reconciliation compares expected cash against actual counted cash. Stocktaking compares recorded
    inventory against physical count. Receivables review checks customer balances and aging.

  • A discrepancy is a problem to explain, not an automatic theft accusation. Causes can include damage/spoilage not
    written off, counting error, receiving mistakes, credit-entry mistakes, employee error or deliberate theft/fraud.

  • Correcting a discrepancy updates the books; the game should not keep a permanent fuzzy value once the business
   has actually counted and reconciled the asset.

 6.6C Record quality and owner information

 Record quality can emerge from bookkeeping workload versus available time/skill, procedures, management attention
 and later office equipment. If administrative work consistently exceeds capacity, books can fall behind or discrepancies
 can remain unresolved. Better books do not increase real sales by themselves; they allow the managing authority to
 understand margin, turnover, receivables, stockouts, cash conversion, maintenance burden and other operating truths
 sooner and more accurately.

6.6D Internal-control decisions

  • Who keeps the books: owner, clerk, manager, dedicated bookkeeper or later portfolio staff.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 27

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 264/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



  • How often cash is reconciled and inventory is counted, including partial/cycle checks versus full stocktake where
    appropriate.

  • Who is allowed to extend customer credit, receive supplier deliveries, handle the till or approve write-offs.

  • How aggressively unusual differences are reviewed and when an outside auditor/inspector is hired.

  • Later cash registers, typewriters and office processes improve accountability/administrative throughput through real
    recordkeeping functions rather than creating demand bonuses.

 6.6E Acquisition and delegated-management consequences

 Books review becomes meaningful diligence. A seller can report strong profit while carrying uncertain receivables, stale
 inventory counts or unrecorded maintenance obligations. Poor records do not necessarily mean fraud; they increase
 uncertainty and may justify deeper diligence. After acquisition, inherited record weakness survives until corrected.
 Delegated businesses also create principal-agent risk. An owner may trust a manager to run routine operations but still
 choose review cadence, reconciliation thresholds and audit triggers. Late-game auditors become valuable because they
 compare reported performance against stock, cash, contracts, staffing and physical condition rather than functioning as
 magical truth buttons.

PART V


 Businesses & Industry Frontier businesses, rural production, lumber, remote industry and mining.

  READING RULE This part is the authoritative home for the systems listed here. Related appendices compress the same
   rules for

 routing and summary; they do not override the body.

 7.1 General Store

 The General Store remains the first fully playable deep slice because it touches the widest set of shared systems at
 once. It is a broad merchant business rather than a forced specialization class. A sufficiently large, well-capitalized store
 may carry food staples, clothing, household goods, tools, hardware, ranch or farm supplies, work goods, selected locally
 produced goods and other period-valid merchandise simultaneously. What it actually carries should emerge from
 physical capacity, working capital, supplier access, freight economics, local demand and owner judgment. Store identity
 therefore emerges from assortment and depth rather than from a Ranch Store or Mining Store upgrade button.
 Special-order capability lets a smaller merchant offer access to goods it does not permanently stock. The current
 managing authority controls the policy; ordinary clerks execute sales, stocking and receiving inside that policy.

7.1A Display, Storage, Bulk/Yard, and dedicated merchandise allocation

 General Store inventory should use normalized physical capacity at a scale large enough to represent a true
 broad-assortment frontier merchant. The three primary pools are Display Space, indoor Storage Space and Bulk/Yard
 Space where the property supports it. Every individual physical unit consumes space according to size; the smallest
 practical packaged goods can use one normalized unit while larger sacks, boots, tools, firearms, stoves, fencing, feed or
 agricultural equipment consume progressively more. Exact size values remain balancing data, not historical claims. A
 proper store may be tuned around a large display pool - approximately the order of 250 normalized display units rather
 than a tiny 20-slot inventory - with proportionally larger storage and bulk capacity, but exact capacities remain open
 until the merchandise catalogue and building footprints are tested. Capacity is tracked as Total, Allocated/Reserved and
 Occupied. Merchandise space is dedicated by product line or fixture rather than treated as perfectly fungible every
 moment. If ten firearms each require ten display units, a 100-unit firearm allocation remains 100 units even after one
 firearm sells; the newly empty ten units are reserved for the firearm line until the managing authority deliberately
 reduces or repurposes the allocation. Employees can automatically refill an allocated display from backstock, but they
 do not replace an empty firearm position with unrelated one-unit goods. The same rule applies to storage and bulk
 areas. Reallocation is an administrative merchandising decision and may consume ordinary worker time for
 rearrangement without requiring a floor-layout minigame.

 7.1B Assortment breadth, sourcing difficulty, landed cost, and pricing

 The store should be allowed to carry as broad an assortment as its property, capital and supply network realistically
 permit. Off-map sourcing is not a magical catalogue. Each product must have a viable supplier or market source, and
 supplier choice should expose price, lead time, reliability, volume, quality, route and freight burden. Common regional
 goods may be easy to replenish while specialized manufactured goods or bulky machinery can be expensive, slow or
 practical only by special order until transport improves. Local goods can be purchased from nearby households or
 producers at negotiated/current local value and can have very different economics from standardized manufacturer or
 wholesaler goods. For MVP retail pricing, the clean rule is acquisition/landed cost plus the managing authority's chosen
 markup. If an item costs the business $1.00 and the authority applies a 50% markup on cost, the retail price is $1.50.
 Landed cost should include the supplier purchase price plus freight, drayage/handling and other supported acquisition
 costs rather than pretending invoice price is the whole cost. Gross merchandise margin and final operating profit
 remain separate; wages, rent/property burden, heat/light, losses, bad debt and other expenses come afterward.
 Historical evidence supports wide variation by product and location, so exact category defaults and blended period
 margins remain a research/calibration hold rather than a universal canon percentage.

 7.1C Replenishment policy, cash reserves, and seasonal profiles

 Routine replenishment should normally run automatically under standing policy rather than require a purchase click for
 every sale. The managing authority can set target stock, reorder point or equivalent days-of-supply logic, preferred and
 backup suppliers, order quantity, emergency/rush tolerance and manual overrides. Each business can protect a
 cash-reserve threshold. While business cash remains above the reserve, approved routine reorders may execute
 automatically; if a purchase would push cash below the reserve or the business is already below it, the system can
 require manual approval and notify the current managing authority. This creates real judgment: a rigid manager can
 protect cash while allowing flour to stock out, while an aggressive manager can preserve availability and leave the




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 29

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 266/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 business unable to meet payroll. Inventory policy should support seasonal profiles. A simple Same All Year option keeps
 one policy; turning it off allows spring, summer, fall and winter overrides for stock targets, reorder behavior, allocation
 and whether a line is stocked at all. Firewood or heavy blankets may become important in winter and unnecessary in
 summer; seed or other seasonal goods can move in the opposite direction. Seasonal reallocation remains a deliberate
 administrative decision rather than an automatic demand bonus.

7.1D Store administration, operating hours, and manager delegation

 The General Store is a principal test case for Business Decision Authority. The managing authority can choose
 assortment, display/storage allocation, markup and pricing posture, suppliers, reorder rules, cash reserve, customer
 credit, special-order policy, delivery policy, operating hours and ordinary staffing. NPC owners use these same controls
 and can make poor decisions. Later managers can receive broad routine authority within owner-set limits, including
 hiring replacement clerks, changing allocation, responding to fast- or slow-selling merchandise, adjusting reorders and
 handling ordinary credit. A stock clerk can refill the rifle rack; only the owner or delegated manager decides that the
 rifle rack should shrink so workwear can expand.

 7.2 Blacksmith

 The Blacksmith covers repair triage, shoes, plow points, wagon parts, hinges, chains, and practical fix work. It has
 emergency repairs, interrupt-driven workflow, medium-high injury risk, and strong spring and fall pressure. Continuity
 remains highly skill-dependent. Without a real journeyman or equivalent smith, normal operation should collapse
 quickly even if the parcel and tools remain.

 7.3 Butcher

 The Butcher handles fresh and preserved meat conversion with spoilage risk and sourcing pressure. It lives on
 perishables, summer spoilage, winter storage advantage, knife injury, and livestock sourcing. It can weaken into a
 narrower provision-counter form when processing skill or supply continuity breaks rather than always failing in one
 step.

7.3A Livestock, carcass and dressed-meat sourcing

 A butcher should be able to operate through more than one sourcing posture. Where local conditions justify it, the
 business can buy live animals and carry the slaughter/processing burden itself, buy carcasses or quarters from another
 slaughtering source, or supplement local supply with preserved or dressed meat brought through wider trade. Those
 choices move costs and risks rather than erasing them. Live-animal purchasing requires holding space, handling labor,
 slaughter capacity and waste management but gives more control over timing and byproducts. Dressed-meat
 purchasing reduces those burdens while increasing dependence on supplier reliability, freight and preservation. A
 frontier butcher tied to an owned ranch can have unusually strong supply security, but the ranch's herd, winter losses
 and sale timing remain real constraints.

 7.3B Whole-carcass economics and product balance

 The butcher cannot turn one animal into only the most profitable cuts. A carcass produces a mixed set of saleable
 meat, fat, bones, hide and other material, with exact detail abstracted to economically meaningful product groups.
 Demand for those groups need not match the physical yield. A strong household market may absorb common fresh
 cuts while a boarding house, mine camp or restaurant can absorb stew meat and larger repeat orders. Slow-moving
 product creates markdown, preservation, wholesale, byproduct or spoilage pressure. The core owner decision is
 therefore not just 'how many cattle to buy' but how much carcass throughput the local customer mix can actually
 absorb before value is lost.

 7.3C Fresh, preserved and seasonal product strategy

 Fresh meat is the highest-turnover local line but is exposed to temperature, delivery timing and uncertain daily
 demand. Salted, cured, smoked or otherwise preserved products can extend sale life where the shop has the required
 skill, time, equipment and inputs. Ice and cold-storage access can materially widen the useful selling window without
 creating modern refrigeration. Winter can reduce spoilage pressure while increasing other supply and travel risks;
 summer can make ice, rapid turnover and disciplined buying much more important. The player can therefore run a
 high-turnover fresh shop, a more preservation-heavy provision business or a mixed operation according to local
 demand and capability.

7.3D Capacity, labor and operating flow

 Butcher capacity should come from distinct but connected work: animal receiving or carcass receiving, slaughter where
 performed, cutting, preservation, cleaning, display/sales and delivery. A skilled butcher is not interchangeable with





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 30

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 267/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 every helper. Assistants can move stock, clean, wrap, deliver and support preparation, but loss of the skilled processing
 role can sharply narrow what the business can do. The business can become backlogged after a large livestock
 purchase, a Saturday demand spike, a mine or hotel contract, or worker absence. Excess throughput can be as bad as
 too little because unfinished or unsold perishable product deteriorates.

 7.3E Wholesale accounts, delivery and cross-business demand

 Household counter sales should not be the only market. Boarding houses, hotels, restaurants, mine camps, logging
 camps, stores and other repeat buyers can create account or supply-agreement demand where the local economy
 supports it. Large recurring buyers improve throughput visibility but can concentrate customer risk and reserve stock
 that might otherwise serve walk-in households. Delivery can be offered when labor and transport exist, creating a
 service advantage at a real operating cost. The player can choose whether scarce supply protects contract customers,
 household trade, internal portfolio buyers or the highest-margin outlet.

 7.3F Byproducts, nuisance, sanitation and continuity

 Hides and tallow remain the principal byproduct categories worth carrying at normal simulation depth. Bones, blood
 and other residues should enter only where a real buyer or disposal problem makes them economically meaningful.
 Slaughtering and meat handling also create odor, waste, water, cleaning and pest pressure. If slaughter occurs on-site,
 those burdens affect site suitability and neighbors; buying dressed carcasses shifts much of that burden upstream.
 Good cleaning and waste removal protect continuity through actual labor and service, not a hygiene buff. Fire,
 equipment failure, ice shortage, livestock shortage, skilled-worker loss or a bad spoilage run can each weaken the
 business through a different causal path. Acquisition diligence should therefore ask not only whether the shop has
 customers, but what part of its supply, skill, cold-storage and account base the buyer is actually inheriting.

 7.4 Crop Farm and Ranch

 Crop Farm and Ranch remain distinct because western South Dakota is not one uniform agricultural surface. Ranching
 and grazing form the broader West River baseline, while crop farming concentrates in suitable valleys, watered ground
 and irrigable sites. Hay and forage are strategic commodities because winter survival, work animals and livestock
 carrying capacity depend on them. Spring 1880 is already a horse-machine agricultural economy. Manufactured prairie
 plows, mowers, reapers, threshing machinery, emerging grain binders, barbed wire and mechanical pumping windmills
 are period-valid. The player does not research these inventions. Adoption depends on acreage, capital, draft animals,
 labor, repair access, freight and whether a machine can be used enough to justify ownership. Agricultural machinery
 changes seasonal work capacity rather than biological yield. Soil, water, seed, weather and crop condition determine
 potential production; plowing, planting, haying, harvest and threshing capacities determine how much can be
 completed before seasonal windows close. Expensive seasonal equipment can be owned, shared, borrowed or hired
 through custom work, creating a real ownership-versus-utilization decision. Ranch technology is primarily about control.
 Fencing is spatial infrastructure that can protect crops, divide pasture, control stock and reduce some herding burden
 but requires wire, posts, labor, gates and repairs. Windmills and wells expand watered range rather than applying a
 generic livestock bonus. Hay storage, sheltering terrain, herd condition and grazing pressure determine winter
 resilience. The winter of 1886-87 is an important historical stress test, not a scripted loss percentage. Overstocking,
 degraded range, poor autumn condition, insufficient hay and severe weather interact to determine mortality.
 Better-prepared ranches can fare substantially better than

 highly exposed open-range operations. Rail changes agriculture through both market access and capital-goods access:
 livestock can reach distant packers, grain can aggregate at elevators where production supports them, and machinery,
 wire and replacement parts become cheaper to obtain. Wagons remain the local feeder system. Horse power remains
 the normal motive force through 1905; steam is specialized and gasoline tractors remain rare cutting-edge technology
 outside the core progression.

 7.5 Business agency standard across industries

 The General Store depth model is a template for agency, not a requirement that every business use shelves. Each
 serious business should expose owner/manager decisions rooted in its real operation so that two otherwise similar
 businesses can perform differently because they are administered differently. A blacksmith can choose service mix,
 backlog priority, contract customers, materials reserve and apprenticeship; a boarding business can choose occupancy
 density, room/board package, meal quality, rates, customer mix and food sourcing; a butcher can choose
 livestock/carcass sourcing, product mix, ice/cold-storage use and household versus business customers; a freight
 company can choose routes, cargo, rates, scheduled versus charter work, team reserves and contracts; a sawmill can
 choose timber source, mill utilization, product mix, storage/drying and customer commitments; a ranch can choose
 stocking, herd composition, water, fencing, hay reserve, winter feeding and sale timing. NPC authorities receive the
 same choices. The design target is not more clicks but more consequential policy.

7.5A Playable Business Depth Gate

  CANON LOCK A business name is not enough to earn playable scope. Before a candidate business graduates from the
   future pool into an active

 player-operable system, the design should be able to answer most of the following in a grounded way: who buys from it
 and why; what physical inputs or information it needs; what labor and specialist capability constrain it; what property,
 capacity or location matters; what recurring owner policies change its behavior; how cash, credit and working capital
 constrain it; what assets can wear or fail; what bad operation looks like before total closure; how rivals or substitutes
 compete with it; how its economics change across season, settlement growth or modernization; and which existing
 systems it feeds or depends upon. Not every business needs equal page count or equal UI, but a player business should
 have more than a unique revenue formula. If the answers are weak, keep the activity background-only, merge it into a
 broader service family or leave it parked until research justifies depth.

 8.1 Boarding and settlement infrastructure

 Boarding House or Hotel is a major settlement and labor-market bridge and remains an active VP expansion target.
 Boarding lets the town absorb single workers, temporary labor, and recent migrants before or instead of household
 ownership, while rental houses and rooms support longer-term family settlement. Housing capacity therefore affects
 the effective labor supply: a worker available somewhere in the region cannot become stable local labor if there is no
 practical place to live. Employer bunks, meals, and lodging can also form part of compensation. Boarding is
 consequently both a daily operating business and productive settlement infrastructure. The 1880 census itself
 distinguished boarders, hotel inmates and hotel cooks/waiters inside real shared-roof/shared-table arrangements, while
 Black Hills evidence includes boarding operations serving mine labor and proprietors who moved between cook,
 boarding-house and hotel roles.

8.1A Accommodation products and physical capacity

 A boarding operation sells use of real accommodation rather than a generic occupancy percentage. Depending on the
 building, it can offer beds in shared rooms, private rooms, room-and-board packages, longer-stay boarding, short
 transient lodging and, where physically suitable, family rooms. The proprietor's own household can occupy part of the
 same building without becoming identical to the boarders. Capacity is bounded by usable sleeping space, beds,
 sanitation, water, heating, fire exposure and meal service. Crowding above a comfortable level may be physically
 possible, especially during a boom, but it increases workload, complaint, fire, illness and turnover pressure instead of
 being blocked by an arbitrary cap.

 8.1B Board, meals and the second capacity bottleneck

 'Board' should matter. A house that includes meals operates both accommodation and food service, creating demand
 for meat, flour, vegetables, coffee, fuel, water, kitchen labor and storage. Bed capacity and meal capacity are separate.
 A proprietor may have empty beds but no practical kitchen capacity to add full-board customers, or a strong kitchen
 may feed nonresident diners when local custom supports it. Menu detail should remain abstracted to meal quality, food
 cost, supply reliability and labor burden rather than becoming a cooking game. Supply agreements with butchers,
 stores, farms or owned businesses can stabilize service through real procurement.

 8.1C Customer mix, stay length and demand pulses

 The customer mix should follow the settlement's reason for existing. A freight stop can receive teamsters and
 short-stay travelers; a mine or railway construction surge can create concentrated single-worker demand; a growing
 town can support clerks, tradesmen and new arrivals who board for weeks or months before renting; a hotel in a
 mature node can draw commercial travelers and higher-paying transient guests. Different customers value rate, meal
 quality, privacy, proximity to work, stable terms and service differently. Major construction, mine expansion, railroad
 surveys or seasonal work can produce arrival pulses that temporarily make every bed valuable, followed by sharp
 vacancy if the project ends.

8.1D Rate, package and occupancy policy

 The owner can set room-only versus room-and-board pricing where the establishment supports both, weekly or
 longer-stay terms, transient rates, meal quality, target customer mix, credit/account tolerance and reservation of rooms
 for expected contract or commercial customers. A low-price crowded house can earn strong short-run revenue while
 creating more wear and service pressure. A higher-price quieter house can preserve capacity but may sit partly empty
 in a weak market. The game should not assign one universally optimal occupancy rate; the right posture depends on
 local demand, labor, food cost, property quality and the owner's strategy.
