 8.1E Labor, household work and proprietor dependence

 Boarding houses are labor businesses. Cooking, cleaning, laundry, bed turnover, heating, water hauling, receiving
 supplies, serving meals, bookkeeping and guest handling all consume work. Small houses can rely heavily on proprietor
 and family labor; larger hotels may need cooks, waiters, cleaners, clerks or other helpers. This creates a meaningful
 scale transition: adding rooms without adding service capacity can reduce quality and retention. Loss of a strong cook,
 housekeeper or proprietor can damage the establishment even when the building is undamaged. Women should be
 fully eligible as proprietors and managers; Black Hills evidence for Lucretia Marshbanks provides a direct regional
 example of a cook, mine boarding-house manager and hotel owner.

 8.1F Boarding as labor-market and project infrastructure

 A boarding house is economically productive because it converts regional or arriving workers into locally usable labor.
 Employers, mines or major projects can reserve or subsidize beds, operate their own lodging or rely on independent
 proprietors. A player who expands boarding ahead of a mine, rail or construction project can profit from the resulting
 labor surge if the project materializes; if it fails, the same rooms can become debt-heavy vacancy. The reverse also
 matters: a profitable mine may be unable to hire to plan because every acceptable bed is occupied. Housing pressure
 should therefore be able to make boarding expansion, employer lodging or permanent rental construction competing
 solutions to the same bottleneck.

8.1G Fire, sanitation, reputation and continuity

 Dense sleeping, stoves, kitchens, lamps, stairs and transient occupancy can make boarding establishments important
 fire and safety exposures. Water, privies, waste removal, cleaning and crowding affect operating quality through real
 property and labor conditions. Reputation should emerge from actual experiences such as clean rooms, reliable meals,
 honored terms, theft/security problems, repeated overcrowding or bad service rather than from a flat hotel-quality
 upgrade. A major fire, illness wave, food-supply failure or proprietor death can displace residents and simultaneously
 damage local labor supply, making boarding continuity a settlement issue rather than only a business-income issue.

 8.2 Lumber chain

 Small Sawmill and Lumber Yard are active near-term chain priorities because they connect construction supply,
 hauling, fuel byproducts, and remote production. Small mill is the entry production site with modest intake, one main
 processing line, limited storage, and stronger vulnerability to labor or hauling bottlenecks. Large mill is the upgraded
 form with higher intake, more workers, more yard pressure, higher maintenance and injury exposure, and a larger role
 in construction supply. Lumber Yard is the town-facing storage and retail arm, either independent or paired with an
 owned mill.

 8.3 Future pool and institutional anchors

 The broader future pool remains Doctor's Office or Town Doctor, Livery or Freight Office, Grain Mill, Saloon, Tailor or Dry
 Goods, Bakery, Bank, Barber, Wheelwright or Repair Shop, Telegraph Office or communication-linked service,
 Telephone Company or private/exchange communications service, Water Company where private utility conditions
 justify it, Electric Light or Light & Power Company, and later luxury or investment-linked businesses that make sense
 once town prosperity becomes visible. Historical availability does not equal implementation priority: telephone and
 water enterprise can be period-valid early while still remaining post-VP systems. Towns can also gain seriousness
 through institutional anchors such as schools, courthouses, depot offices, hospitals, military or federal presence. These
 are not VP-core requirements, but they are valid later-phase growth multipliers. Doctor service remains active early as
 a grounded town service. The player does not begin with a doctor business. The doctor's office can be acquired later as
 a service business. It remains a small service business, not a hospital simulation, and matters because treatment
 access reduces labor loss, treatment delay, and medical burden across the town and later across the portfolio.

 8.3B Future-pool width discipline

 The future pool is a research and opportunity map, not a promise that every named enterprise receives its own shallow
 management screen. A bakery, saloon, barber, tailor, grain mill, telephone company, water company or prestige
 business should become directly playable only when it passes the Playable Business Depth Gate in 7.5A or when its
 ownership creates a genuinely new strategic relationship. Otherwise it can remain a simulated NPC service, a
 component of another business family or a parked candidate. Revision XIV explicitly prefers six deep businesses over
 twelve businesses that differ mainly in icon, recipe and revenue rate.

8.3A Secondary settlement services and remote civic emergence

 The broader service pool should no longer be read only through the lens of the starting town. Remote nodes that cross
 enough population, boarding, freight, and permanence thresholds should be able to support their own local store,




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 33

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 270/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 butcher, blacksmith support, doctor outpost, schoolhouse, freight office, or other practical services. The exact
 combination should depend on why the node exists. A mine settlement, a farm-service hamlet, and a freight-side
 crossroads should not all evolve the same way even if they briefly sit in similar population bands. Institutional anchors
 matter here as well. Schooling, formal platting, civic office, a church meeting hall, a freight yard office, or a small town
 hall should emerge from local pressure and usefulness rather than as arbitrary unlocks. These responses should be
 softened by randomized trigger windows so that settlement life feels discovered and negotiated rather than gamified
 into exact breakpoints.

 8.4 Byproduct markets

 Keep byproducts practical rather than overbuilt. The important VP forms remain butcher hides and tallow plus sawmill
 slabs and offcuts as fuel wood or low-grade sale output. Later deepening of bark, sawdust, blood, bones, or other
 residues should happen only where it materially improves the economy rather than bloating the tree.

 8.5 Logging, timber, sawmills, and lumber-chain additions

 Logging and sawmills form a practical supply-chain layer rather than a decorative business type. Construction, repairs,
 mines, rail, storage, housing and industrial expansion depend on lumber, beams, boards and related byproducts.
 Timber extraction uses stand/worksite logic where supported, with terrain, vegetation, road access, hauling distance,
 season, daylight, weather and local timber quality affecting viability. Logging labor is outdoor work whose practical day
 can be limited by usable light, travel, physical conditions and available timber rather than a universal shift. Sawmills
 remain shared-shell businesses with log supply, power source, saw capacity, lumber output, yard or pond storage,
 green-lumber handling/drying, machinery condition, labor, maintenance and hauling strain. Mining progression
 increases the strategic value of timber, and large expansion can create real logging, hauling and sawmill booms rather
 than a flat lumber-demand modifier.

8.5A Sawmill power, water sites, log handling, and bottlenecks

 Sawmill configuration should follow period technology and site economics rather than a linear Water -> Steam ->
 Electric upgrade ladder. Water-powered mills are historically valid where a site provides adequate flow and head and
 may require a dam or impoundment, mill pond, headrace/millrace, wheel or turbine arrangement and tailrace. Mill or
 log ponds can also hold raw logs before sawing. Steam-powered mills are already plausible at the 1880 opening in the
 Black Hills and can be portable or more fixed; they trade water-power geography for boiler, engine, fuel, water,
 maintenance, skilled operation and machinery-logistics requirements. Black Hills-specific prevalence and exact mill
 forms remain subject to targeted research before generation weights are locked. The causal chain should distinguish
 standing timber -> felling -> extraction/skidding/hauling -> log landing or pond -> mill intake -> power availability ->
 sawing -> green lumber handling -> stacking/drying -> finished inventory -> outbound freight. Felling, extraction, mill
 throughput, power, handling, drying/storage and outbound transport can each become the active bottleneck. Improving
 the saw does not create logs, and hiring more loggers does not help if the yard or mill cannot absorb their output. This
 is contained systemic depth: it reuses labor, transport, storage, property, time and machinery rather than creating a
 detached mill minigame.

 8.6 Commercial, cold-storage, and office technology progression

 Commercial modernization is gradual and should reinforce ownership problems rather than become a gadget tree. The
 1880 General Store remains strongly ledger-, barrel-, sack- and crate-oriented while manufactured packaged goods
 already exist. Branded boxes, tins and standardized packaging become increasingly visible during the 1890s and early
 1900s as rail distribution and national brands deepen. Natural ice harvesting, icehouses and iceboxes remain the
 normal local cold-storage system. Refrigerated railcars exist in the wider world before local Black Hills rail and later
 expand the practical market reach of perishables where the railway and icing network support them. Mechanical
 refrigeration remains capital-heavy and exceptional before 1905. Mail-order competition becomes a serious
 late-campaign pressure, especially in the 1890s. Catalog merchants compete strongly for standardized manufactured
 goods when mail, express and rail can deliver them, but the local store retains immediate availability, small quantities,
 emergency supply, local exchange and household credit. Cash registers exist at the opening edge of commercial
 technology but are not normal for a tiny frontier store. They become increasingly useful in larger late-1880s and 1890s
 businesses because they improve employee cash accountability and reconciliation rather than demand. Typewriters
 similarly exist before the campaign but become increasingly common in banks, railway offices, mines, utilities and
 major commercial offices as administrative scale grows.

 21.1 Mine placement, districts, and opening chronology

 Mines are remote industrial businesses tied to mineral districts, claims, processing and freight rather than magic
 resource nodes. The spring 1880 region is already industrializing: placer mining remains possible and small prospects
 exist, but substantial hard-rock mining and large stamp mills are already operating in the northern Black Hills. Mining is




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 34

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 271/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 therefore historically present immediately even though ownership of a serious mine remains a capital-heavy later
 player path. District generation should care about deposit family, geological confidence, access difficulty, extraction
 style, metallurgical character, treatment requirements, freight burden and boom potential. Claim logic comes first;
 settlement consequences follow. Mine camps can grow into nodes when labor, boarding, freight and services
 concentrate, and can later decline or convert if the deposit or economics weaken.

 21.2 Mine identities and metallurgy

 Gold remains the dominant Black Hills mining identity. Lead-silver and other polymetallic deposits are secondary and
 localized, with distinct smelter and treatment economics. Tin is speculative and should emphasize the difference
 between promotional samples, representative bulk grade and actual mill recovery. Coal is strategically important as
 fuel but often regional/imported or geology-conditional. Iron is niche and does not create a local integrated rail-steel
 economy. Ore grade alone is insufficient. A meaningful deposit also has metallurgical character and treatment
 compatibility. Free-milling gold may support stamp crushing and amalgamation, while refractory or sulphide-bearing
 material can require custom treatment, smelting, chlorination, cyanidation or other appropriate routes. Ore mined is
 not identical to recovered metal. The system should distinguish geological mineralization, physically mineable material,
 treatable material and economic ore. Technology and freight can lower the economic cutoff without changing the
 geology, allowing old stockpiles, dumps, tailings or marginal sections to acquire value later.

 21.3 Functional bottlenecks and development

 Mining technology removes actual constraints rather than granting mine levels. Important capacities include geological
 confidence, development rate, drilling/blasting, ground support, internal haulage, hoisting, water control, crushing,
 treatment, power, freight and technical labor. Improving one can expose another: pneumatic drilling can create more
 broken rock than the hoist or mill can handle; a larger

 hoist can expose treatment capacity; a larger mill can expose fuel, water, timber or freight limitations. Stamp milling,
 amalgamation for suitable ore, steam machinery, blasting, timbering, mine cars and serious powered hoisting are
 already available at major operations near the opening. Heavy machinery can be purchased before local rail by sending
 it to a distant railhead and hauling it overland at high cost and delay. Rail improves delivered cost, replacement parts,
 fuel and bulk shipping rather than unlocking industrial machinery. Mine water is site- specific. Hydrology, season and
 workings determine inflow; pumping becomes necessary where drainage or existing capacity is insufficient. Timber
 demand likewise derives from geology, opening geometry and support needs rather than a universal per-ton rule.

 21.4 Technology chronology, 1880-1905

 Hand hammer-and-drill work remains credible at important operations well into the early 1890s. Compressed-air drilling
 and compressor plants become increasingly significant during the 1890s and mature toward 1900-05, raising
 development capacity while creating new power, maintenance and skill dependencies. Electricity enters mining first on
 a limited scale, especially lighting. Homestake's 1888 dynamo is a useful regional anchor. Steam, water and mechanical
 drives remain important for years; broader electric motive power becomes increasingly plausible near the turn of the
 century but does not replace steam universally by 1905. Gold treatment overlaps rather than advancing in one switch.
 Stamp/amalgamation is opening-era technology for suitable ore. Black Hills chlorination becomes significant around
 1889; specialized matte smelting expands around 1890; an early Deadwood cyanide plant exists in 1892 but is
 intermittent; cyanidation becomes increasingly successful and widespread in the late 1890s and early 1900s.
 Availability, ore character, expertise, plant economics and reliability determine adoption. The Homestake interests also
 demonstrate that a private industrial narrow-gauge railway can become rational around 1881-82 when a company
 needs to connect mine openings, mills and timber supply before common-carrier rail reaches the region. Internal mine
 track, industrial railway and regional common-carrier rail remain three separate transport scales.

 21.5 Labor, safety, and professionalization

 Mines are labor-hungry and increasingly specialized. Early operations can rely on miners, laborers, teamsters,
 blacksmith/repair support, bosses and assayers; larger operations add hoist operators, millmen, boiler operators,
 machinists, timber crews and superintendents; later sophisticated plants may require engineers, metallurgists,
 compressor personnel and electricians. Regional mining education and technical professionalization deepen during the
 1880s and 1890s without creating a player research tree. Safety is causal. Ground failure, blasting, hoisting, machinery,
 fire and water hazards arise from geology, equipment condition, maintenance, explosives handling, support,
 supervision, fatigue and site conditions rather than one universal annual accident percentage. The game should
 represent the ownership consequence without becoming a mine-engineering simulator.

 21.6 Mining company and portfolio operation





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 35

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 272/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 Each mine remains an owned operating business inside the shared business model, with operating information for
 deposit family, claim/development state, accessible workings, metallurgical character, output, stockpiles, workers,
 foreman or superintendent, support/timber, power, hauling, road/rail access, treatment route, condition and
 shutdown/hold/expand/sell decisions. A portfolio mining overview can summarize output, shortages, hauling, claims,
 debt, investors, technical coverage and risk without merging every site into one hive mind. Starting a mine uses a
 staged path: district information or rumor -> prospecting/claim control -> assay and representative sampling ->
 feasibility -> financing/investor structure -> initial works -> production -> expansion. A mine may own its mill, use a
 custom mill, ship selected ore to a smelter, stockpile difficult material or later build specialized treatment. Vertical
 integration reduces real procurement and coordination burdens only where the player actually controls those inputs; it
 also transfers those operating risks into the portfolio.

7.2A Repair, Fabrication & Technical Services - shared economic system

 The Blacksmith remains a core opening-era craft business, but Revision XI broadens the design from one shop type into
 a shared Repair, Fabrication & Technical Services economy. Actual maintainable assets generate work orders; shops
 satisfy that demand according to their people, tools, facilities, materials and capabilities. The design should not force
 historically overlapping crafts into artificial hard classes. Blacksmithing, horseshoeing, wagon repair, wheelwright work,
 harness work and later machine-shop repair can be combined or specialized according to settlement scale and market
 demand. Direct Black Hills evidence supports this width before the campaign even begins: an 1878 Deadwood business
 directory lists multiple blacksmith/repair shops, blacksmith-and-wagon-repair businesses, a wagon maker and
 saddle/harness makers. A tiny 55-95-person opening node may still have only one flexible craftsperson or no resident
 specialist; a larger mining/commercial node can support several competing specialists.

 7.2B Capabilities rather than rigid shop classes

  • Smithing capability requires a forge, appropriate tools/material and a qualified smith; it supports iron hardware,
    practical fabrication, tool/implement repair and other compatible work.

  • Horseshoeing/farrier capability requires the relevant skill, tools and animal-handling setup; the work is recurring
   because the horse- powered economy physically uses shoes and hooves.

  • Wagon/wheel capability requires woodworking/wheel skills, workspace and appropriate components; iron-tire work
   may overlap with the smith.

  • Harness/tack capability requires leatherworking skill, workbench/tools, leather and hardware; harness is a real
    transport asset rather than invisible equipment.

  • Machine-work capability becomes increasingly important as mines, mills, utilities and rail create demands beyond the
    traditional smithy; powered tools, machinists and larger facilities can emerge without a Blacksmith Level upgrade
    ladder.

 7.2C Repair work orders and Physical Truth

 Each meaningful repair is represented as a work order with customer, asset/component, reported problem,
 actual/diagnosed problem, urgency, required capability, materials, location, queue position, estimated labor and agreed
 price/terms. The job resolves only when the asset or repairperson reaches the correct location, the materials/tools are
 available and the labor is actually performed.

  • A horse being shod physically visits the smith/farrier and is temporarily unavailable for work.

  • A wagon with ordinary damage travels to a shop; a wagon immobilized miles away may require temporary field repair
    or a repairperson/tools to travel to it.

  • Large fixed machinery can be repaired on site, or a component can be removed and hauled to a capable shop. The
   game should not teleport a broken pump or axle to town.

7.2D Diagnosis, queue, urgency and pricing freedom

 Customers can report symptoms without knowing the defect. Diagnosis can reveal additional work and convert a rough
 estimate into a proper quote. Shop capacity is therefore a queue of real jobs competing for skilled labor, workstations,
 material and time. Routine shoeing, plow work and fabrication can be interrupted by a freight wagon or mine
 component whose downtime is economically urgent. The managing authority may set any price the market can
 plausibly accept. If an ordinary job commonly sells for $2, the player may ask $8; a desperate monopoly customer may
 pay, ordinary customers may wait or travel elsewhere and sustained exploitation can create a profitable opening for a
 competitor. Price limits should come from contracts, law where relevant and customer alternatives, not designer caps.

 7.2E Accounts, recurring contracts and reserved capacity





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 36

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 273/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 Repair trades can use the shared commercial-credit system. Farms, ranches, freight companies and mines may hold
 running accounts where historically appropriate rather than paying cash for every shoeing or small repair. Larger
 customers can negotiate recurring service: priority repair, reserved capacity, agreed pricing or regular fleet/animal
 work. Guaranteed demand can stabilize shop income but reserving capacity for one major client can increase waiting
 time for everyone else.

 7.2F Materials, parts, fabrication, refurbishment and salvage

 Repair shops hold real materials and parts: forge fuel, metal stock, common hardware, wagon components, shoeing
 supplies, leather/harness inputs where supported and increasingly manufacturer replacement parts as machinery
 standardizes. A shop can choose to carry expensive slow-moving parts because emergency local availability is valuable;
 obsolete parts can become dead inventory.

  • Repair restores an existing asset; fabrication creates a needed component; replacement installs a purchased new
   component; temporary repair restores limited function; refurbishment combines multiple repairs to restore a used
    asset for continued use or resale.

  • A shop may buy broken or worn wagons/equipment, repair them and resell them, or dismantle uneconomic assets for
    parts/scrap. Used-equipment commerce therefore grows naturally out of the maintenance and repair systems.

7.2G Skill formation, apprenticeship and competitive labor

 Craft continuity depends heavily on real people. Apprentices/helpers can initially perform support and simple
 compatible work, then gain capability through actual experience where historically calibrated. Exact apprenticeship
 terms, years and titles remain a research hold. A highly skilled employee can demand higher compensation, leave, be
 poached or eventually open a competing shop if capital/property become available. Buying a craft shop does not
 automatically buy the craftsperson. Diligence should ask whether the smith, wheelwright or machinist will remain after
 sale. Customer relationships may partly follow the individual whose skill created them, making key-worker retention
 strategically important.

7.2H Repair-market evolution, 1880-1905

 The opening economy can rely heavily on flexible hand craftspeople. As standardized farm machinery, steam
 equipment, mines, mills, rail and utilities expand, more work shifts toward diagnosis, manufacturer parts, heavier repair
 and machine-shop capability. The traditional smith does not disappear by 1905 because horses, wagons and practical
 fabrication remain essential; the mix of work changes. A large mine or mill can internalize blacksmith/machinist
 capacity as a maintenance department while smaller operators continue to buy service externally.

7.4A Rural Production Economy - square-off doctrine

 Crop Farm and Ranch remain the two core rural production businesses, but Revision XI broadens them into a Rural
 Production Economy. Agriculture should have comparable width and depth to mining without turning the game into a
 manual farming simulator. The player decides land use, herd/field strategy, seasonal priorities, capital equipment,
 hiring, storage, contracts, sales and risk posture; workers and animals physically perform the work. Farm and ranch
 identity emerges from land, water, biological production, market access and owner decisions rather than from one
 generic rural-business template.

 7.4B Ten rural participation lanes

  • Crop farming: produce marketable crops through land suitability, biological growth and successful completion of
    seasonal work windows.

  • Hay/forage production: convert summer land and seasonal labor into feed that supports the horse/livestock economy
   and winter reserves.

  • Cattle ranching: manage herd composition, forage, water, winter preparation, sales and biological growth.

  • Sheep ranching: retain only if research and mechanics give it genuinely distinct output, labor, market and
   management characteristics rather than reskinned cattle.

  • Local/market produce: supply nearby households, stores, lodging and service businesses through proximity and
    perishability.

  • Custom agricultural work: own seasonal machinery/capacity and sell work to other farms when the player is not using
      it.

  • Livestock commerce: buy, assemble, hold and move livestock for resale without necessarily owning the breeding
    operation.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 37

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 274/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



  • Agricultural supply: sell seed, wire, machinery, parts, tools and other historically supported inputs through existing
   merchant businesses or specialized operations where demand supports them.

  • Processing/storage: mill, aggregate, store or otherwise handle agricultural output where the local production volume
   and historical business form justify it.

  • Rural property/infrastructure: own productive land, water improvements, pasture, storage or supporting assets and
     profit from their real usefulness; leasing/use-right variants remain a targeted research hold.

 7.4C Field authority and crop operating cycle

 Cultivated land should be represented by meaningful field/parcel production state rather than a farm-wide output
 meter. A field or field group knows area, suitability/soil, moisture/water state, current crop/use, current seasonal
 operation, work progress, crop condition, access and ownership. The engine can use detailed values internally while the
 owner receives practical agricultural reports. Crop production separates biological potential from work completion. Soil,
 water, seed, weather and crop condition determine what the land could produce; plowing/ground preparation, planting,
 cultivation where supported, harvest, threshing/processing and hauling capacity determine how much of that potential
 is actually realized before the relevant windows close. A machine does not create yield; it lets the farm complete more
 work in time.

7.4D Seasonal capacity and priority

 Seasonal jobs compete for workers, horses and machines. If 80 acres are ready but the current crew/equipment can
 harvest only 12 acres per day, rain, illness or a breakdown can make field priority consequential. The managing
 authority can choose which acreage is worked first according to value, vulnerability, access or owner judgment. Missed
 work reduces realized production through the crop/field state rather than a Farm Efficiency percentage.

 7.4E Machinery ownership, hire and custom work

 Expensive seasonal machinery creates a utilization problem. Ownership provides schedule control but ties up capital,
 storage, maintenance, horses and repair capacity. Hiring custom work avoids fixed ownership cost but exposes the
 farm to contractor queues and weather-driven

 schedule shifts. An owner with excess machine capacity can sell custom service to neighbors, converting an underused
 capital asset into a seasonal business. The schedule itself becomes valuable. A contractor can book several farms; rain
 or breakdown at the first job propagates delay to later clients. Urgency rises as seasonal windows close. Exact period
 Black Hills custom-work practices and pricing remain a research/calibration question, but the ownership-versus-hire and
 utilization logic is canonical.

 7.4F Hay and forage as first-class strategic commodities

 Hay/forage is not merely another crop. It links summer land productivity to winter survival of horses and livestock. A
 ranch can produce its own hay, buy from nearby producers, maintain recurring agreements or enter the spot market
 during shortage. Self-sufficiency uses more land, machinery and seasonal labor; purchased feed frees land/capital but
 increases market and supplier exposure. Hay production should include enough physical stages to make timing
 meaningful - standing forage, cutting, drying/curing, collection/stacking or period-appropriate storage and movement -
 without requiring manual farming actions. Weather during the process can matter differently from weather during
 growth. Exact equipment and storage practices remain crop/period research items.

7.4G Herd structure and biological capital

 Ranch livestock should not collapse into one Cattle count. Use cohorts or economic groups appropriate to the supported
 species: breeding animals, young stock, market animals and other meaningful categories. Exact cohort definitions and
 reproductive timing require historical livestock research, but the principle is that animals can be both productive
 biological capital and saleable assets. Breeding is therefore a retention/allocation decision rather than a reproduction
 buff. A cash-starved ranch may sell breeding-quality animals to raise money today and weaken future herd growth. A
 better-capitalized operation may retain them. Biological growth, deaths, purchases and sales change the herd over
 time.

7.4H Range, water and carrying capacity

 Rural land value and usable livestock capacity depend on forage, water, terrain, access, season, weather and prior
 grazing pressure rather than acreage alone. A large tract with poor practical water access can be less useful than a
 smaller watered property. Wells, pumps and windmills expand usable range because they create actual water access;
 they do not grant a generic livestock bonus. Overstocking should be allowed. Excess grazing pressure reduces actual
 forage condition, which can weaken animal condition, winter resilience and future pasture availability. A distressed





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 38

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 275/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 rancher may knowingly maintain too many animals because an immediate sale is financially painful. The game allows
 the gamble and follows the land/animal consequences.

 7.4I Fencing and spatial ranch control

 Fencing remains physical infrastructure with gates, boundaries and maintenance. It can protect cultivated land,
 partition pasture, control stock and reduce certain labor burdens. The player chooses which boundaries justify capital.
 Broken or neglected sections create actual control problems rather than a flat ranch penalty. Barbed wire is
 opening-era available technology, but adoption remains property- and capital-dependent.

 7.4J Winter preparation and the 1886-87 stress test

 Winter preparation should become one of the most consequential recurring rural decisions. Before winter, the ranch can
 evaluate herd size, animal condition, stored hay, remaining pasture/forage, water reliability, sheltering terrain and
 forecast uncertainty. Expertise and records can improve the feed/resilience estimate, but future winter severity remains
 unknown. The owner can buy feed, sell animals, reduce exposure or gamble. Severe winter consumes reserves and
 changes animal condition over time; it does not apply a scripted mortality percentage. The 1886-87 winter remains a
 historical stress test in which poorly prepared, overstocked operations can suffer far more than well-prepared ones.

7.4K Livestock sales, holding and physical market movement

 Livestock sale is a capital-allocation decision. Market-ready animals can generate cash; selling breeding stock may
 damage future production; holding animals keeps potential upside but continues feed/water/land burden. Animals sold
 remain physical animals requiring appropriate movement to buyers, aggregation points or later rail interfaces. Rail
 changes feasible market reach and transport economics rather than magically raising livestock value.

 7.4L Agricultural storage and sale timing

 Harvested crops, feed and other outputs require commodity-appropriate storage rather than entering a global inventory
 pool. Storage capacity and condition determine whether the producer can hold output, protect it and wait for a later
 market. A bumper harvest can create a storage/freight problem and weak harvest-time prices; selling immediately may
 be necessary for debt/cash even if the owner expects better prices later.

7.4M Rural credit and seasonal cash flow

 Agriculture should be one of the strongest demonstrations of irregular cash timing. Seed, wire, feed, repairs, wages and
 machinery needs can occur before crop/livestock proceeds. Merchants and lenders can extend appropriate credit based
 on the real operation. A failed harvest or weak livestock sale can then propagate into overdue merchant accounts,
 rent/mortgage pressure, lender distress and reduced purchasing power.

7.4N Family labor, hired surges and workload

 Family farms/ranches can combine owner/household labor with hired permanent and seasonal workers. Family
 members are not free generic labor slots; age, household duties, health, schooling where relevant and other
 employment still matter. Seasonal work can create temporary demand spikes far above the normal workforce,
 generating migration, boarding and wage pressure in the overlapping labor market.

7.4O Repair, weather and settlement feedback

 Agriculture feeds the repair economy through wagons, harness, plows, mowers, pumps/windmills, fencing and other
 equipment. Repair pressure should become particularly visible before/during seasonal work windows, when a two-day
 delay can be far more expensive than the same repair in winter. Weather acts on the physical process it affects.
 Drought changes soil moisture, pasture growth, hay production and water pressure; rain can improve moisture while
 simultaneously delaying field work; hail or frost damages exposed crops; severe winter acts through forage, shelter and
 animal condition. Do not implement global Farm Output -30% events.

 7.4P Agricultural settlement identities and downstream businesses

 Rural production should shape settlement business mix without an Agricultural Town trait. Ranch-heavy hinterlands
 create demand for livestock service, hay, freight, repair, wire/hardware and lodging. Productive crop valleys can
 support storage, milling, seasonal labor, machinery/custom work and heavier freight. General Stores become
 agricultural suppliers through actual assortment. Grain-mill/storage and livestock-commerce business forms require
 targeted regional research before exact operational templates are locked.

7.4Q Rural land, leasing and water-right research holds

 Rural property value should derive from usable acreage, soil, water, forage, terrain, access, improvements, fencing,
 storage/buildings and market distance rather than a single Land Quality score. Acquisition diligence inherits pasture
 condition, hay reserves, equipment condition, water-system reliability and other operating baggage. The project should
 research Dakota/Black Hills agricultural leases, grazing leases, crop-tenancy/share arrangements, ditch/irrigation
 organization and water rights before adding detailed mechanics. These have high width potential but must not be
 invented from generic western assumptions.

7.4R Rural square completeness test

 Every serious rural enterprise should be able to answer ten depth questions: productive land/resource, biological state,
 seasonal timing, labor, draft/machinery, inputs, storage, maintenance, market/logistics and capital/authority. Across
 the width dimension, the current design pool is crop farming, hay/forage, cattle, sheep where distinct, local produce,
 custom work, livestock commerce, agricultural supply, processing/storage and rural property/infrastructure. This is a
 completeness matrix, not a requirement for one hundred exposed UI features.

 21.7 Mining Economic Ecosystem - square-off doctrine

 Mining remains one of the deepest physical systems in the canon, but Revision XI broadens it from primarily mine
 ownership into an economic ecosystem. Mineral discovery creates value and risk across claims, finance, technical
 information, treatment, trade, supplies, contracting, property and settlement. The player and NPCs may participate at
 any economically legitimate point without owning a producing mine. Vertical integration is an available strategy, not
 the assumed endpoint.

21.7A Ten mining participation lanes

  • Prospecting & Claim Development: finance discovery, control legitimate claims, improve geological information and
     sell, partner, hold or develop the property.

  • Mine Ownership & Operation: develop workings, extract material and manage the existing bottleneck-rich mine
    system.

  • Mining Investment & Promotion: provide risk capital through historically appropriate ownership/investor structures,
    taking partial upside without operating every mine.

  • Assay & Technical Services: sell credible analytical/technical information to prospectors, mines, investors, lenders and
    buyers.

  • Custom Milling & Treatment: own treatment capacity and process other mines' material for fees or negotiated
    arrangements.

  • Ore & Concentrate Commerce: buy physical mineral lots, assemble/route compatible material and bear
    working-capital, assay and market risk.

  • Mining Supply & Equipment Trade: serve the district through historically supported tools, consumables, parts, clothing,
   hardware and industrial supply, usually through flexible merchant identity rather than a Mining Store class.

  • Mining Contract Services: sell freight, timber, repair, construction and technical capability to mines through the same
    shared businesses used elsewhere.

  • Mine-Camp Property & Services: profit from housing, boarding, stores, freight yards and other settlement demand
    created by mining without owning the deposit.

  • Reprocessing, Salvage & Failed-Mine Redevelopment: acquire remaining value in claims, plant, dumps/tailings,
    machinery, roads, buildings, housing and other distressed industrial assets.

21.7B Exploration, development and production as separate capital uses

 A mineral property should distinguish exploration (learning what may exist), development (physically
 exposing/accessing and understanding the deposit while preparing production) and production (extracting currently
 economic material). A cash-starved owner may exploit known high-value material and postpone learning; a
 well-capitalized company may deliberately fund development ahead of immediate output. These decisions change
 information and physical access rather than adding a Research percentage.

21.7C Claim information history and valuation uncertainty

 Claims preserve evidence histories: discovery, surface work, trenching/development, assay reports, previous
 production, abandoned workings and prior-owner records where available. Mineral-property value can remain
 extremely uncertain because the future deposit is not fully known. Asking price can be exact while fair-value estimates
 remain wide. Better representative sampling and development narrow geological uncertainty; Expertise cannot reveal
 unobserved rock.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 40

21.7D Work fronts, geological confidence and operating allocation

 Operating mines can contain economically meaningful work areas or fronts rather than one mine-wide
 grade/confidence score. North Workings can be well understood and expensive to support while a deep extension
 remains uncertain and water-prone. Owner/superintendent allocation among fronts becomes a strategic decision
 without requiring the player to draw tunnels.

 21.7E Ore classes, stockpiles and economic cutoff

 Mine output should preserve enough classification to make treatment and future economics matter: high-value/special
 lots, normal mill feed, lower-grade stockpile, material requiring different treatment and waste where appropriate. The
 owner can stockpile material that is currently uneconomic rather than automatically discarding or processing it. Later
 freight, treatment or price changes can make old stockpiles, dumps and tailings valuable. Cutoff/selection decisions
 should affect what material is mined or processed under current economics, but exact geological implementation and
 period terminology require specialist research. Avoid a simplistic High Grade Mode bonus; the physical ore and mine
 plan should carry the consequence.

 21.7F Assay and technical-information business

 An assay office should be a real professional-service business where demand supports it. Samples are received,
 registered, queued, prepared/analyzed and reported. The key distinction is sampling quality versus analytical quality: a
 competent assayer can accurately test an unrepresentative hand-picked sample. Investors and mine owners therefore
 care both about who assayed the material and how the sample was obtained.

  • Assay capacity creates queues during booms; rush turnaround can be sold if the office has capacity.

  • Professional reputation affects how lenders, investors and buyers treat reports because credibility is the service being
    sold.

  • Large mines can internalize assay capability; small operators can purchase it externally. The same information system
    supports both.

21.7G Custom milling and treatment as independent industry

 The existing canon already allows a mine to use a custom mill. Revision XI makes the provider side fully playable. A
 custom mill has treatment compatibility, physical capacity, power, water, labor, maintenance, receiving/storage,
 customer queue and tailings handling. Its central financial problem is utilization: an oversized mill with insufficient ore
 feed can be a disastrous investment. Customer agreements can reserve capacity, establish price/fee structure and
 define priority subject to historical research on exact forms. When total customer demand exceeds mill capacity, the
 managing authority chooses how commitments, owned mines and spot work are prioritized. Treatment specialization
 means not every ore lot is economically suitable for every plant.

21.7H Mineral commerce and physical lots

 Ore/concentrate commerce remains a research-sensitive lane but is preserved because the economic role is powerful.
 Mineral lots are physical: source, weight, location, sampled/assayed characteristics, treatment compatibility, ownership
 and intended destination. A trader who buys material ties up working capital until it is hauled, treated or resold. Value
 depends on expected recovery minus treatment/freight and on confidence in the sample/assay. Aggregation can create
 value by combining economically compatible small lots into commercially useful shipments where historical practice
 supports it. Exact Black Hills ore-buying, settlement and sampling arrangements remain a targeted research hold rather
 than being invented from a corporation name alone.

 21.7I Mining supply and contract-service marketplace

 Mining supply should mostly broaden existing merchants instead of creating a rigid Mining Store class. A district can
 create unusual value for locally stocked slow-moving parts or consumables because a small component can prevent
 days of industrial downtime. The merchant chooses whether to stock, special-order or require a deposit; exact
 catalogue items must be historically researched. Mines also issue real demand for freight, timber/lumber, repair,
 construction and technical work. The mine can self-perform, contract externally or acquire the supplier. Service
 companies compete on actual capacity, reliability, price and timing. Internal ownership moves the cost/risk into the
 portfolio rather than making the service free.

 21.7J Mine-camp property and independent commercial ecosystems

 A remote mine can generate enough workers and freight to create a settlement opportunity for landlords, boarding
 operators, merchants, repair shops and other services. Independent investors can speculate on transferable nearby
 property and build ahead of expected employment. If the mine disappoints, vacancy and business failure follow. A mine




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 41

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 278/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 company can instead provide some housing/services internally, trading greater capital/control for less independent
 local enterprise; detailed company-town arrangements require targeted regional research.

21.7K Failed mines, reprocessing and breakup value

 Mine failure leaves physical and informational history rather than deleting the site. Claims/mineral rights, workings,
 roads, buildings, mill plant, machinery, stockpiles, dumps/tailings, housing and utilities can retain separate values. A
 distressed owner, lender or estate may sell them together or separately. Restart cost depends on actual condition:
 flooded workings, deteriorated support and exposed machinery can make an apparently cheap mine extremely
 expensive to reactivate. Later treatment economics can make surface material valuable even if underground
 production never restarts. Rights to tailings/dumps/reprocessing should be treated as distinct economic interests where
 historical/legal research supports them.

 21.7L Mine management hierarchy and operating posture

 A small prospect and a large industrial mine should not use the same management granularity. Small operations can be
 owner/boss led. Larger mines need superintendents, foremen and specialized operators. The superintendent can
 allocate labor among work fronts, manage routine purchasing/maintenance, schedule shifts and respond to ordinary
 operating conditions within authority; the owner controls major expansion, financing, treatment strategy, acquisition
 and shutdown. Mine operating posture can include development-heavy, normal production, reduced operation,
 temporary idle or closure rather than a simple on/off switch. Idling may still require pumping, inspection, security,
 maintenance or preservation. Shutting a wet mine without adequate pumping can allow water to make later restart
 progressively harder.

21.7M Shifts, safety and maintenance integration

 Mining can use longer or multiple shifts where historically/operationally justified, but added scheduled hours do not
 automatically multiply production. Labor, supervision, hoisting, mill capacity, light, power and maintenance windows all
 need to support the schedule. Exact Black Hills shift patterns remain a research/calibration item. Safety should remain
 the outcome of actual ground support, equipment condition, explosives handling, water control, supervision,
 fatigue/workload and skill. The player can defer support/maintenance when physically possible. The game should not
 hide the risk behind a Safety Budget slider or universal accident modifier.

21.7N Mining labor, information and acquisition diligence

 Mine expansion creates differentiated labor demand: general labor, miners, teamsters, timber/support workers,
 hoist/boiler operators, smiths/mechanics, mill workers, supervisors and later technical specialists. A district can have
 abundant labor but lack one critical skill. Better wages, board/housing, recruitment and training/promotion where
 appropriate are causal responses. Mining information should preserve provenance: rumor, visual showing, promotional
 sample, independent assay, development exposure, bulk test/treatment and actual production history carry different
 evidentiary weight. A major mine acquisition therefore becomes a premier diligence challenge involving claim/title
 review, records, independent assays, machinery/condition inspection and technical reports while rival bidders or time
 pressure can still exist.

21.7O Roads, water, power and industrial rail as capital forks

 Remote access is a mine capital decision. The owner can expand wagon capacity, improve road/bridge/drainage, later
 pursue industrial rail or seek common-carrier connection. Water can be both resource and hazard: pump capacity and
 actual inflow determine accessibility over time. Power can come from steam, water where site permits, private
 generation or later purchased electric service. These choices alter physical operating costs and dependencies rather
 than applying mine modernization bonuses.

21.7P Mining boom, closure and regional contagion

 A credible successful discovery should attract NPC prospectors, investors, landlords, freighters, merchants and service
 providers through visible evidence, raising claim prices, wages, housing pressure and service demand. Claim rushes
 therefore emerge from information rather than a scripted Gold Rush event. Rumor alone can produce speculation, but
 stronger evidence produces stronger capital response. Closure propagates in reverse. A large mine shutdown can
 reduce worker income, empty housing/boarding, weaken stores, free freight capacity, cut timber/repair demand and
 damage bank loans. The district keeps roads, buildings and distressed assets, allowing later redevelopment rather than
 resetting the map.

21.7Q Mining accounting and portfolio concentration





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 42

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 279/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 Mining reports should separate major economic causes such as exploration/development, extraction labor,
 support/timber, hoisting/haulage, pumping, power/fuel, treatment, freight, maintenance and administration.
 Bookkeeping/Expertise can improve owner interpretation, but the costs themselves come from the real operation. A
 vertically integrated mining empire can own mines, mills, timber, freight, repair, housing, industrial rail and power. This
 improves control and may reduce external margin/coordination costs, but it can create severe correlated exposure: a
 mineral downturn can hit nearly every supposedly diversified business at once. Risk analysis should recognize vertical
 concentration rather than treating business count as diversification.

21.7R Mining square completeness test

 Every mining lane should answer ten depth dimensions: information, physical capacity, labor/skill, inputs/logistics,
 customers/contracts, cash/finance, condition/reliability, time/lifecycle, authority/delegation and regional consequence.
 Across the width dimension, the ten current lanes are prospecting/claim development, mine operation, investment,
 assay/technical services, custom treatment, mineral commerce, supply, contract services, mine-camp property and
 failed-mine/reprocessing. The square is a design-completeness test rather than a requirement for one hundred
 separate controls.

PART VI


 Supply, Trade & Logistics How goods move, how supply chains are controlled and how shortages emerge from real
 causes.

  READING RULE This part is the authoritative home for the systems listed here. Related appendices compress the same
   rules for

 routing and summary; they do not override the body.

 9.1 Supplier classes and sourcing logic

 Stores and production businesses should not receive goods from nowhere. Supplier classes remain internal
 player-owned suppliers, other local businesses, hired local hauling or freight services, and off-map regional suppliers.
 Core sourcing logic remains unit price, hauling and transfer cost, lead time, reliability, quality, volume limit, and market
 reach. Owned hauling can lower marginal transport cost and provide stronger control when shipment volume keeps
 teams, wagons, and labor productively used, but it creates continuing feed, labor, maintenance, stabling, and storage
 costs even when idle. Hired hauling avoids those fixed burdens but charges a commercial rate and offers less direct
 control. The better mode therefore depends on route, volume, frequency, and utilization rather than ownership always
 being cheaper in the long run.

9.1A Landed cost and source geography

 The economy should distinguish supplier quote from landed cost. Landed cost is the actual acquisition burden after
 supported freight, transfer, drayage/handling, route and other direct procurement costs are included. This distinction
 matters especially before local rail: an inexpensive distant item can be less profitable than a higher-priced regional or
 local source once overland transport is counted. Standardized manufactured goods may have relatively legible
 wholesaler/manufacturer pricing, while local food, timber, livestock, repair inputs and household-produced goods can
 be negotiated or driven by current local availability. Product profitability therefore emerges from source, route,
 turnover, credit and selling price rather than from one hard-coded margin property.

 9.2 Recurring local orders

 Recurring local orders belong in VP because they make the town economy feel connected without needing full formal
 freight contracts. Each agreement should store buyer, seller, goods category or item, target quantity, cadence, next
 due date, price mode, hauling responsibility, and breach history. Useful examples include boarding houses buying meat
 and staples, butchers sourcing livestock from a ranch, blacksmiths keeping repeat repair work with farms and ranches,
 and general stores supplying nearby service nodes on a repeat basis. Agreements can succeed, partially fill, arrive late,
 fail, or be cancelled; those outcomes should affect trust, Business Reputation, and future renewal odds.

9.2A Supply agreements, internal chains, and visible commitments

 Recurring local orders should now expand into a full Supply Agreements system. Agreements are the standing policy
 layer between businesses, while actual shipments are the execution layer. A ranch can commit slaughter animals to a
 butcher, a butcher can commit preserved output to a general store or boarding house, a sawmill can commit lumber to
 a yard or project, and a store can maintain recurring inbound agreements with local or off-map suppliers. The player
 should be able to see the agreement, the route, the cadence, the target quantity or percentage, the reserve rule at the
 source, the priority rank, the hauling mode, and the recent fulfillment history. This system must work for
 owned-to-owned chains, owned-to-non-owned sales, non-owned-to-owned procurement, and background non-owned
 trade that still affects the player indirectly. The point is not just to move goods; it is to let the player deliberately shape
 supply chains, protect critical buyers, prioritize internal vertical integration, and decide where overflow goes when a
 preferred destination is full or absent.

 9.2B Commercial Commitment Authority

 Supply agreements are one instance of a broader Canon concept: meaningful commercial commitments consume
 future freedom. A commitment should answer who is obligated, what is promised, when or over what period, how much,
 where performance occurs, whose assets perform the work, who pays which costs, what is reserved or prioritized,
 which risks each side bears and what happens when circumstances change. Employment, freight service, leases,
 custom processing, construction, lending, partnerships, priority repair and other high-value relationships can use the
 same conceptual grammar without sharing one generic contract screen.

 Contract state is not execution state. Signing a promise can reserve stock, money, labor time, processing slots,
 transport capacity or property use, but the promised outcome still requires the real people, assets, materials and travel




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 44

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 281/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 to perform it. This makes future capacity strategically saleable where the resource is real: a mill can reserve treatment
 time, a freight business can reserve haul capacity, a repair shop can reserve priority slots and a warehouse can reserve
 space. There are no generic Future Capacity points.

 9.2C Discretionary-control reporting

 For important resources, the player should be able to distinguish what exists, what is physically usable now, what is
 already promised or legally burdened, what ordinary operations require, what policy deliberately reserves and what
 remains genuinely redirectable. A wagon scheduled for tomorrow's contract is owned but not freely available. Cash
 pledged to a project is not equivalent to uncommitted cash. A leased room is owned but not vacant. A breeding herd
 may be saleable property while still being strategically necessary biological capital. These states should remain
 resource-specific rather than collapsing into one universal Capacity or Discretionary Control meter.

9.2D Performance, breach and recovery

 Commitment performance should allow more than Success/Failure. Depending on the relationship, outcomes can
 include on-time performance, late performance, partial performance, substitution, renegotiation, cancellation, excused
 nonperformance where historically/contractually appropriate and unexcused breach. Communication, records, urgency,
 prior history and available alternatives can influence whether the parties renegotiate or end the relationship. Missed
 commitments should damage the specific relationship or commercial standing they actually affect rather than subtract
 from one global reputation bar.

 9.3 Asset markets and rush response

 Asset markets should cover wagons and transport assets, livestock classes, seed sources, and later more specialized
 equipment. A wagon is never enough by itself; it also needs animals, harness, upkeep, storage space, and assigned
 labor. Rush orders remain a meaningful emergency lever that can protect against stockouts, off-map leakage, and trust
 erosion at a real cost. In Land & Ledgers, rush response is one of the clearest ways supply, cash flow, and reputation
 collide in a readable management decision.

  CANON LOCK

9.3A Trip-based logistics and non-teleporting freight

 Important goods cannot teleport. A delivery order has a source, destination, cargo class, route, loading window, travel
 time and unloading step, and destination inventory updates only when the goods physically arrive or complete a
 justified off-map leg. A delivery can contain multiple transport legs. Distant goods may move by outside rail or river
 service to a regional transfer point, then complete the final journey by hired or owned wagon. Each local wagon leg
 derives practical capacity and travel time from vehicle type, draft team, cargo, load, route quality, grade,
 surface/weather, animal condition and the availability of water, feed, bridges, crossings and stopping infrastructure.
 Severe

 conditions can stop a route rather than merely applying a speed percentage. For locally represented movement, the
 actual person, animal and vehicle state remains authoritative enough to validate departure and arrival. Agents should
 travel beyond the player's normal field of view toward a hidden regional boundary before converting to coarse/off-map
 simulation. Returning agents should re-enter from the corresponding boundary and continue physically. Abstraction
 changes simulation resolution, not identity, cargo, route or reality.

 9.3B Transport assets, draft power, roads, and the Livery / Freight
backbone

 Freight wagons are already mature commercial technology at the opening. The 1880-1905 transport story is primarily
 changing route length, road quality, team economics, rail interface and commercial organization rather than Wagon I ->
 Wagon II -> Wagon III. Heavy freight, farm wagons, local drayage and passenger/stage equipment can differ by job
 without becoming a technology tree. Draft animals retain economic identities. Oxen are slow but strong and useful for
 heavy haul where speed matters less. Mules are hardy professional freight animals. Horses support faster local delivery,
 farm work and time-sensitive movement. Practical load depends on vehicle, team, grade, road condition, weather,
 cargo and animal condition rather than a universal capacity. Road improvement is a physical project. Horse- drawn
 scrapers and graders are already period-valid, but rural roads remain predominantly dirt and weather-sensitive through
 1905. Grading, drainage, culverts, bridges and selective surfacing improve reliability, feasible load and travel time
 through real route conditions rather than an abstract freight bonus. As rail approaches, long wagon segments shorten;
 after a depot arrives, wagons shift toward drayage, farm/ranch collection, mine and timber feeder service and
 secondary settlements. Blacksmiths, farriers, wheelwrights, harness makers and local repair remain important
 throughout the campaign. Factory-standardized parts increasingly change repair from fabrication toward diagnosis,
 ordering and installation without eliminating local skilled work.

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 282/346 ====================

 9.4 Business-to-business logistics and internal routing

 Business-to-business routing should become a general ownership system, not a mining-only exception. The player
 should be able to direct outputs from one business to another, to off-map buyers, to projects, or to storage where the
 chain makes sense.

  • Owned businesses may route output by percentage, fixed quantity, cadence, priority, reserve rule, destination,
    transfer price, and hauling responsibility. Cadence can be daily, weekly, monthly, or another supported interval.

  • Same-owner transfers can use a flexible price modifier: free/0%, at cost, below market, market value, or above market
   where the current economy supports it. There should not be an artificial minimum price if both businesses are
    player-owned, but ledgers must remain honest so profit is not magically created.

  • Split routing should be supported where feasible. A ranch can send part of livestock output to an owned butcher and
    the rest off-map. A sawmill can reserve some lumber for projects, send some to mines, and sell excess locally or
    off-map. A butcher can supply a general store, a boarding house, households, or outside buyers.

  • Local inventory remains real. Global summaries can reveal portfolio-wide stock and shortages, but goods should not
   become a magic shared warehouse. Transfers require actual source stock, reserve checks, destination capacity, route
    access, loading/unloading ability, transport assets or hired freight, labor, cost, and lead time.

  • Business-to-business logistics should support owned-to-owned, owned-to-non-owned, non-owned-to-owned, and
   background non-owned trade that affects player-facing supply, prices, relationship memory and opportunity pressure.

9.4A Internal allocation, opportunity cost and related-party governance

 Wholly owned businesses do not need to fake-negotiate with one another. Their managers can advocate, warn and
 expose local consequences, but the owner with legitimate authority allocates. Internal ownership does not make the
 resource free. Physical cost, accounting transfer value and opportunity value are separate questions. Lumber sent
 internally still consumed logs, labor, mill capacity and freight, and it may displace an outside sale. Internal transfer
 pricing must never create consolidated profit from nothing.

 Where outside or minority ownership exists, the rule changes. A player cannot use control of one partly owned
 company to strip value for the benefit of a wholly owned company without the other owners caring. Material
 related-party transfers, distributions, new obligations or asset sales should respect the control rights and protections
 established by the ownership agreement. This connects partial ownership, bookkeeping, internal transfers and
 governance.

 9.5 Livery / Freight business and professional hauling

 Livery / Freight should function as the professional hauling layer of the town and region. It is both infrastructure and a
 business opportunity. Businesses can self-haul if they have assets and labor; otherwise they can hire freight, rely on
 buyer pickup, or use a player-owned or NPC- owned hauling service.

  • The hauling business should be able to serve multiple clients: player businesses, NPC businesses, households or
    institutions where relevant, construction projects, mine camps, sawmills, ranches, farms, stores, and later rail or depot
    interfaces.

  • A hauling trip should account for cargo class, distance, route difficulty, grade, road condition, wagon/cart fit, animal
   and team requirements, labor, loading/unloading time, feed and upkeep, water or stopping access, storage or stabling
    capacity, and lead time. The shortest geometric route is not always the cheapest or most reliable route.

  • Self-hauling can reduce out-of-pocket freight cost, but it still consumes paid labor, animal use, wagon time, feed,
    upkeep, and opportunity. It is cheaper only when the player has the assets and can spare the capacity.

  • A player-owned Livery / Freight business can profit from the town economy's movement needs. As mines, sawmills,
    farms, butchers, stores, and construction projects grow, demand for professional hauling should rise.

  • The system should support source-delivers, destination-pickup, hired freight, and route assignment modes where
    current implementation permits. It should avoid teleporting important cargo unless an early underlying simulation
    placeholder is clearly marked as temporary.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

 9.6 Causal supply pressure and price formation

 CAUSAL PRICING Supply pressure changes real output, availability, demand, transport capacity, reliability, or delivered
 cost first. Price reacts afterward. Supply pressure is a consequence, not an arbitrary event modifier. The game must not
 simply decide that livestock, grain, lumber, or another commodity costs more. A grounded condition must first change
 actual output, available supply, demand, transport capacity, reliability, or underlying delivered cost. Market and
 supplier prices then respond to those changed conditions. Do not implement logic equivalent to "cattle disease -> beef
 price +25%." Prefer a chain in which disease reduces usable livestock supply; procurement becomes tighter; buyers




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 46

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 283/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 compete for fewer animals; butcher throughput may fall; and price pressure emerges according to the actual market
 state.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

9.6A Livestock disease

  • Livestock health problems may reduce animal condition, sale eligibility, reproduction, herd output, usable slaughter
    stock, or survivorship depending on the supported simulation depth. Named diseases should only be used where their
    period, geography, and transmission are historically justified; do not rely on one generic cattle-epidemic event.

  • A disease affecting one ranch should normally damage that ranch and dependent buyers without automatically
   moving the entire regional market.

  • Several affected local ranches can create a settlement/local shortage.

  • Only an outbreak large enough to affect the broader regional supply pool should materially constrain off-map livestock
    availability or pricing.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

 9.6B Crop failure and infestation

  • Grounded causes can include infestation, crop disease, drought, excessive rain, frost, poor harvest, or other supported
    environmental conditions.

  • The first-order effect is reduced yield or usable output. Supplier availability and price pressure follow from the
    resulting supply situation.

  • Commodity specificity matters. A wheat problem does not automatically raise every agricultural price. Secondary
    effects may occur later through substitution, feed demand, transport competition, or connected supply chains.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

 9.6C Geographic shock scale

  • Supplier/business scale: one producer or supplier is impaired. Dependents may suffer even if the wider market barely
   moves.

  • Local/settlement scale: enough nearby production or transport is impaired to move local availability. Off-map sourcing
   can remain an escape valve, usually with longer lead time and higher freight or acquisition cost.

  • Regional/off-map scale: the problem is large enough to affect the broader supply pool. Outside capacity, price, and
    lead time can now deteriorate as well. These events should be much rarer because they remove a major player
    fallback.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

9.6D Diversification and vertical integration

 Supplier concentration should create a real risk/reward tradeoff. One cheap primary supplier can maximize margin but
 increase exposure. Multiple suppliers can cost more while increasing resilience. Vertical integration is another response,
 but owning the ranch, farm, mill, or freight business transfers the underlying production and labor risk into the player
 portfolio rather than deleting it.

 9.6E Market reach, information, cold chain, and price propagation

 Each good or service has a practical market reach determined by value-to-weight ratio, perishability, transport cost,
 route reliability, information speed, customer mobility and available substitutes. A store stockout, settlement shortage,
 regional shortage and wider-market shock remain distinct. Rail can greatly expand market reach by reducing bulk
 freight cost; telegraph and telephone can reduce information delay without moving goods. Natural ice, icehouses and
 later refrigerated rail extend the practical reach of perishables where the required cold chain exists. Refrigeration
 should therefore change spoilage horizon and reachable buyers rather than act as one global technology toggle.
 Existing inventory and replacement cost remain separate. A merchant may hold stock bought cheaply while new
 supplier quotes rise, or may choose not to reprice until replacement cost becomes relevant. Outside-market influence
 grows as transport and communication

 networks deepen, making late-campaign local prices more exposed to distant conditions without erasing local route,
 quality and shortage effects.

 9.6F Shock severity, buffers, and recovery





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 47

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 284/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 Economic adversity should not carry a predetermined percentage effect. Severity emerges from the condition's
 geographic footprint, which assets or people are actually exposed, timing within a production cycle, available inventory
 or forage reserves, spare labor and route capacity, substitute suppliers or goods, the affected share of the relevant
 market, and the time required for recovery. Two businesses exposed to the same weather, illness, financial condition,
 or transport failure can therefore experience very different outcomes.

  • Acute shocks include hail, injury, bridge loss, sudden supplier failure, and other fast-onset capacity losses.

  • Developing shocks include drought, pasture deterioration, supplier unreliability, labor scarcity, and inventory depletion
   and should usually move through Early -> Mounting -> Action signals.

  • Seasonal culmination occurs when months of exposure become decisive at harvest, wintering, roundup, or another
    timing- sensitive point.

  • Structural shocks include oversupply, prolonged credit tightening, route decline, or persistent population loss and can
   remain for months or years rather than expiring on a short event timer.

  • Surplus is a real pressure family. Bumper harvests, overbuilt services, or excessive livestock supply can weaken sale
    prices and storage economics even when physical output is strong.

 10.1 Storage rules and spoilage

 Interior storage remains safest and limited. Exterior or yard storage remains valid for appropriate bulky goods but can
 carry greater weather, loss, spoilage or security exposure. Every physical inventory unit should consume normalized
 capacity appropriate to its size and storage type rather than existing as weightless database stock. Spoilage should
 begin with perishables such as meat and vulnerable prepared goods. Spoiled goods should be removed automatically
 but reported clearly in the ledger so the player can understand why a business is bleeding value.

10.1A Capacity authority: total, allocated, occupied, and unallocated

 Inventory-capable businesses should distinguish total physical capacity from allocated/reserved capacity and actual
 occupied capacity. Unallocated capacity is genuinely free for a new line. Reserved-but-empty capacity belongs to an
 existing line and stays unavailable to unrelated goods until the managing authority deliberately changes the allocation.
 This prevents unrealistic perfect packing after every sale and gives layout/assortment decisions economic meaning
 without requiring manual shelf placement. The same authority can be reused for display, backroom storage, warehouse
 space, yard/bulk storage, cold storage or other business-specific pools.

10.1B Stocking execution versus administrative allocation

 Routine shelf stocking is execution work. Employees should refill displays from available backstock according to the
 owner/manager's target and allocation when workload allows. They do not decide to shrink a slow product line, add a
 new category, convert a firearm fixture to cigarettes or consume reserved capacity with unrelated stock. Those are
 administrative decisions. Temporary special orders may use receiving/holding capacity without establishing a
 permanent merchandise allocation, provided the business has somewhere to stage the item until collection or delivery.

 10.2 Stock discipline and stockout memory

 Households and business buyers should not simply fail a purchase and forget it. Repeated stockouts should contribute
 to weaker household preference, softer renewal odds on recurring orders, and broader erosion of local trust. Bad stock
 discipline should create a soft but persistent drag rather than only a one-time lost sale. This gives the player a reason to
 care about consistency, not just occasional high- margin spikes.

 10.3 Saturday readiness

 Saturday should remain a recurring readiness opportunity, not a guaranteed demand multiplier. Historical practice
 supports Saturday-night marketing and late store hours in many communities, but routine household shopping remains
 reserve-driven and does not occur on a rigid weekly script. Rural travel patterns, household routines, income timing,
 local custom, weather, seasonal work, and available cash determine whether a particular Saturday becomes unusually
 busy. Readiness still matters: stock, staffing, urgent requests, local supply stability, visible condition, and operating
 hours can turn a concentrated shopping day into opportunity or lost trust.
