PART VII


 People, Households & Labor People as households, workers and economic actors rather than decorative population.

  READING RULE This part is the authoritative home for the systems listed here. Related appendices compress the same
   rules for

 routing and summary; they do not override the body.

 12.1 People simulation

 Each visible NPC should be a simulated person with identity, age, relationships, origin and migration path, skill
 formation, employment, schedule, health, location, household burden, housing state, economic relationships, risk
 markers and succession flags. The individual person is the fundamental social and labor actor. The player should not
 know everything about a person immediately; some truths should emerge through references, employment history,
 observed performance, account records, reports and time rather than magical full-info UI. A person who works at the
 sawmill is the same person whose wage supports a household, who can shop, travel, become ill, quit, be poached,
 relocate, age or die.

12.1A Household economy versus individual action

 The household is the fundamental ordinary consumption and domestic economic unit, while individuals perform the
 actual actions that make that economy work. Food, fuel, clothing, rent, household credit and many purchases are
 planned at household level so the simulation does not create one independent grocery need per person. A specific
 member can then be chosen to shop, work, deliver, travel or seek service according to schedule, location, ability and
 household circumstances. Household members can have separate jobs and life histories while contributing to shared
 resilience and dependency. Exact personal-versus-pooled cash detail can remain abstract unless a later mechanic
 needs a separate purse; the default design priority is truthful household cash flow and individually truthful
 work/movement.

 12.2 Households as economic units

 Households are labor systems, consumption units, care networks, and sometimes mixed domestic-commercial
 enterprises, but family, household, and dwelling should remain distinct authorities. A family represents kinship and
 dependency relationships; a household represents people sharing domestic and economic life; a dwelling represents
 the physical residential space. A boarding proprietor family and six unrelated boarders can therefore share one building
 without becoming one biological family. Household strength should depend on earning capacity relative to dependency
 load, reserves, housing burden, debt, and household production rather than on household size alone.

12.2A Household budgets, cash timing, substitution, and hardship

 Households do not generate money because they have a need. They spend actual cash, use available account credit,
 sell goods or labor, draw reserves, substitute, delay purchases, reduce quantity or go without. Income timing matters
 as much as annual income: clerks and wage workers can receive relatively regular pay while ranch, farm, freight or
 business households can experience irregular large settlements. This makes merchant credit, rent, fuel and seasonal
 purchasing meaningful. Financial stress should propagate through real choices: unemployment can reduce
 discretionary buying, increase use of store credit, threaten rent, change work search and eventually contribute to
 relocation rather than applying one generic poverty modifier.

 12.3 Settlement ladder and household improvements

 Boarding is a major bridge between immigration and permanent settlement, but not the only bridge and not a
 mandatory first stage. New arrivals can board, rent, join kin, move directly into stronger accommodation, use employer
 housing, or arrive with enough means to buy. Rental housing is a normal durable tenure state rather than a temporary
 failure state. Vacant rental-capable properties, rooms above businesses, boarding capacity, and employer bunks
 therefore matter as distinct settlement infrastructure. Household improvements such as chicken coop, kitchen garden,
 root cellar, or boarder rooms remain useful where the game supports them.

 12.4 Family labor and winter pressure

 Helper-age children should begin contributing through chores and light work as soon as it is historically plausible.
 Family businesses should benefit from this, especially general stores, farms, ranches, and households with coops or
 gardens. Each household should carry heat retention, stove tier, fuel reserve, preferred fuel, and winter strain. Heat
 retention is driven by house type, size, and condition. Small tight houses can outperform larger drafty ones. When fuel




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 49

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 286/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 drops below critical, urgency rises and the household may overpay, shift to lower- quality fuel, or cut spending
 elsewhere. Winter strain should feed illness pressure, work efficiency, and financial instability rather than acting as a
 fail state.

 12.5 Demographic generation and migration networks

 Population composition should emerge from settlement function, migration history, housing, and employment rather
 than fixed statewide quotas. The 1890 South Dakota population was strongly migration-driven and somewhat
 male-skewed, but individual nodes should vary substantially. Mining camps, freight nodes, and construction booms can
 attract disproportionate numbers of single working adults; agricultural and mature service communities can support
 more families, children, renters, owners, and older residents. The opening target of roughly 14-22 households and
 55-95 residents, with a likely sweet spot around 70-85, remains valid. The improvement is in composition: varied family
 sizes, single workers, couples, children and youth, widows or widowers, adult relatives, boarders, renters, owner
 households, and a small older population should combine into the total rather than cloning one average household.
 Historical regional averages are guardrails, not generator quotas. Migration should have a reason. Job vacancies,
 wages, kin relationships, land or business opportunity, institutional employment, displacement from another node, and
 existing community/language networks can all pull specific people. Origin and nationality shape biography and
 relationships, not predetermined skill bonuses. Growth changes composition as well as headcount: a mine or railroad
 project may first produce boarder-heavy labor growth, while stable work and housing later encourage kin migration and
 durable household formation. Decline should work in reverse as transient workers leave before deeply rooted
 households.

12.5A Household lifecycle, formation, aging, and succession

 A twenty-five-year campaign requires households to change. People can marry, have children, age into new work or
 schooling stages, leave home, form new households, take boarders, combine with kin, become widowed, inherit,
 relocate or die. The town in 1905 should not be the 1880 roster with older portraits. Children at the opening can
 become adult workers, owners or managers by the late campaign. Exact schooling, child-work and age thresholds
 require historical calibration, but the lifecycle authority should be preserved from the start so demographic continuity
 can emerge without turning the game into a genealogy simulator.

 13.1 Health matters economically first

 Health should matter economically before it becomes medically elaborate. Minor illness reduces efficiency for roughly
 one to two weeks. Moderate illness causes missed work, household income dip, and a higher doctor-visit chance.
 Severe illness can create long absence, rare death chance, and possible lasting weakness.

 13.2 Injury pools and job risk

 Low-risk jobs include clerk, store work, and office work. Medium-risk jobs include butcher, delivery or cart work, and
 basic farm labor. High- risk jobs include blacksmith, ranch work, construction, and heavy hauling. Profession-based
 injury pools should remain grounded. Ranch and horse work risks kicks, trampling, falls, rope-hand injuries, crush
 injuries, and head trauma. Farm work risks tool cuts, wagon accidents, livestock injuries, strains, and crushes. Butchery
 risks deep cuts, infection, and finger loss. Blacksmithing risks burns, eye injuries, crushes, and repetitive hand damage.

 13.3 Doctor service and employer relief

 Medical service remains active early as a grounded town service. The player does not begin with a doctor business. The
 doctor's office can be acquired later as a service business. Office visits handle most cases. House calls are reserved for
 severe illness, severe injury, immobility, and later special cases. Employer relief should be a policy or choice mechanic
 rather than a universal legal guarantee. Some employers may cover treatment or partial wages after serious workplace
 injuries to retain labor, improve trust, or maintain employment relationship history.

13.3A Time, travel and practice capacity

 A doctor primarily sells scarce professional time and judgment. Office care concentrates patients around the doctor; a
 house call consumes travel time as well as treatment time. In a small wagon-and-foot town the difference is
 economically important. A doctor who spends half a day riding to a remote mine cannot simultaneously serve ordinary
 office patients. The player should therefore see a queue and coverage problem rather than a magical healing radius.
 Roads, weather, horse availability, distance and later telephone access can change how efficiently calls are arranged
 without removing physical travel. Historical North American practice strongly supports the home-visiting model and the
 gradual efficiency advantage of office practice.

13.3B Urgency, triage and incomplete treatment





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 50

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 287/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 The medical layer should distinguish enough severity to create scheduling decisions without becoming a diagnosis
 simulator. Minor and routine cases can wait or self-manage; moderate cases are more likely to seek care; severe injury,
 immobility, childbirth complications where modeled and serious illness can justify urgent house calls or immediate
 attention. When demand exceeds capacity, some patients wait, travel elsewhere or go untreated. Treatment can
 reduce absence, complications or death risk where historically plausible, but it never guarantees recovery and should
 not erase the underlying severity.

13.3C Fees, accounts and who pays

 Medical service can be paid at the visit, carried on an account, paid partly later, covered by an employer in selected
 workplace cases or supported through a specific institutional arrangement where historically justified. Exact fee levels
 and collection customs remain calibration items, but the economic consequence is clear: a busy doctor can hold
 substantial receivables while lacking cash. A generous credit posture can improve access and reputation but create
 bad-debt exposure. A mine or large employer can create dependable business through a service arrangement while
 also consuming priority during a serious accident or illness cluster.

13.3D Practice inputs, facilities and professional continuity

 The doctor's office needs modest but real supplies, equipment, heat, clean working space and transport for house calls.
 The design should not track every medicine bottle, but shortages of basic dressings, commonly used medicines or
 transport can reduce what the practice can do. More important is the doctor themselves: professional skill and local
 trust are not contained in the building deed. If a doctor leaves, dies or is incapacitated, an acquired office may retain
 premises, records and some goodwill while losing the core professional capacity. Hiring or attracting another qualified
 practitioner is therefore a real continuity problem.

 13.3E Reputation, information and referral

 Households should learn about the doctor through direct treatment, neighbors, employers and local reputation rather
 than omniscient quality scores. Better medical expertise can improve treatment odds and recognition of serious cases,
 but uncertainty remains. Some cases can be referred or sent to a larger off-map center when local capability is
 inadequate and travel is feasible. A reputable practice can draw patients from nearby nodes, while repeated absence,
 poor outcomes or inability to respond can weaken trust even if the doctor remains technically competent.

 13.3F Public-health load without a public-health minigame

 Illness waves should matter primarily because they create simultaneous household and labor disruption. They can also
 overload the doctor, consume supplies, raise demand for house calls and expose the difference between one small
 practice and a settlement with deeper medical capacity. The player should not run a modern health department
 through the doctor screen. The useful ownership choices are staffing/support, transport, credit, employer
 arrangements, practice location, service priorities and whether capital is justified to expand or attract another
 practitioner.

 13.4 Labor continuity

 Businesses should feel labor strain through absences, reduced efficiency, coverage weakness, and continuity risk. A
 worker shortlist or watchlist is a valid owner-planning tool and should remain consistent with partial knowledge and
 staged discovery. Health therefore becomes part of labor realism, not a detached medical minigame.

13.4A Employee turnover, poaching, and management vacancies

 Employees are not permanent building attachments. They can quit, accept a competitor's offer, relocate, retire,
 become unavailable through illness or injury, or die. Competitors can poach capable workers by making real
 employment offers, and the player can do the same. Compensation, working hours, role/status, conditions, stability,
 distance, housing and household circumstances can affect whether a worker changes jobs. Ordinary vacancies can be
 handled by a delegated manager within authority; losing the manager or another unique administrative/skill-critical
 person should escalate because the authority or function itself has disappeared.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

 13.5 Player mortality gameplay-tolerance lock

 GAMEPLAY TOLERANCE NPC mortality remains simulated. Random player mortality does not end a campaign.

 NPC mortality remains simulated and can generate estates, widow ownership, inheritance, labor loss, property sales,
 succession problems and business-continuity consequences. Mortality should not be a uniform random employee-death
 roll. Where implemented, risk should arise from age, period-appropriate disease, childbirth, living conditions, exposure





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 51

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 288/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 and occupation-specific accidents, with exact cause weights calibrated from historical evidence. Western Plains
 mortality evidence supports meaningful infectious-disease and pneumonia risk

 as well as exposure and accidental/violent death; dangerous work such as mining, heavy hauling, forestry, ranching
 and industrial machinery should carry different accident profiles from clerical or retail work. Random player mortality
 must not end the campaign. The player can remain a normal human within the fiction without subjecting a long
 economic save to random death Game Over.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

 13.6 Human illness as an economic shock

 Existing health rules remain authoritative, but illness should connect more directly to production, logistics, service
 coverage, and supply. The preferred causal chain is: illness -> worker absence or reduced capacity -> operating-role
 weakness -> lower output / lower hauling capacity / reduced service -> downstream delays, shortages, or price
 pressure where the market is tight enough.

  • Illness among teamsters or freight workers can reduce transport capacity and reliability.

  • Illness among sawmill workers can reduce lumber output.

  • Illness among farm labor during harvest can reduce crop output or leave part of the harvest unrealized.

  • Illness among miners can reduce extraction and increase remote-site strain.

  • Illness among retail/service staff can reduce hours, service quality, and operating-role coverage even without
   changing commodity production.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

13.6A Timing and seasonal consequence

 The same disruption should not have identical consequences at every point in the calendar. Illness, injury, transport
 failure, or labor loss can matter much more during harvest, roundup, Saturday trade, a construction surge, a mine
 expansion, or another capacity-sensitive period. Timing should modify the economic consequence through the work
 that fails to occur, not through an arbitrary "bad season" penalty.

PART VII - REVISION XII INTEGRATED ADDITION


 12.6 Household, Accommodation, Kinship & Demographic

 Lifecycle REVISION XII AUTHORITY This section is the governing interpretation layer for earlier Sections 12.1-12.5A and
 for the Residential Property system in 12.7 wherever those passages use household, dwelling, housing state or family
 more narrowly. It does not delete the earlier systems. It clarifies the entities and relationships they operate on. A
 person survives a change of household; a household survives loss of a dwelling; a family relationship can survive
 separation across households; and an accommodation can exist without conventional real-estate ownership. Core
 doctrine: A household is a social-economic domestic unit, not a building and not a parcel. Accommodation is the current
 relationship that answers where a person or household is sheltered. A building can contain several economically
 meaningful accommodation spaces and several households. Systems should modify relationships and states rather
 than treating a household as an object owned by the Housing system.

12.6A Household identity, minimum size and lifecycle output

 A household may consist of one adult maintaining a distinct domestic economy or any larger group of people who
 actually pool important domestic resources, obligations and consumption. A one-person merchant above a store,
 widower in a cabin, laborer renting a room or adult boarder who keeps a distinct budget can therefore be a one-person
 household. Dependence on wages, remittances, kin support or credit does not by itself merge that adult into another
 household. Household size has no arbitrary fixed maximum. A household can legitimately contain parents, many
 children, a widowed parent, an orphaned niece or nephew and another dependent relative if those people actually
 operate as one domestic economy. Large households should remain uncommon because marriage timing, fertility
 variation, mortality, migration, children leaving home, widowhood, economic pressure and household splitting naturally
 limit them - not because the simulation imposes a maximum-member rule.

  • Household size is generated by life events, not selected directly. Birth, marriage, death, widowhood, adoption/care
    placement, adult children staying or leaving, migration, household split, household merger and kin hosting change
   membership.

  • Family and household remain separate. Related people can live in different households. Unrelated people can share a
    building or even accommodation without becoming one household if their domestic economies remain substantially
    separate.

  • Household formation and residential formation are independent. Two people can marry and initially remain with kin or
    in boarding before establishing a new domestic unit or acquiring separate accommodation.

  • Household split and merger can occur without migration. Adult children can establish a new household next door; a
   widowed parent can merge into an adult child's household; two households can share a dwelling temporarily without
   merging finances. The existing spring-1880 population envelope of roughly 55-95 residents, with 70-85 preferred,
   remains a stronger opening constraint than the older 14-22 household count. The household range becomes an
    indicative calibration target rather than a hard generator gate. A seed with many one-person workers or boarders may
    legitimately exceed it; another with several large family households may fall nearer the old band. The generator
    should preserve believable people and relationships rather than force an obsolete household count.

12.6B Kinship graph and family authority

 Kinship should be explicit enough to support inheritance, dependency, migration, household formation, family labor and
 succession. Each local person can carry direct parent/child and spouse relationships where known. Siblings,
 grandparents, grandchildren, aunts/uncles, nieces/nephews and other useful relationships can then be derived rather
 than stored redundantly.

  • Surname is evidence for generation, not proof during simulation. World generation may use matching surnames as
   one clue when intentionally creating related local families, but once the world exists the relationship graph is
    authoritative. A maternal uncle with another surname can be closer kin than an unrelated person sharing the child's
   surname.

  • Off-map kin are valid lightweight records. A person can have a parent, sibling, aunt, uncle or adult child elsewhere in
   Dakota or beyond the simulated region without requiring the whole United States to be simulated. Such kin can matter
    for chain migration, emergency care, inheritance correspondence and later return migration.

  • Kinship does not command household membership. The game should never automatically merge everyone related to
   one another. Family is a network; household is a current domestic/economic arrangement. This is a high-value shared
    authority: the same small relationship graph can support orphan placement, succession, estate claims, family
    migration, caregiving, remarriage, household creation and business continuity.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 53

12.6C Dependent minors, loss of responsible adults and care resolution

 When a child or other dependent minor loses the last locally responsible adult, the death system should not assign a
 random household directly. It should create a Dependency Resolution Case. The case preserves the minor, their current
 accommodation, sibling group, estate interests, known kin and immediate shelter while the simulation seeks a
 workable care arrangement. The preferred simulation search order is a social-plausibility priority, not a claimed
 statutory kin hierarchy: surviving parent or existing lawful guardian where one exists; suitable close adult kin;
 established non-kin relationships such as a household already closely connected to the child or parents; another
 suitable local household; then an off-map relative, public, charitable or institutional path where historically appropriate.
 Suitability considers accommodation, resources, existing dependents, health, willingness, relationship strength, travel
 practicality

 and the ability to provide care. Sibling groups receive a strong preference for placement together, but the simulation
 may separate them when no plausible arrangement can take all of them. The receiving household does not
 automatically acquire the minor's inherited assets. Care, guardianship, estate ownership and property management are
 different relationships. A child can live with an aunt while an estate remains legally distinct and a guardian or other
 lawful authority administers the minor's property. When relevant status changes later, direct control can pass according
 to the legal regime. Historical anchor: the 1887 Compiled Laws of Dakota Territory contains a dedicated Chapter 13,
 Guardian and Ward, including an article on Guardians of Minors. This establishes formal guardianship as a real
 territorial legal institution by 1887. Exact spring-1880 procedures, appointment priority, county practice and
 property-management rules remain a LEGAL RESEARCH HOLD rather than being inferred backward from the 1887
 compilation.

12.6D Child contribution, dependency and adult authority are separate

 Do not use one Age >= X switch for work, independence and legal authority. The simulation should distinguish at least
 three concepts: economic contribution, residential/domestic independence and legal/contracting authority. A child can
 help a household or earn wages before being capable of an autonomous adult household or full legal control of
 property. The 1880 U.S. Census instructions required an occupation entry for each person age ten and upward and
 further instructed enumerators to record a younger boy or girl's occupation when that child was regularly earning
 money, contributing to family support or appreciably assisting in mechanical or agricultural industry. The same
 instructions also warned that ordinary chores or errands should not automatically be treated as a gainful occupation.
 This is an unusually useful design boundary: age ten is historically old enough that meaningful work can exist, but it is
 not a canon declaration that every ten-year-old works or that a ten-year-old becomes an independent household head.

  • Very young dependent: primarily consumes care and cannot meaningfully cover ordinary productive workload.

  • Child/helper stage: can perform appropriate chores and, where actual circumstances support it, meaningful
    family-business or agricultural work.

  • Youth stage: broader wage work, apprenticeship or regular productive contribution becomes increasingly plausible,
    subject to occupation, schooling, health, household need and legal context.

  • Independent adult stage: can normally form a one-person household and exercise the ordinary adult authority
    permitted by the current legal regime. Exact age boundaries, territorial/state legal majority, independent contracting
    capacity, schooling requirements and occupation-specific child-labor restrictions remain a targeted research hold. The
    important canon lock is that contribution begins before full independence and that those states cannot be collapsed
    into one threshold.

 12.6E Fertility is person/couple based, not household based

 Births arise from actual people. The household does not roll for a baby merely because two adults are present. The
 demographic system identifies a biologically compatible reproductive couple and evaluates conception over time using
 age, pregnancy state, fertility variation, time since a prior birth, health and whether the partners are actually
 co-resident or otherwise in a plausible relationship for conception. A multigenerational household can contain more
 than one reproductive couple; an elderly couple, widow household or one-person household does not generate births
 simply because the Household entity exists. Do not assign every couple a visible Desired Children = 6 quota and do not
 impose a universal child cap. Individual variation should emerge from marriage timing, age-specific fertility, spacing,
 underlying fertility, widowhood, separation, mortality, migration and chance within historically calibrated rates. Some
 couples will have no children, some one or two, many several and a minority very large numbers of births. The
 distribution should be calibrated at the population level rather than scripted at household creation. The simulation does
 not need a reproductive physiology minigame. A monthly or similarly low-frequency demographic review is enough.
 Conception creates a pregnancy state; birth creates a persistent new Person; subsequent conception becomes possible
 only when the previous pregnancy and a plausible recovery/spacing interval allow it. Exact spacing distributions are a
 research/calibration question rather than a fixed two-year rule.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 54

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 291/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



  • Birth has real crossover consequences. Dependency and domestic workload rise; consumption changes;
   accommodation suitability/crowding can change; the pregnant or postpartum person's available work can change for a
    period; later the child becomes a helper, worker, heir, migrant or business owner.

  • Maternal and child risk are causal demographic risks. Pregnancy, birth, infancy and childhood must be materially
     riskier than in a modern setting, but outcomes should be historically calibrated and not staged as constant dramatic
    roulette.

  • Birth count is not resident-child count. Children may die, leave home or live elsewhere. Family history and current
    household membership are therefore different datasets.

 12.6F Historical demographic calibration anchors, not quotas

 Revision XII adopts several broad historical anchors for automated calibration while explicitly refusing to treat national
 values as exact Black Hills rules.

  • Fertility: the Social Security Administration's historical U.S. series gives total fertility of about 4.24 children per woman
    in 1880, 3.87 in 1890 and 3.56 in 1900, with a modest rebound to about 3.50 in 1905. The same series adjusted to
    count children surviving to age ten is about 2.96 in 1880 and 2.78 in 1900. Use these as aggregate
    order-of-magnitude targets and evidence that births and surviving children must not be conflated.

  • Marriage timing: Census Bureau historical estimates place median age at first marriage around 26.0 for men and 21.9
    for women in 1890, with very similar 1900 values. Use the late-nineteenth-century pattern - women generally early
    twenties, men generally mid-twenties - as a national calibration anchor, not a frontier hard age.

  • Family-size context: the 1890 census reported 5.04 persons per census family nationally in 1880 and 4.93 in 1890.
   The 1900 census reported South Dakota rising from about 4.7 in 1890 to 4.8 in 1900 and specifically observed that
   newly settled communities could begin with smaller average families and grow as settlement matured. This supports a
   young frontier seed with many single or small domestic units without making it ahistorically childless.

  • Census terminology warning: the 1880 census definition of family is not identical to the game's Household authority.
   Census instructions counted a person living alone as a family, but could also count all hotel inmates as one census
    family under a common roof/table. Land & Ledgers deliberately separates distinct domestic economies inside
    boarding/hotel buildings. Historical family-size values therefore require translation before balance use. These values
    are calibration envelopes. Opening age/sex structure, migration selectivity, settlement maturity, local mortality and
    household formation can move a particular seed away from national averages. The correct test is whether repeated
    25-year simulations produce plausible distributions and trends, not whether every household resembles the national
   mean.

12.6G Opening population generator: people first, relationships second

 World generation should not begin by selecting Family of Five, Single Miner or Large Ranch Family as opaque household
 templates and then filling them with decorative people. The preferred order is:

  • 1. Generate the resident population envelope appropriate to the spring-1880 settlement, including age, sex,
    origin/migration status, occupation potential and the frontier-biased presence of single/transient adults.

  • 2. Establish explicit kinship and marriage relationships consistent with ages and migration history.

  • 3. Generate prior children/birth histories where parental ages and demographic calibration support them, including
    children who are deceased or off-map when that history matters.

  • 4. Form households from actual domestic/economic relationships, allowing one-person, nuclear, multigenerational and
    kin-extended households.

  • 5. Assign accommodation based on property, rent/board offers, employer lodging, kin hosting, temporary shelter,
    household size, affordability and suitability.

  • 6. Validate aggregate outputs - residents, household-size distribution, single adults, child share, boarders,
    renters/owners, age structure, labor supply and housing pressure - then reroll or rebalance only when the seed is
    structurally implausible. This order gives every household an explanation. A 51-year-old couple with adult and teenage
    children looks different from a 25-year-old couple with two small children because their actual ages and history differ,
    not because a household archetype selected a sprite set.

12.6H Accommodation relationship ontology

 A household does not require ownership or occupancy of a conventional dwelling to exist. Household identity persists
 through boarding, renting rooms, employer accommodation, kin hosting, doubled-up housing, temporary shelter,
 displacement and periods without stable shelter. Housing systems must therefore model the relationship between
 household/person and accommodation rather than embedding the household inside a house. The canonical relationship
 chain is conceptually: Person -> Household membership -> Residential Occupancy / Accommodation Arrangement ->
 Accommodation Space -> Building -> Parcel The layers answer different questions. A Person is one human being. A




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 55

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 292/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 Household is a domestic/economic grouping. Family/Kinship is the relationship network and does not require
 co-residence. Residential Occupancy records who is sheltered where and on what terms. An Accommodation Space is
 an economically meaningful place capable of sheltering people. A Building is the physical structure that may contain
 commercial, storage and accommodation spaces. A Parcel is the property geography and legal land interest beneath it.
 A change at one layer should not silently rewrite the others. A fire can destroy an accommodation space while the
 household, kinship, employment, debts and ownership rights remain. The resulting loss of accommodation then creates
 migration, boarding, construction, credit and labor consequences through their own systems.

 12.6I Accommodation states and housing security

 Residential arrangement is not a class. A household can move among forms over its history according to money, work,
 family size, availability and expected permanence. Supported states include owner-occupying, independent rental,
 partial-building or room rental, boarding/lodging, employer lodging, kin-hosted accommodation, doubled-up/shared
 occupancy, transient lodging, temporary shelter/camp, precarious accommodation and no stable shelter.

  • A tent or rough temporary shelter can be real accommodation. Do not implement HasHouse = false -> Homeless =
    true. A tent can have a location, weather protection, heating limitations, storage limits, fire exposure and
    season-specific suitability even though it is not conventional real estate.

  • Housing security is separate from tenure. Owner-occupation can be precarious under foreclosure pressure; employer
    lodging can be stable while the job lasts; kin hosting can be stable or temporary; boarding can be durable for a single
    worker. Use actual termination,

 affordability, crowding and dependency conditions.

  • No stable shelter is a pressure condition, not a permanent population state. Displacement should trigger attempts to
    board, rent, stay with kin, use temporary shelter, seek employer accommodation or leave the node according to actual
    options. A permanence ladder must never become a linear upgrade ladder. A transient worker may rationally prefer a
   bunk or tent despite being able to afford more; a merchant family may value a secure private dwelling strongly.
    Suitability is actor-specific.

 12.6J Shared buildings, separate households and multi-location members

 Two households can occupy the same physical dwelling or accommodation space without becoming one household. If
 the Carter household temporarily stays with the Thompson household after a fire but keeps separate earnings, debts,
 shopping and future plans, they are two households sharing accommodation. They merge only when their domestic
 economy actually merges. Conversely, not every member of one household must sleep at the same coordinates every
 night. A ranch family member can lodge near seasonal work or a worker can maintain weekday lodging near a mine
 while remaining economically attached to a primary family household. Architecture should therefore allow a
 household-level Primary Domestic Anchor plus person-level current residence assignments when needed. Most people
 will simply inherit the household's primary accommodation; exceptions should be supported without inventing a second
 household. Boarding houses demonstrate the distinction. One building may contain the proprietor household, several
 one-person worker households, a married couple household and transient people whose permanent household is
 elsewhere. Shared meals or a common roof do not automatically merge their finances. This deliberately differs from the
 1880 census enumeration convention that could count a hotel and all inmates as one census family. Mixed-use
 buildings are equally valid. A General Store can contain a commercial operating space, owner quarters and one or more
 rentable rooms where the authored building plausibly supports them. Parcel owner, building owner, business operator
 and residential occupant can all be different parties. The simulation tracks only economically meaningful functional
 spaces; it does not need to model every bedroom, hallway or closet as a separate management object.

12.6K Accommodation Space capabilities and emergent suitability

 Accommodation should expose real capabilities rather than a universal Housing Quality score. Depending on the space,
 relevant characteristics include shelter/sleeping capacity, weather protection, heat source/capability, water access,
 sanitation, cooking capability, storage, privacy/shared status, condition, fire exposure, yard/outbuilding access,
 proximity to work/services and seasonal accessibility. Suitability emerges from household/person x accommodation x
 season. A one-person worker can tolerate a summer tent that is unacceptable for a large family in winter. A room over a
 store may provide excellent town access but poor yard access. A remote employer cottage can be secure yet tie the
 household closely to one job. The property does not contain a magic Suitability = 54 value; the same physical facts are
 evaluated differently by different households. Crowding remains a consequence rather than an arbitrary lock.
 Accommodation capacity should represent practical sleeping/shelter ability and increasing strain, not a gamey hard
 maximum that prevents emergency doubling-up. Severe crowding can increase privacy loss, domestic workload,
 sanitation/fire pressure and the incentive to move or build without erasing the emergency option.

 12.6L Accommodation pressure, migration and practical labor supply





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 56

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 293/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 Settlement housing pressure should be measured by accommodation match, not Population - Beds. A node can have
 two vacant cabins, three rented rooms, four boarding beds, employer bunk space and temporary camp capacity yet still
 face a severe shortage for households with several children. Single workers and family migrants therefore see different
 opportunity sets. Migration becomes a real search problem: can this person or household identify accommodation they
 can afford, access and accept? A single miner may accept a bunk. A merchant family may need stable private space. A
 wealthy entrant may purchase or build. A desperate household may double up with kin. The same town can attract
 transient labor while failing to retain families. This directly modifies effective labor supply. An employer may know that
 twenty-five workers are willing to take the wage, but only nineteen can relocate immediately because practical lodging
 is scarce. Others can commute if geography permits, wait, accept camp conditions or refuse. Employer-provided
 lodging therefore has real recruitment value because it changes the accommodation constraint, not because it applies
 a labor bonus. Temporary camps allow settlement to grow ahead of permanent housing. A mine or rail/construction
 surge can produce tents, rough shelters, saturated boarding and doubled-up dwellings rather than a hard No Housing
 -> No Migration gate. The resulting crowding, weather exposure, sanitation strain, fire exposure, lumber demand, food
 demand and construction opportunity should be visible and should create the economic pressure that causes the node
 to harden into a town - or fail if the employment pulse disappears.

12.6M Lifecycle continuity and relationship persistence

 Demographic and household change should preserve the continuity of actual people and relationships over the full
 campaign. Birth, death, marriage, migration, household formation, household separation, displacement, guardianship
 and changes of accommodation should alter the relevant relationship without erasing unrelated history. A person
 remains the same person when they leave a household, move into boarding, change jobs or inherit property. A
 household remains the same domestic unit when it moves from one accommodation to another unless the domestic
 economy itself splits or merges.

 The player should experience these changes through people, notices, leases, payroll, housing pressure, succession,
 estate events and visible town life rather than through administrative screens. The design must preserve enough
 historical continuity that later systems can answer who lived where, who worked for whom, who is related, who owes
 what, what property is owned and why a current arrangement exists.

12.6N Calibration loop and research-hold register

 Demographic balance should be tested by running many full 1880-1905 simulations and evaluating distributions rather
 than hand-authoring a few plausible households. Calibration reports should include births per woman, surviving-child
 distribution, first-marriage timing, age structure, household-size distribution, one-person households, boarders/lodgers,
 renters/owners, widow/widower share, household splits/mergers, orphan/dependency cases, migration by life stage and
 total population growth. Targeted research holds before exact constants are locked: Dakota/Black Hills marriage and
 remarriage patterns; childlessness and parity distribution; birth spacing; maternal, infant and childhood mortality by
 place and subgroup; territorial/state legal majority and contracting capacity; school-attendance and child-work law
 chronology; spring-1880 guardianship procedure and county/charitable placement practice; detailed boarding/lodging
 household enumeration; and how census-family statistics should be translated into the game's narrower
 domestic-economic Household definition. The canon is already strong enough to build the architecture without
 inventing these constants. Where evidence is absent, preserve the causal relationship and label the calibration open.
 This follows the project-wide rule: understand real process depth first, then simplify only where the surviving
 abstraction keeps the important cause-and-effect.

 REVISION XII RESEARCH BASIS - PRIMARY/HIGH-AUTHORITY ANCHORS

 U.S. Census Bureau, 1880 Census Instructions to Enumerators: defines persons living alone in cabins, huts, tents or
 rooms above stores; defines census-family conventions; requires occupation reporting for persons age ten and upward
 and permits recording younger children doing regular productive work. U.S. Census Bureau, Compendium of the
 Eleventh Census: 1890 - Progress of the Nation: national persons per census family 5.04 in 1880 and 4.93 in 1890. U.S.
 Census Bureau, 1900 Census, Volume 2: Population, Part II: South Dakota average census-family size 4.7 in 1890 and
 4.8 in 1900 and discussion of smaller average families in newly settled communities. U.S. Census Bureau historical
 first-marriage series: 1890 medians approximately 26.0 men and 21.9 women. Social Security Administration historical
 fertility series: total fertility approximately 4.24 in 1880 and 3.56 in 1900, with a survival-to-age-ten adjusted series
 around 2.96 and 2.78 respectively. Compiled Laws of the Territory of Dakota, A.D. 1887: Chapter 13 Guardian and
 Ward, including Guardians of Minors. These anchors support architecture and broad calibration; they do not erase Black
 Hills-specific research holds.

 12.7 Residential Property, Tenancy & Housing Markets

 Housing is now a full household, property and investment system rather than only a settlement-support variable. Every
 physical dwelling or residential unit should know its owner, occupant household/person, tenure arrangement, agreed
 rent/board terms where applicable, condition, maintenance, debt/encumbrance state and physical housing




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 57

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 294/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 characteristics. A household does not simply have HousingState = Rented; it occupies an actual unit owned by an
 actual person, estate, company or other entity.

12.7A Historical tenure calibration

 The federal census did not systematically ask ordinary households whether homes were owned or rented until 1890, so
 there is no defensible exact 1880 Dakota renter percentage. The 1890 South Dakota nonfarm benchmark is
 nevertheless strong: approximately 45.12% of all reported nonfarm homes were rented; outside cities of 8,000 or more,
 about 44.13% were rented and 55.87% owner- occupied; in the larger-city category, renting was higher. The 1900
 known-tenure nonfarm data still indicate roughly 40% renting. For the fictional tiny 1880 gateway settlement, the
 provisional design calibration is approximately 35-45% of independent nonfarm households renting and 55-65%
 owner-occupying, with roughly 40% renters as a useful initial target. This is an inference anchored to the nearest direct
 census evidence, not a claim that an 1880 census measured exactly 40%. Boarders, lodgers and transient workers are
 additional housing arrangements and should not be counted as independent renter households in that percentage.

12.7B Who owns rented housing

 The census tenure tables identify occupancy tenure more reliably than landlord type, so Revision XI does not invent
 landlord percentages. Historically supported ownership forms include private individuals/investors, ordinary households
 owning an additional property, widows/heirs/estates, boarding proprietors, employers or mining companies in
 contextual settings, and lenders/receivers that acquire housing through distress. Black Hills records include
 purpose-used rental houses and boarding businesses, demonstrating that owner and occupant can be different real
 economic actors.

12.7C Residential units and tenure products

  • Owner-occupied dwelling: the household owns the accommodation it occupies.

  • Independent rental dwelling: a household rents a house or self-contained residential unit and runs its own domestic
   economy.

  • Rented room/lodging: an individual or small household rents part of a larger property without necessarily receiving
    meals.

  • Boarding: accommodation plus services, especially meals where included, with its own capacity and
    operating-business economics.

  • Employer lodging: bunkhouse, cottage, room or board supplied as part of or alongside an employment relationship.

  • Kin/doubled-up housing: people stay with relatives/another household without becoming a normal commercial
    tenancy; this can relieve housing pressure while increasing crowding. One building can support more than one
    residential relationship only where the authored physical structure supports it: owner residence plus rooms,
   commercial ground floor plus rooms above, boarding arrangement or multiple suitable units. The simulation structure
    should permit this without generating anachronistic apartment patterns by default.

12.7D Rent freedom and market formation

 Landlords set actual asking rents rather than receiving a townwide rent modifier. The player may ask whatever amount
 they choose, subject to applicable period law or contract. Households compare available options and may refuse, move,
 crowd elsewhere or leave the node. Estimated market rent can exist as analysis, but it is not an enforced maximum.
 Average town rent is an output of real agreements. Housing shortage can cause landlords to ask more and households
 to accept more because alternatives are scarce; new construction responds with delay because it requires land, capital,
 lumber/hardware, labor and time. If many investors respond at once, a later housing surplus can create vacancies and
 rent competition.

 12.7E Household housing choice

 Household choice should consider affordability, size/suitability, crowding, location relative to work and services,
 condition, heating burden, water/sanitation arrangement, yard/outbuilding usefulness where relevant, relationship/kin
 factors and available alternatives. Cheap nominal rent is not always the cheapest household option if a drafty distant
 house consumes far more fuel and travel time. Suitability is household-specific. A small room may be reasonable for a
 single worker and poor for a family with children. The game should avoid a universal House Quality score as the sole
 decision input.

 12.7F Crowding as consequence, not occupancy lock

 Reasonable capacity can be estimated from usable residential space and sleeping arrangements, but it should not be a
 hard maximum. Families can double up, take relatives or accept crowded housing when scarcity demands it. Crowding





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 58

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 295/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 can increase wear, domestic burden and, where historically/medically justified, sanitation/health risk; exact health
 effects require targeted research. The important rule is freedom with consequence rather than Cannot Move In because
 capacity is exceeded.

12.7G Rental-property owner decisions

  • Set rent and change it when the current agreement/law permits.

  • Choose applicant-review policy and whether an agent/manager can accept ordinary tenants automatically under
    standing criteria.

  • Set tolerance for arrears, partial payment or case-by-case exceptions; exact eviction/removal process remains a
    Dakota/South Dakota legal research hold.

  • Maintain, repair, refurbish, expand, connect utilities, convert or sell the property.

  • Decide whether rooms/properties are furnished or services/fuel are included where historically appropriate; exact
   common arrangements require research.

  • At scale, delegate rent collection, vacancy letting and minor repairs while retaining approval for rent policy, major
    renovation, sale, debt and exceptional tenant situations.

12.7H Rent arrears and household cash allocation

 Rent is an actual household obligation paid from actual cash or negotiated arrears. A household with $11.40 that
 simultaneously owes $8 rent, needs $5 of winter fuel and owes a merchant account cannot satisfy every claim
 magically. Household priority, urgency, credit access and landlord policy determine what is paid or postponed. Missed
 wages can therefore propagate from employer to household to landlord to lender and merchant. Rental ledgers should
 track current rent due, past-due balance, partial payments, last payment and arrears age where the system supports it.
 Arrears are structurally similar to commercial receivables but should follow the historically correct tenancy/legal
 process rather than automatically using merchant-credit rules.

 12.7I Vacancy, turnover and physical moves

 Vacancy is a real cost. When a tenant leaves, rent stops until a new household agrees and physically occupies the
 property. A landlord can re-rent immediately, hold the unit vacant for repairs/refurbishment or deliberately wait for a
 higher-paying market. High asking rent may increase income per occupied month but also increase vacancy/turnover
 risk. Moves follow Physical Truth. The household leaves one actual dwelling and enters another. Close moves can be
 represented at an appropriate abstraction with people and household goods/cart movement; off-map migration follows
 the established hidden-boundary transition. The simulation should not change address while the people visibly remain
 elsewhere.

 12.7J Landlord maintenance, exploitative operation and market
consequence

 Residential property plugs directly into the Asset Condition system. Roofs, stoves/chimneys, structure, weatherproofing,
 privies/water arrangements and later utility connections can require real work. Vacancy can be a valuable repair
 window. A landlord may deliberately defer work and extract high rent during scarcity. The game does not need a
 Slumlord class or morality perk; exploitative landlord behavior emerges from high rents, crowding, low maintenance
 and short-term cash extraction. Such a strategy can genuinely succeed while housing is scarce. Longer-run
 consequences emerge through deterioration, fuel burden, fire/sanitation exposure, tenant willingness to remain,
 competition from better housing, future capital repairs and any historically grounded civic/legal pressure. The game
 should not apply an automatic moral penalty merely because the player chose an unpleasant strategy.

12.7K Employer housing and labor-market integration

 Employers may build or control housing where geography and business scale justify it, especially remote mines or
 industrial sites. Housing can be offered as part of compensation or rented separately according to historically
 appropriate arrangements. It can make recruitment feasible where jobs exist but accommodation does not. It also
 creates dependence: shutdown can remove both income and employment- linked housing. Company housing is not a
 universal requirement. A sawmill beside a functioning town can rely on independent landlords; a remote mine twenty
 miles away may need bunkhouses or cottages. The choice depends on land, capital, labor need and existing settlement
 supply.

 12.7L Residential construction, speculation and boom/bust

 NPC and player housing construction should be an investment decision driven by land, expected occupancy/rent,
 construction cost, finance, maintenance and market outlook. The simulation should not spawn the exact housing




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 59

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 296/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 quantity demanded. Supply responds with delay and can overshoot. This makes speculative housing possible. A player
 can build near a proposed depot or mine before demand exists. If the project arrives, occupancy and land value can
 surge. If the railroad bypasses the town or mine fails, the player owns empty buildings with debt and maintenance.
 Housing surplus can then lower rents, improve household accommodation and push weak landlords toward sale/default.

12.7M Utilities, neighborhoods and nuisance without zoning

 Water, sewer, electricity and telephone connections can become property-level landlord investments when the network
 reaches the site. Connection may support higher rent/lower vacancy or reduce household burden, but it costs capital
 and does not automatically pay back. Partial adoption allows wealthy and poor streets to modernize unevenly.

 Residential preference can respond to nuisance, manure, smoke, industrial noise, rail yards, slaughtering, fire exposure
 and traffic without a modern zoning lock. Lower rents/land values can make undesirable areas economically acceptable
 to some households. Neighborhood form emerges from price, access, externalities and land use.

12.7N Distress, foreclosure, estates and tenant-to-owner movement

 Rental property participates fully in the property/finance system. A distressed landlord can sell one house, a package or
 an entire portfolio, refinance, defer maintenance or default. Estates can inherit occupied rentals. Lenders can acquire
 property through the appropriate foreclosure process and then temporarily collect rent or resell where legally
 supported. Existing tenancy treatment through foreclosure remains a legal research item. Households are not
 permanently typed as renters. A renter can accumulate savings, obtain period-appropriate financing, buy an occupied
 house from the landlord or purchase elsewhere. An owner can lose property and become a renter. Tenure is a
 life/economic state, not a social class.

12.7O Residential holdings at portfolio scale

 Early rental property can remain directly owned income-producing property rather than requiring a formal business
 entity. As holdings expand, the player can hire historically appropriate agents/property managers if research supports
 the title/structure. Portfolio UI should show property, occupant, rent, payment status, vacancy duration, condition, debt
 and exceptions so dozens of units remain manageable without losing the ability to inspect one household/property in
 detail.

PART VIII


 Markets, Competition & Adversity Demand, rivals, pricing and conditions that can push back against accumulation.

  READING RULE This part is the authoritative home for the systems listed here. Related appendices compress the same
   rules for

 routing and summary; they do not override the body.

 14.1 Household shopping logic

 Households should buy from the business that makes the most sense, not automatically from the player. Demand
 resolves mainly at household level for clarity and performance, but a specific person performs the local trip. Household
 choice should consider price, stock, operating hours, distance or convenience, Business Reputation, remembered
 experience, credit availability, urgency and accessible substitutes. A local purchase should not complete before the
 shopper actually reaches the business and the business is still able to serve the purchase. If normal local options are
 closed, unavailable or unsuitable, the household can wait, substitute, seek another local merchant or, when urgency
 and travel economics justify it, obtain goods through an off-map trip or channel. Owner Reputation remains a smaller
 trust modifier or tie-breaker, not the main store-choice driver.

14.1A Customer urgency, information, and remembered relationships

 Not every need has the same urgency or tolerance for delay. A household can postpone discretionary cookware, but
 food exhaustion, winter fuel shortage or a work-critical replacement can justify higher prices, unusual travel,
 emergency credit or inconvenient hours. Customers should act on information they plausibly possess rather than
 omniscience. Repeated successful purchases, stockouts, accepted credit and other direct experience can shape future
 choice without requiring one exposed loyalty score. The player likewise should not receive exact private household
 cash or rival books without an information source; ownership, account records, employment and later banking or
 professional reports determine what can be known precisely.

 14.2 Reserve-based shopping and pricing

 Target stock is what the household would ideally like to hold. Reserve stock is the point where the category joins the
 shopping list. Critical reserve is where urgency spikes and faster shopping attempts become likely. Routine shopping
 should remain threshold-driven rather than scripted to a rigid weekly day. Overpricing should push households toward
 alternatives when they exist; underselling can still sink the business through margin failure.

 14.3 Commercial accounts, credit posture, and early-game action density

 Customer credit is a shared commercial capability rather than a General Store-only mechanic, but it should appear only
 where historically appropriate for that business relationship. The current managing authority can choose cash-only
 versus credit, broad credit posture, customer/household limits, exceptions, collection tolerance and whether ordinary
 staff may approve small transactions. General Stores use

 household book accounts; doctors and service trades can carry billed or running accounts; blacksmith/livery-type
 services can maintain repeat-customer accounts where appropriate; merchants and wholesalers can use
 business-to-business trade credit; sawmills or lumber sellers can extend account terms to repeat buyers. Ordinary store
 tabs do not automatically accrue interest unless a specific agreement warrants it. Credit creates accounts receivable,
 liquidity risk, customer retention and competitive differentiation. A generous NPC can report strong sales while starving
 itself of cash; a stingy NPC can drive reliable customers to a rival. Repayment emerges from actual cash-flow events,
 not a universal weekly script. Early-game action density still matters, but account decisions should be mostly
 policy-driven rather than a popup for every purchase.

 14.4 Rival response and market causality

 Rival openings and expansions should emerge from the same town logic the player reads. A rival should not open a
 business merely because a hidden number crossed a threshold. The rival should appear to be acting on visible backlog,
 weak coverage, rising wages, housing strain, supplier slack, newly available land, financing access, or a distressed
 acquisition opening. Rival action is one of the cleanest ways an opportunity becomes pressure. This preserves the
 player fantasy that the town is alive and reactive rather than procedurally decorative. It also ensures that defeating or
 buying out a rival yields inherited real conditions rather than fake clean resets.

 14.5 Category markets, customer segments and practical market share





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 61

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 298/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 There should be no single universal Market Share number for the player's empire. Competition is specific to a good or
 service, a reachable customer group and a geography. A general store can dominate workwear while losing food
 staples; a butcher can own household trade while a rival controls hotel accounts; a freight firm can dominate one mine
 corridor and have little presence in farm hauling. Market share should therefore be a derived analysis built from actual
 transactions, unmet demand and reachable alternatives. Customer segments matter only where they change behavior:
 households, repeat business accounts, remote camps, institutional buyers, travelers and project demand can value
 different combinations of price, reliability, credit, location and volume.

 14.6 Substitution, leakage and the outside option

 A weak local market should not trap customers into buying from the nearest business. Households and businesses can
 substitute products, postpone demand, repair instead of replace, use household production, buy from another node or
 leak demand off-map when price, urgency and transport make that rational. Likewise, strong local merchants can
 capture demand from surrounding nodes. Rail, road improvement and communication can therefore increase
 competition as well as opportunity: the same connection that brings cheaper inventory can make outside sellers more
 accessible. Market reach is a two-way door.

14.6A Credible alternatives as bargaining power and resilience

 Market power should be understood primarily through the counterparty's best credible alternatives, not through an
 abstract Influence or Monopoly meter. A worker with several employers has bargaining leverage. A mine with one
 practical treatment provider is vulnerable. A borrower with several willing lenders can reject poor terms. A rancher with
 one reachable merchant has fewer options. A town served by two viable freight routes is more resilient than one
 dependent on a single carrier. The same principle explains distress: as liquidity, suppliers, workers, buyers, lenders or
 sale options disappear, the actor's remaining choices become worse. Power and distress should therefore emerge from
 the structure of alternatives.

14.6B Bounded awareness and practical choice sets

 People do not evaluate the entire simulation every day. A practical decision process is Trigger -> Awareness ->
 Feasibility -> Shortlist -> Choice. A person reconsiders a supplier, employer, store, lender or service when something
 gives them a reason. They know alternatives because of prior use, travel, direct observation, family/acquaintance
 networks, coworkers, advertising, directories, correspondence, solicitation or other supported information channels.
 Distance, hours, stock, transport, housing, qualifications, credit eligibility and urgency then determine which known
 options are actually feasible. Choice occurs among a bounded shortlist rather than through omniscient optimization.

 14.7 Rival strategy and capital constraints

 Rivals compete through the same kinds of levers available to the player: price, assortment, stock reliability, hours,
 location, customer credit, delivery, service specialization, recurring contracts, labor recruitment, supplier relationships,
 property acquisition and capital investment. They should not receive hidden demand, production or cost bonuses. A
 rival with deep cash reserves can survive a price war or carry more inventory; a weak rival may be unable to respond
 even when the opportunity is obvious. Rival strategy should reflect its assets, information, owner preferences,
 relationships and financing access. This makes an aggressive competitor dangerous because it is actually well
 positioned, not because difficulty mode grants it a multiplier.

 14.8 Price competition, service competition and destructive rivalry

 Price is one competitive dimension, not the whole market. Two stores at similar prices can differ through stockouts,
 credit, hours, delivery, location and trust. A price war is valid when businesses deliberately cut margin to defend or
 capture trade, but it burns cash and can make both firms weaker. Deep pockets therefore matter, as do purchase cost
 and supplier terms. Conversely, a high-price business can remain viable if it offers scarce goods, better reliability,
 convenient credit, superior location or a service package customers actually value. The game should allow
 predatory-feeling strategies to fail economically without requiring an invisible fairness rule.

 14.9 Advertising and commercial information

 Advertising should change who knows an offer exists, not manufacture demand from nothing. The Black Hills press
 already carried business advertising in the opening era, including hotels, banks, blacksmiths, groceries, restaurants and
 professional services. Newspaper notices, signs, handbills and later faster communications can therefore announce
 openings, new stock, special terms, routes, services or sales to customers who might otherwise remain unaware.
 Advertising works best when the underlying offer is useful. Repeated promotion of empty shelves or bad service can
 waste money or even spread disappointment faster. The value of advertising rises when the reachable market is large
 enough to justify the cost and when information is otherwise fragmented.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 62

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 299/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


 14.10 Entry, overcapacity, exit and market succession

 Profitable unmet demand should attract capital eventually, but entry requires a suitable property, startup capital, labor,
 supply and a willing owner or investor. New businesses therefore arrive with delay and can overshoot. Several
 merchants may all respond to the same boom, creating later overcapacity, margin pressure and vacancy. Weak firms
 can narrow their service, seek credit, merge or sell, change location, accept a buyer, close or fail through distress. Their
 customers, workers, supplier commitments and property then become opportunities for others. This creates market
 succession: a strong player can win not only by undercutting rivals, but by surviving a downturn, buying a distressed
 location, hiring displaced workers or absorbing abandoned accounts.

14.10A Entry requires a business thesis

 NPC entry should not occur merely because a margin statistic crossed a threshold. A plausible entrant needs awareness
 of the opportunity, an operator or investor willing to act, capital/credit, property or equipment, labor, supplier access,
 customer reach and an expectation that the enterprise can survive likely incumbent response. If nobody can assemble
 a credible business thesis, a profitable-looking gap may remain open. Successful player dominance therefore does not
 require the simulation to spawn a challenger for balance alone.

 14.11 Competitive memory and reputation repair

 Customers and counterparties should remember economically meaningful experiences rather than accumulate one
 permanent loyalty score. Successful fills, fair handling of credit, reliable contracts, repeated stockouts, surprise closure,
 poor repair, bad lodging or missed deliveries can all shape future choice. Memory should fade when the event is old or
 when new evidence contradicts it, allowing businesses to recover from a bad period through sustained better operation.
 Ownership change can reset expectations only partially. A new proprietor may create curiosity, but inherited
 employees, location, stock, debts, service failures and local stories remain until real operation proves otherwise.

14.11A Commercial memory types

 The economy should preserve memory selectively rather than invent one permanent Reputation score. Personal
 memory is what a person remembers or has learned. Relational memory is what two counterparties know about dealing
 with each other. Recorded memory is preserved in books, correspondence, contracts, account histories and reports.
 Procedural memory is embedded in experienced employees and routines. These forms survive different disruptions.
 Losing the founder may remove personal knowledge while records and staff preserve continuity. Losing both staff and
 records can genuinely reduce organizational capability.

14.11B Reputation-score interpretation lock

 Where earlier Canon wording uses Business Reputation, Owner Reputation, employment relationship history or similar
 shorthand, Revision XIV interprets that term as a summary of specific commercial evidence and remembered history,
 not as one universal permanent scalar that mechanically modifies every interaction. A seller can trust the player's
 closing record; a worker can distrust one employer's treatment; a bank can value repayment history; households can
 remember stockouts. Those facts may be summarized for readability, but the causes remain relationship-specific.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

 3.2B Strategic failure doctrine

 The simulation should be willing to let the player permanently lose individual battles without ending the campaign.
 Strategic failure is an essential source of consequence and should arise through the same grounded economic causality
 as success.

  • Property or acquisition opportunities can be lost to rivals or seller decisions.

  • Businesses and collateral can be sold, seized, foreclosed, closed, or otherwise lost.

  • Important workers can resign, die, become unavailable, or accept competing opportunities.

  • Supplier relationships or scarce supplier capacity can be lost.

  • Household preference, customers, market share, and recurring commitments can shift to competitors.

  • Rail corridors, financing opportunities, investment opportunities, and settlement momentum can be lost.

  • A settlement can stall, decline, ghost, or be surpassed without automatically creating player defeat.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

 3.2B-1 Distress as deterioration of alternatives Business distress should be legible as a shrinking set of credible
 responses rather than a universal Business Health meter. Cash disappears, lenders tighten, suppliers shorten terms,
 managers leave, collateral is already pledged, customers defect, asset buyers vanish or a dependent market collapses.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 63

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 300/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 The business becomes dangerous because fewer good moves remain. One entity can lose its options, be sold, closed,
 liquidated or taken by creditors while the owner continues elsewhere.

 3.2B-2 Failure creates recombination Failure should often redistribute useful economic pieces instead of deleting them.
 A closed enterprise can release property, machinery, wagons, inventory, workers, managers, customer relationships,
 supplier capacity and local demand. Creditors, rivals, employees, managers or the player can recombine those pieces
 into new ownership structures. Distress can therefore be both destruction and opportunity, giving the economy
 continuity across booms and downturns.

 3.2C Adversity as part of the ownership loop

 The economy is not considered proven if the dominant loop is only profit -> expansion -> more profit. MVP must include
 enough grounded adversity to demonstrate that external and internally generated forces can weaken the player, create
 difficult ownership decisions, produce strategic losses, and occasionally push a portfolio toward distress. Adversity
 should primarily emerge from simulation state and readable economic cause. It should not become a random disaster
 deck or a constant popup stream. MVP adversity families

  • Rival competition: rivals can open or expand businesses, acquire distressed competitors, compete for parcels, recruit
    workers, compete for supplier capacity, alter prices, and act on visible profitable openings. Rival causality rules from
    Revision IV remain authoritative.

  • Supply pressure: real production, supplier, transport, or availability problems can make procurement harder and can
    eventually affect prices. Revision V causal-supply rules below are mandatory.

  • Labor pressure: illness, injury, resignation, competing wage offers, and skilled-worker scarcity can reduce
    operating-role coverage. Severity depends on the business and the role lost.

  • Financial pressure: payroll, debt service, inventory purchases, expansion, project costs, and disruption can create
   genuine liquidity stress that makes owner cash, business cash, refinancing, transfers, and asset sales meaningful.

 REVISION V INTEGRATED

3.2D Persistent conditions, not notification spam

 Economic problems should normally exist as persistent conditions that evolve through the existing signal ladder. The
 player should be interrupted when a meaningful threshold is crossed, not every time the same underlying problem
 updates.

  • Early signal: condition is visible but not urgent.

  • Mounting signal: repeated evidence shows the town or business is compensating badly.

  • Action signal: the condition has crossed a threshold where ownership response is warranted. One continuing freight or
    supply problem should mature from weakening to mounting to critical rather than generating a fresh alert every day.
    UI should explain cause and trend while the world provides physical or behavioral evidence where practical.

 3.2E Fire, conflagration, and physical recovery

 Fire must not operate as a universal annual disaster probability. Ignition comes from credible building, heating, lighting,
 cooking, industrial, machinery, or environmental conditions; spread then depends separately on combustible contents,
 construction, spacing, neighboring uses, wind, detection, water access, and firefighting response. Randomness may
 decide whether a credible hazard actually ignites, but it must not bypass the physical conditions that make the fire
 plausible. Wood-frame frontier construction is inexpensive and historically appropriate but creates greater conflagration
 exposure when buildings are dense. Brick and stone can materially improve containment without making a building
 fireproof. Water mains, hydrants, organized volunteer fire companies, hose or hook-and-ladder equipment, and
 response distance are real settlement infrastructure and should protect only the properties they can practically reach.
 Fire damage should resolve against physical authorities separately: inventory can burn while a structure survives; a
 building can be lost while the business continues in temporary premises; workers or residents can be injured or
 displaced; neighboring properties can suffer partial losses; and utility or freight assets can be damaged independently.
 Insurance can exist as a later risk-transfer product, but exact period premiums remain a tuning/research question.
 Major fire can also create opportunity and restructure a node. Rebuilding can drive lumber, masonry, hauling, labor,
 finance, temporary-premises, and land demand; strong towns may rebuild quickly and in more permanent form while
 weak nodes can lose businesses or population. Wildland and prairie fire should remain a separate environmental hazard
 family whose behavior depends on vegetation, dryness, wind, terrain, and ignition rather than the urban structure-fire
 model.

 3.2F Fire service progression and municipal fire rules
