 Fire protection can mature from ad hoc bucket response to an organized bucket brigade, volunteer hook-and-ladder or
 hose company, hydrant-supported response and, only in sufficiently large late-campaign towns, paid professional
 service. Volunteer organization should remain normal through most of the campaign. Fire-company capability, water
 coverage, equipment and actual response distance affect suppression; the existence of a town fire organization is not a
 universal percentage reduction. Growing territorial towns can impose specific fire-prevention rules without adopting
 modern zoning. Historically grounded powers include regulation of dangerous stoves or stovepipes, ashes, explosives
 and combustible storage, requirements for practical fire equipment, inspection and, where local pressure justifies it,
 more fire-resistant construction in vulnerable commercial blocks. These rules should emerge from actual fire pressure
 and civic action rather than a settlement-rank unlock.

PART IX


 Finance & Capital Credit, banks, investors, collateral, distress and the 1880-1905 legal environment.

  READING RULE This part is the authoritative home for the systems listed here. Related appendices compress the same
   rules for

 routing and summary; they do not override the body.

 18.1 Finance before player banking

 Off-map finance should exist before on-map banking. Early in the game the player is borrowing from an established
 outside finance system that already functions as part of the world. The first on-map bank will usually arrive because the
 town has matured enough to support it, not because the player immediately has the capital to found one. This keeps
 banking from arriving as a fantasy power too early and better supports the town's own growth arc.

 18.2 Multiple banks and lender personalities

 The finance market should support more than one lender over time, but not necessarily multiple equal full-service
 banks from the first moment the town becomes bankable. The grounded version is one local bank or banker first,
 followed later by a second bank, private banker, stronger outside lender presence, or a player-founded bank once
 population, rail access, and regional seriousness justify it. Different lenders can have different reputations, collateral
 appetite, payment schedules, willingness to finance land versus business versus infrastructure, and tolerance for
 distress or speculation. This makes finance a real strategy layer rather than a flat interest-rate slider.

18.2A Deposits, confidence, and regional credit ecology

 The lending market is a regional credit ecology, not merely a source of outbound loans. Banks compete for deposits,
 hold different reserve postures, carry different loan quality and sector exposure, and depend to varying degrees on
 correspondent or outside capital access. Solvency and liquidity are separate: a bank can own sound loans yet still be
 unable to satisfy a sudden concentration of withdrawals. Bad debt, overexposure to one boom sector, rumors, nearby
 suspensions, wider money-market stress, or repeated failures can therefore tighten lending through real balance-sheet
 and confidence channels. The UI may summarize these interacting conditions through a readable Regional Credit
 Climate such as Easy, Normal, Cautious, Tight, or Crisis, but the label must be derived from actual lender states rather
 than acting as a global modifier. Individual banks can still react differently. A strong conservative bank may continue
 excellent collateral lending during a tight climate; an overexposed rival may stop new credit or suspend payment.
 Acute bank-run liquidity stress and a longer credit depression are different phases and should not share one short event
 timer.

 18.3 Founding versus acquiring a bank

 Both bank paths are valid. The player can eventually acquire an existing bank if conditions, seller motives, or strategic
 pressure make that possible. The player can also found a bank once wealth, collateral, labor, and reputation justify it.
 Founding one should be capital-heavy and prestige-heavy, not a quick side-business. Acquisition may be cleaner in
 some runs; founding may be more attractive where there is no strong incumbent or where the player wants tighter
 policy control.

18.3A Silent partners, external investors, and subscription capital

 Not all growth should be financed through debt alone. Before the full late-capital stock-and-bond layer arrives, the
 game should support outside investors, silent partners, subscription drives, and profit-share funding for suitable
 projects. These structures are especially useful for riskier ventures such as mine development, mill expansion, remote
 service clusters, boarding expansion, or speculative district plays where a conservative lender may be unwilling to
 advance enough capital. The important distinction is that lenders protect downside while investors buy into upside.
 Debt preserves control but burdens repayment. Equity-like outside capital reduces ownership purity but shares risk and
 can accelerate growth. This should become a meaningful strategic fork in the player's financial life rather than a flavor
 variation on the same loan mechanic.

 18.4 Loan review, automation, and delegated thresholds

 Bank ownership should create two overlapping play styles. First, the player can personally review important loans, read
 the application, inspect the borrower's creditworthiness, collateral, trade prospects, and existing obligations, and
 approve or deny the request. Second, the player can automate ordinary lending through staff thresholds. Small loans
 under a chosen amount can be processed or denied automatically according to policy. Larger loans break the threshold




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 66

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 303/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 and trigger a player review notice. This mirrors the project's business-cash automation logic: ordinary repeatable work
 can be delegated, while high-consequence exceptions still surface to the owner.

 18.5 Collateral, bad debt, and instruments

 Collateral should be real, varied, and instrument-specific. A borrower may pledge land, a building, a business,
 inventory, tools, livestock, wagons, machinery, or later paper instruments where law and local practice support them.
 Each debt should know whether it is secured or unsecured, what property supports it, priority where relevant, and
 whether the borrower carries personal liability. A pledged asset can remain in productive use before enforcement;
 missed payment does not instantly make the lender its owner. Bad debt should happen, and creditor recovery should
 proceed through workouts, judgments, seizure, chattel or mortgage foreclosure, negotiated surrender, and sale as
 appropriate.

 18.6 Banking additions

 Banking remains a late-capital and institutional power layer. Off-map finance exists before player banking; local
 banking arrives when a settlement becomes economically serious enough; player banking becomes a way to shape
 regional credit rather than a simple money button.

  • Add a settlement or node bankability ladder: too small for formal banking, regional lenders watching, private banker
     likely, ready for first local bank, strong enough for competing banks, and regional finance hub. The ladder should
    consider population, business count, payroll volume, deposit demand, land value, debt demand, rail or industrial
    seriousness, and local confidence.

  • Use explicit loan categories: working capital, property purchase, business acquisition, construction or project, rescue
     liquidity, infrastructure, speculation, mine or rail development, and refinance or consolidation. Each category should
   have distinct lender appetite, collateral preference, repayment logic, and risk.

  • Expose lender posture in player-readable terms. Lenders may prefer land collateral, known borrowers, commercial
    expansion, distress lending, relationship lending, rail or mine development, or conservative low-risk loans.

  • Player-owned banks should support policy controls and automation thresholds. Routine loans can be handled by staff
    policy; significant, risky, strange, or strategic loans should trigger owner review.

  • Loan review should include borrower identity, loan purpose, repayment source, collateral quality, existing debt,
    reputation, market outlook, strategic value, and risk to the player portfolio.

  • Add competitive-conflict review. If an applicant seeks funding to open, expand, or strengthen a business that
   competes with a player-owned or player-controlled industry, a player-owned bank can deny, reduce, delay,
    counter-condition, or approve the loan. This is a real advantage of owning a bank, but repeated self-serving denial can
   damage bank reputation, civic trust, deposit confidence, local growth, or invite rival lenders.

  • Banking should create opportunities and problems across the wider sim: funding rivals, rescuing weak businesses,
    creating distressed assets, supporting mines or rail, accelerating secondary settlements, tightening credit after
    shocks, and exposing the bank to sector or node risk.

  • Before enforcement, banks may attempt workouts such as revised schedules, partial payment, added collateral,
    refinance, or negotiated voluntary asset transfer. Manager replacement, tighter operating control, or
    debt-to-ownership structures should appear only where agreement, acquisition, receivership, or the business structure
   makes them legitimate rather than as automatic creditor powers. Recovered assets should become gameplay through
    resale, temporary operation, strategic hold, split liquidation, or acquisition paths.

 18.7 Credit enforcement and institutions across the 1880-1905 campaign

 The spring 1880 economy begins under a developed Dakota Territorial legal framework. Mortgages, liens, exemptions,
 separate property, corporations, banks and municipal institutions already exist. Real-estate mortgages are liens rather
 than automatic title transfers, and foreclosure or chattel enforcement is asset-specific and staged. A one-year
 real-estate redemption period is a strong territorial anchor; exact notice and court procedure can be compressed where
 gameplay does not need the detail. The Black Hills interest regime changes during the campaign: the general opening
 framework uses seven percent as the legal/default rate and permits written contracts up to twelve percent; from 1881
 through June 30, 1887, covered Black Hills written contracts may set any mutually agreed rate; the general ceiling
 returns July 1, 1887. Lenders still price loans according to actual risk and liquidity rather than automatically charging
 the legal maximum. Banking and corporate organization predate statehood. A First National Bank operated in
 Deadwood before the campaign, demonstrating that the absence of a bank in the player's tiny opening town is an
 economic bankability issue rather than a legal or technological one. Congress's July 30, 1886 territorial restrictions
 matter to civic finance and railroad promotion: territorial local governments face a four-percent general debt ceiling
 and cannot treat municipal credit or corporate subscription as an unlimited subsidy instrument. South Dakota statehood
 on November 2, 1889 preserves existing contracts, corporations, rights, litigation and obligations rather than resetting
 them. The state constitutional framework uses a five-percent general local debt ceiling and later amendments expand




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 67

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 304/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 flexibility for specified infrastructure. The campaign begins in the 1878-1898 federal bankruptcy gap, so most early
 distress resolves through workouts and territorial/state creditor remedies. The Bankruptcy Act of 1898 takes effect July
 1, 1898 and adds a federal bankruptcy route for qualifying late-campaign debtors. It is not modern Chapter 7/11 and
 should not become a universal reset. Commercial Ruin remains based on the actual exhaustion of ownership and
 recovery capacity.

 18.8 Bank balance sheet and liquidity doctrine

 A player-owned bank must operate as a business with both assets and liabilities. Deposits are money the bank owes to
 depositors, not free owner cash. Loans and other earning assets can generate income while tying up funds. Cash and
 liquid correspondent balances protect the ability to meet withdrawals and settle obligations but usually earn less.
 Recovered property can have value without being liquid. The central banking decision is therefore how aggressively to
 turn available funds into earning assets while preserving enough liquidity to survive ordinary and stressed withdrawals.
 Do not reduce this to one Reserve slider that directly grants profit or safety; policy should matter through the actual
 composition and timing of the bank's commitments.

 18.9 Loan-book construction, concentration and maturity mismatch

 Loan quality is portfolio-specific. A bank can be profitable yet dangerously concentrated in one mine district, cattle
 market, railroad project, speculative property boom or connected borrower group. The player should be able to review
 exposure by borrower, purpose, collateral family, settlement node and sector without receiving perfect future
 knowledge. Short working-capital lending, longer property debt and major infrastructure financing create different
 timing. A bank that funds long, illiquid assets with deposits that can be withdrawn quickly carries liquidity risk even
 when most borrowers remain solvent. Seasonal agriculture, payroll cycles, construction and tax or trade timing can
 create predictable cash-demand periods that a prudent banker learns to prepare for.

 18.10 Deposit relationships and confidence

 Deposits should come from actual households, businesses, institutions and counterparties that choose where to keep
 money when local banking exists. Their choice can reflect convenience, safety perception, relationship, service,
 confidence, the bank's owner reputation and available terms where historically supported. Large depositors create
 useful funding but concentration risk: losing one mine payroll account or major merchant balance can matter more than
 many small withdrawals. A bank run is therefore an extreme acceleration of a real liability, not a random event card.
 Rumor can matter only because depositors already have funds they can attempt to withdraw. Confidence can recover
 through credible liquidity, continued payment, outside support, improved balance sheet condition and time; a cosmetic
 reputation purchase should not stop a real run.

 18.11 Correspondent access, outside capital and panic transmission

 Local banking remains connected to wider finance. Correspondent or outside balances can support settlement,
 remittance and liquidity, while dependence on those relationships can transmit distant stress inward. Historical banking
 panics show interior banks withdrawing balances from money-center banks and money-center strain then restricting
 currency back to the interior. Land & Ledgers should preserve that two-way dependency without simulating the national
 financial system bank by bank. During an outside panic, correspondent availability, withdrawal demand, asset
 saleability and new-loan appetite can all worsen through separate channels. A conservative local bank may remain
 open but tighten credit; an overextended bank may suspend or fail.

 18.12 Bank income, operating cost and the cost of being conservative

 A bank earns through interest, fees and other supported financial services while paying staff, premises, communication,
 legal/collection and loss costs. Holding more liquidity can reduce earnings because fewer funds are deployed; pushing
 nearly every available dollar into loans can increase short-run income while making withdrawal stress dangerous.
 Lending to familiar insiders may reduce information cost and also create concentration or conflict. The player should
 face real tradeoffs between growth, liquidity, credit quality, customer service and strategic influence rather than
 maximizing a single interest-rate control.

 18.13 Workouts, foreclosure assets and bad-debt resolution

 A defaulted loan does not instantly turn collateral into cash. Workouts can preserve value when a viable borrower needs
 time, but they can also delay an inevitable loss. Enforcement can leave the bank holding a house, farm, store,
 inventory, machinery or business that requires management, maintenance, rent collection, sale effort or temporary
 operation. Recovered assets can depress reported loan losses while creating new liquidity and management problems.
 The player can liquidate quickly at a discount, hold for a better market, appoint management, restructure the borrower
 or sell to another investor when law and the asset permit it. This makes bad debt part of ownership gameplay rather





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 68

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 305/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 than a red number that disappears after foreclosure.

 18.14 Bank governance, conflicts and institutional reputation

 Owning a bank creates power and scrutiny. The player can finance projects, rivals, suppliers, customers and
 settlements, but repeated self-serving credit denial or unsafe insider concentration can weaken depositor confidence,
 relationships and institutional standing even when technically legal. The game should not apply a moral score to
 aggressive banking. Consequences should arise because counterparties notice patterns, rival lenders recruit
 customers, depositors protect themselves, borrowers seek alternatives and the bank's own risk becomes concentrated.
 Delegated officers can handle ordinary underwriting inside policy while large connected loans, strategic conflicts,
 workouts and unusual collateral rise to the owner.

 18.15 Banking completeness test

 Banking is deep enough when the same nominal level of deposits can support very different outcomes depending on
 liquidity posture, loan quality, sector concentration, maturity, confidence, correspondent access and management. A
 bank should be capable of failing while owning valuable assets, surviving a panic while reducing new credit, earning
 less because it deliberately holds more liquidity, or becoming regionally influential because its underwriting and deposit
 relationships are strong. It must never function as an infinite-money business merely because the player owns the
 institution.

PART X


 Rail, Communications, Utilities & Capital Development Networks that reshape geography, information, power and
 capital command.

  READING RULE This part is the authoritative home for the systems listed here. Related appendices compress the same
   rules for

 routing and summary; they do not override the body.

  CANON LOCK

 2.4 Railway arrival design lock

 Rail is not present locally at the spring 1880 start and should never be treated as a cosmetic flip. The wider Black Hills
 economy still relies heavily on distant external railheads and long overland wagon legs, while industrial rail inside the
 Hills and outside common-carrier penetration are only beginning to develop. Regional railway expansion therefore
 affects the player before local track arrives: the nearest practical rail interface can move closer, shortening wagon legs,
 changing delivered cost, supplier choice and market reach. Local service remains an independent corporate decision
 shaped by network strategy, engineering, land access, rival towns, expected traffic, townsite opportunity and railroad
 finance.

 2.5 Telegraph follow-through and electricity timing

 Telegraph, telephone, electricity and civic infrastructure should no longer be written as sequential steps behind rail.
 Telegraph already exists unevenly in the Black Hills by 1880; telephone lines and exchange enterprise also appear
 exceptionally early; electric lighting becomes commercially available during the 1880s; waterworks already exist in
 exceptional dense towns. Rail commonly accelerates all of these by improving transport, capital and corridor
 economics, but each network has its own adoption logic and can move ahead or lag behind the others.

 20.1 Private but public-facing rail

 Railways in Land & Ledgers should feel private, profit-seeking, and strategically independent while remaining deeply
 entangled with land politics, approvals, town pressure, freight demand, and capital markets. The player can eventually
 become a railway promoter, land assembler, financier, founder, owner, or controlling industrial customer once wealth
 and opportunity justify it. Outside railway companies should evaluate the region for their own network reasons; a
 commercially strong town can gain negotiating leverage and still be bypassed.

 20.2 Corridor projects rather than freehand city-builder track

 The player should not become a city-builder track painter. The stronger design is corridor projects. Inside town, the
 player secures rights-of- way, acquires strips, chooses depot and station sites, and approves corridor segments and
 sidings. Outside town, expansion becomes an abstracted rail project to named off-map destinations. Distance, grading
 difficulty, bridges, river crossings, tunnels, and route-choice modifiers affect cost and viability. Some routes will be
 straightforward, some will be expensive, some will demand a bridge or tunnel, and some may simply not be worth the
 capital at the current stage.

 20.3 Required facilities and commercial geography

 A rail company should need more than track alone. Core facilities can include depot, freight handling area, maintenance
 shed or light service building, fuel and water support, sidings and later more specialized service infrastructure. Rail
 arrival creates new commercial geography, but depot location is only potential gravity: road access, available land,
 distance from the old core and established business strength determine whether a second commercial center actually
 forms.

 20.4 Materials integration and owned supply chains

 Rail construction and operation should benefit from owned supply chains, but only where the portfolio actually controls
 a historically plausible input. Player-owned timber, lumber, grading/earthwork capacity, hauling, land, blacksmith
 repair, local hardware, and in some runs regional fuel can make a project cheaper or more reliable. Rails, heavy
 machinery, and much finished iron or steel normally remain wider- market manufactured inputs; owning a local
 iron-bearing claim does not create an integrated rail-steel industry. Internal ownership should reduce real middleman,
 transport, and coordination costs rather than granting a generic construction discount.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 70

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 307/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


 20.5 Off-map expansion logic

 The player should be able to expand from the current named town to off-map destinations without the project needing
 a full simulated region of hand-built towns. Off-map destination projects should calculate distance, base materials and
 labor needs, route modifiers, and

 expected commercial value. The line therefore becomes a strategic frontier infrastructure project rather than a
 requirement to fully simulate every settlement along the way.

 20.6 Railroad corporate strategy, negotiation, and bypass

 Outside railroad interest should become visible before commitment. A plausible progression is regional observation ->
 preliminary interest -> survey activity -> competing-route consideration -> local negotiation -> conditional
 commitment -> construction. Surveyors, newspaper discussion, land speculation, rival-town lobbying, depot
 negotiation, and right-of-way requests should make the decision readable before track appears. The player can
 materially improve Commercial Attractiveness and reduce Construction/Acquisition Burden by generating recurring
 freight, assembling or donating right-of-way, providing depot land, supporting grading or local materials, contributing
 capital, or organizing public aid. The player cannot directly command an outside company's Strategic Interest. A
 railroad may choose cheaper terrain, a rival town, a railroad-controlled townsite, or another network direction even
 when the player's town is commercially useful. A bypass can create a new depot node whose warehouses, hotels,
 yards, businesses, and housing pull activity away from the original settlement. Valuable regions can also attract
 competing railroads. Separately, a large mine, logging operation, smelter, or industrial portfolio may justify a captive or
 industrial railway before a full public common-carrier route becomes attractive.

 20.7 Moving railheads and the 1880-1905 regional chronology

 Every settlement should know its current practical rail interface rather than only whether local track exists. Useful
 access states include remote from rail, distant railhead access, nearby regional railhead, approaching/surveyed
 corridor, local depot service and junction or competing service. Freight can change railheads as new lines open, so a
 store may receive cheaper or faster goods years before its own town gains a station. The regional historical guide is
 deliberately non-scripted: distant railheads dominate around 1880; Homestake-style industrial narrow-gauge operation
 becomes plausible around 1881; outside rail reaches the southern Black Hills in 1885, Rapid City in 1886 and
 Whitewood in 1887; local/interurban lines appear by the late 1880s; major Deadwood, Belle Fourche, Hot Springs and
 Hill City connections develop around 1890-91; and by 1900 the Hills possess a substantial multi-company network.
 Major east-west South Dakota integration is still being built in 1905: work on the Chicago & North Western temporary
 Missouri River crossing at Pierre begins in November 1905 and the first official train crosses shortly before Christmas,
 with the permanent bridge following later. Industrial rail, local/interurban rail and regional common-carrier rail are
 distinct business scales. Wagons remain important after rail by shifting toward depot drayage, feeder routes and
 secondary-node distribution. These dates govern plausibility and outside-world pressure, not automatic calendar
 unlocks for the fictional town.

 20.8 Railway operation after construction

  CANON LOCK Completing track begins a railway operating business; it does not finish one. A working line must turn
   traffic into enough revenue to cover crews,

 fuel, water, stations, maintenance, rolling stock, administration, debt and periodic capital repair. A lightly used but
 expensive corridor can therefore become a financial burden even if it was strategically satisfying to build. The railway's
 core management loop should be traffic, rate/service policy, capacity, reliability, maintenance and capital allocation -
 not full train dispatch.

 20.9 Freight classes, tariffs and rate policy

 Rail freight historically used explicit rates and commodity/classification systems. The game should compress this into a
 manageable set of economically distinct traffic classes rather than price every historical tariff line. Bulk low-value
 freight, livestock, ordinary merchandise, higher-value goods and unusually difficult or perishable traffic can differ in
 rate, handling and capacity burden. Rates should normally be quoted by route and class with enough visibility that a
 mine, ranch, merchant or competing town can compare rail with wagon or another carrier. Cheap rates can stimulate
 traffic but consume capacity at low margin; high rates can protect margin while driving shippers toward alternatives or
 political pressure.

 20.10 Shipper commitments, traffic base and line utilization

 A new line should be bankable partly because someone is expected to ship on it. Mines, mills, ranches, merchants,
 grain shippers, lumber businesses and later connecting railroads can provide anchor traffic through expected volume or




                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 71

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 308/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 formal commitments where appropriate. The player can build speculative capacity ahead of demand, but the financial
 risk remains. Line utilization should emerge from actual traffic rather than a generic railway-level stat. A railway may be
 busy in one season and weak in another, profitable on one segment and underused on a branch, or dependent on one
 mine whose closure suddenly destroys the traffic base.

 20.11 Service frequency, reliability and rolling capacity

 Customers care not only that track exists, but how often and how reliably service actually moves. More frequent service
 can reduce inventory waiting and improve shipper value, but it requires locomotives or motive power, cars, crews,
 fuel/water and maintenance capacity. Too little equipment creates delays and lost traffic; too much creates idle capital.
 Breakdowns, washouts, bridge trouble, fuel shortage, crew shortage or congestion can reduce service through real
 operating constraints. The player should decide broad service posture and capital additions rather than route individual
 trains minute by minute.

 20.12 Depot handling, sidings and wagon interface

 The depot is a transfer machine between rail and the rest of the regional economy. Freight still has to be received,
 stored where necessary, loaded, unloaded, documented and moved by wagon to its final local destination. Siding,
 platform, yard and storage capacity can become bottlenecks even when the main line has spare capacity. Good road
 access and drayage services increase the practical value of a depot. This preserves the wagon economy after rail
 arrival and gives freight firms a new role rather than making them obsolete.

20.12A Rail transforms old businesses rather than merely obsoleting them

 Rail arrival should recontextualize the wagon economy. Long-haul wagon routes can decline while depot drayage,
 farm/ranch collection, mine feeder service and secondary-node hauling grow. Warehouses and commercial frontage
 may relocate. The original store can gain access to distant manufactured goods while facing mail-order or outside
 competition. Old freight businesses can pivot into local distribution. This is the preferred modernization pattern
 throughout Land & Ledgers: history asks new questions of existing assets before it adds a replacement business
 category.

 20.13 Passenger, mail and express as secondary service layers

 Passenger, mail and express traffic can exist where corridor scale and historical circumstances justify it, but they should
 not displace freight as the main commercial reason most player rail projects matter. Passenger service can support
 settlement access, commercial travel and town prestige while carrying its own equipment, schedule and station
 burden. Mail or express contracts can provide useful recurring revenue where researched. These layers should enter
 only when they create a meaningful operating decision rather than because every railway menu is expected to contain
 every historical department.

 20.14 Competition, interchange and route capture

 A second railroad can change the economics of the first even without duplicating every track. Competing service can
 force better rates, improve shipper options, redirect through traffic or weaken a monopoly depot district. Junctions and
 interchange can add traffic but also make the line dependent on another carrier's connection. Large shippers can gain
 bargaining leverage when carriers compete for their traffic. A captive industrial line has different incentives from a
 public common carrier: its main purpose may be lowering an owned mine or mill's logistics cost rather than maximizing
 third-party freight revenue.

 20.15 Interstate Commerce Act boundary after 1887

 Where a player common carrier participates in interstate commerce, the Interstate Commerce Act of February 4, 1887
 changes the legal envelope. The Act requires just and reasonable charges, public rate schedules, prohibits special
 rebates and undue preferences, restricts long-haul/short-haul discrimination and creates the Interstate Commerce
 Commission. Historical enforcement was imperfect and contested, so this should constrain available rate practices
 rather than create perfect regulation. A purely local industrial or intrastate operation may sit under a different legal
 regime. The player should not be asked to litigate rate cases routinely, but a railroad strategy that relies on secret
 discriminatory rates should become legally and reputationally riskier after 1887.

 20.16 Maintenance, renewal and capital discipline

 Track, bridges, culverts, water/fuel facilities, rolling stock and depots are durable assets that wear and can become
 unreliable. Deferred maintenance can preserve cash during a bad year while increasing delay, failure and later repair
 burden. Heavy traffic can accelerate wear and justify stronger maintenance capacity. Expansion, replacement and debt
 service compete for the same capital. This ties railway ownership back into the shared condition, bookkeeping, finance





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 72

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 309/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 and executive systems instead of making the railroad a separate empire game.

 20.17 Railway completeness test

 Railway ownership is deep enough when a player can make a good corridor fail through bad rates, weak service,
 overbuilding, poor maintenance or dangerous debt, and can make a modest corridor valuable through strong traffic
 commitments, disciplined capacity, reliable interchange and useful depot geography. The intended fantasy is owning
 and directing a transportation business, not painting track or dispatching every train.

 22.1 Telegraph timing and corridor logic

 Telegraph is already part of the wider Black Hills communications environment in spring 1880. Deadwood and other
 important corridor nodes received telegraphic service in the 1870s, so the opening town is information-poor because
 direct access is uneven, not because the technology does not exist. Telegraph tends to follow useful stage, military,
 mining, federal, commercial or railway corridors. A line passing a region, practical access to an office and a functioning
 local commercial office are separate states.

 22.2 Gameplay effects

 Telegraph changes the speed and reach of information, not the physical movement of goods. Market quotations,
 supplier availability, distressed-sale notices, bank or lender messages, railroad negotiations, and other short
 commercial information can arrive much sooner, while actual inventory still follows the freight system. Information
 should carry an age and source: a market quote received by telegraph this morning is different from a newspaper or
 letter several days old. Telegraph access does not create omniscience; messages can be brief, costly, incomplete,
 mistaken, promotional, or strategically misleading.

 22.3 Business implications

 A telegraph office or communication-linked service can exist as its own business or service node where demand
 supports it. The normal 70- 85-person opening settlement should not have a direct office unless a specific stage,
 military, mining, federal or through-corridor reason justifies it, but it can still use indirect service by physically carrying
 urgent messages to the nearest wired node. Faster communication improves supplier negotiation, emergency sourcing,
 credit decisions and rail operations while also accelerating rumor and financial contagion.

 22.4 Telegraph access states and information age

 Telegraph access should progress from mail/traveler only -> courier-to-wire access -> regular access through a nearby
 telegraph node -> local telegraph office -> rail-integrated/mature communications node. The first and last leg of a
 message can therefore remain physical even when the long-distance portion travels by wire. Important information
 should retain source, sent time, received time and information age. Telegraph reduces delay rather than granting a
 market-awareness bonus. It remains best for short urgent written messages; letters, invoices, contracts, catalogues and
 other detailed documents continue to use physical mail. National telegraph coverage expands rapidly through the
 1880s and 1890s, so the outside information network becomes denser even when the player takes no direct action.

 22.5 Telephone as a parallel communications network

 Telephone technology is already exceptionally early in the Black Hills at the spring 1880 opening. Deadwood sources
 record telephone lines by 1878, the 1880 federal census records a Deadwood telephone exchange with subscribers,
 and a Rockerville/Rapid City telephone and telegraph company was incorporated in April 1880. The exact organizational
 date of the earliest Deadwood exchange is disputed, so canon locks only the broader fact that regional telephone
 service exists by the opening years of the 1880s. Telephone and telegraph are complementary. Telegraph is the
 stronger mature long-distance written network; early telephone is primarily immediate spoken communication among
 local or shorter-distance connected endpoints. A telephone call can eliminate messenger delay between a store, bank,
 freight office, hotel, manager or mine, but goods, workers, doctors and wagons still travel physically. Spoken calls also
 do not automatically create the documentary record of a telegram or signed letter. Telephone service should be
 subscriber-based and physical. Adoption can begin with a private point-to-point line between high-value sites, then
 grow into a local exchange with switchboard and operators, expanded subscriber coverage, toll/inter-town connections
 and later regional or rural/mutual service. Network value rises as more useful subscribers join, while sparse extensions
 still carry real pole, wire, maintenance and staffing costs.

 22.6 Telephone ownership, competition and late-campaign growth

 A Telephone Company is a legitimate infrastructure ownership path. Early networks can face stronger proprietary or
 licensing barriers; independent-company formation becomes much more plausible in the mid-1890s as key patent
 restrictions weaken. Competing Bell- associated, independent or mutual systems may have different coverage and





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 73

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 310/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 need not automatically interconnect, making subscriber base, compatibility, toll access and acquisition meaningful
 business assets. Rural/mutual telephone expansion becomes increasingly plausible around 1900-05, allowing remote
 farms or ranches to gain voice service before they gain electric utility service. Telephone should also support the
 executive-management transition. As the portfolio grows, connected managers can report and coordinate remotely,
 giving the later UI a physical historical reason to move from constant owner travel toward delegated oversight.
 Technology reduces communication delay; it does not create free automation or perfect knowledge.

  CANON LOCK

 23.1 Electricity eligibility and narrow rollout

 Electricity is absent from the normal spring 1880 opening settlement for both chronological and economic reasons.
 Commercial electric lighting is only beginning nationally, so period technology availability and local viability must be
 treated separately. The player does not research electricity as an invention; equipment and engineering become
 purchasable through the wider economy over time, while concentrated paying demand, capital, generation opportunity
 and distribution economics determine whether a particular node adopts it.

 23.2 Generation paths and existing industrial power

 Generation depends on local resources and existing industrial infrastructure rather than one universal coal-steam
 template. Black Hills precedent strongly supports waterpower, steam power, and combined water/steam systems,
 including dynamos added to mills or mining facilities. A dedicated steam central station remains valid where fuel supply
 and demand justify it, but coal should not be the mandatory first fuel. Large mines, mills, hotels, or other concentrated
 users can justify isolated generation before a broad town utility exists and may later become the foundation of wider
 service.

 23.3 Ownership and business model

 The first broad town service will most often be a privately financed Electric Light or Light & Power Company operating
 under a local franchise or permission to use streets and rights-of-way, although municipal ownership remains possible.
 Founding or acquiring the utility requires a viable plant site, generating equipment, capital, anchor demand, operator
 coverage and physical distribution. Early effects begin with illumination rather than universal motor power. Arc lighting
 is especially appropriate for streets and large spaces; incandescent lighting expands the useful interior customer base
 as equipment becomes available. Electricity does not create a universal productivity modifier or instant rural
 modernity.

 23.4 Distribution geography, load, and reliability

 Electricity is delivered through generation, poles/wires and specific connected customers rather than a townwide
 boolean. Early local systems are geographically compact, making plant location, customer density, water/fuel access
 and distribution buildout strategically important. Connected load matters more than customer count: a mine, mill, hotel
 or street-lighting contract can justify more capacity than many small houses. Improved alternating-current equipment
 during the late 1880s and 1890s gradually makes more distant generation and larger service territories economical
 without requiring the player to configure voltage, frequency or transformer engineering. Early service need not operate
 continuously. Some plants can produce primarily during evening lighting hours or industrial shifts. Generator, boiler,
 water, machinery, operator, pole, or line failures should affect the customers actually dependent on that system.
 Kerosene, candles, and other lighting fuels should decline gradually in connected districts rather than disappearing
 from the regional economy.

 23.5 Electrical technology progression, 1880-1905

 Spring 1880 is near the beginning of commercial electric-light adoption. The normal opening settlement has no electric
 service. Deadwood electric lighting in 1883, Rapid City and Homestake-era late-1880s installations, Hot Springs wiring
 around 1891, Spearfish hydroelectric development around 1893, Black Hills AC-era projects in the 1890s, the
 Deadwood-Lead electric local railway around 1901 and

 utility/steam-turbine consolidation around 1904-05 define a widening capability envelope rather than scripted unlock
 dates. Arc lighting can precede broad incandescent interiors; electricity begins primarily as lighting rather than instant
 motorization. Steam engines, water wheels, belts and line shafts remain useful for years. By 1905 a strong town or
 mine can plausibly possess a meaningful electrical network, but rural electric service remains unusual and a nearby
 primitive settlement can still have none. The intended end state is a mixed-power frontier- industrial economy rather
 than a universal electrified modern world.

 23.6 Utility consolidation, labor and changing markets





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 74

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 311/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 Electrification creates new skilled work for operators, electricians and line-maintenance staff. Small early utilities and
 isolated generators can later be purchased, merged, enlarged, relocated or retired as networks mature. A player can
 therefore evolve from an isolated mill or mine dynamo into a local light company and eventually a multi-node utility,
 while old generating equipment may retain resale or relocation value. Electricity should alter existing markets
 gradually. Connected businesses can operate effectively later into the evening; lighting-fuel demand weakens first in
 serviced commercial districts while rural and unconnected demand persists; and obsolete inventory risk can emerge for
 merchants that overstock products whose demand is being displaced. These effects arise from actual service coverage
 and customer behavior rather than generic modernization bonuses.

 24.1 Capital-command phase

 Late game in Land & Ledgers is the capital-command phase. The player has delegated routine operations to managers
 and trusted staff, relies heavily on reports, audits, and portfolio oversight, and begins shaping the town through
 institutions and infrastructure rather than only through individual storefront optimization. Major late-game ventures
 include banks, railway companies, mines, utility plants, remote industrial chains, and later luxury or investment-linked
 commerce.

 24.2 Luxury, investing, and civic-commercial prestige

 As wealth grows, new late-game opportunities become plausible: jewelry or precious-goods trade linked to gold and
 silver output, investment office functions linked to stocks or bonds, finance-market intermediation, or other prestige
 commercial institutions that make sense once the town and the player both command substantial capital. These should
 not arrive as random rich-person toys. They should grow out of the same ownership-led logic as everything else: control
 of supply, financing power, information advantage, and regional seriousness.

 24.3 The town still matters

 Even in the late game, the player should not mentally leave the town behind. The town remains the proving ground. A
 railway changes its geography. A bank changes its credit environment. A mine changes its labor and service pressure. A
 utility changes its night economy. The fantasy is not escaping the simulation; it is becoming powerful enough to
 redirect it.

 24.4 Final late-game lock

 The late game should not simply be bigger menus. It should be the phase where earlier businesses, land, supply chains,
 and reputation finally pay off in institutions that reshape the town and region. That is the full commercial arc this
 edition is intended to preserve. Appendices The appendices below are intentionally practical. They are not decorative
 filler. They are quick-reference surfaces meant to preserve current locks, future late-game identity, and scope-aware
 caution.

PART XI


 Executive & Portfolio Management Delegation, diagnosis and owner attention at portfolio scale.

  READING RULE This part is the authoritative home for the systems listed here. Related appendices compress the same
   rules for

 routing and summary; they do not override the body.

 19.1 Why the executive layer exists

 Late game in Land & Ledgers should not mean the player manually revisits every store to check margins one by one
 forever. Once the portfolio is large enough, the player should be able to rely on trusted staff and contracted specialists.
 This is the difference between owning several businesses and running an actual frontier business empire.

 19.2 Auditor and inspector roles

 An auditor, inspector, or efficiency specialist is a strong late-game role. The player can hire one as payroll staff or
 contract one for a one-off review. That specialist can inspect a business, mine, livery, hotel, or other operation and
 return a grounded report on margins, staffing, stock discipline, supplier drag, local demand fit, condition, management
 weakness, and whether the business should be stabilized, expanded, sold, or closed. The auditor should not be a
 magical truth button. They are an informed professional lens that shortens diagnosis and helps the player act at
 portfolio scale.

 19.3 Delegated approvals and policy bands

 Delegated authority begins below the executive-office scale. A business manager can receive owner-defined permission
 over routine staffing, operating hours, merchandise allocation, reorder policy, supplier changes, pricing bands,
 customer-credit decisions and minor repairs. The owner can set thresholds or require approval for new product lines,
 large customer exposure, major supplier changes, capital projects, debt, asset sales or other strategic commitments.
 Executive office roles later extend the same principle across the portfolio: small cash transfers, low-risk loans, routine
 supply contracts or modest repairs can be handled under policy while high-value acquisitions, major distress actions,
 railway corridors or infrastructure commitments rise to the owner. Delegation should preserve owner agency by making
 exceptions and policy boundaries meaningful rather than turning management into a flat automation bonus.

 19.4 Closure, sale, and turnaround recommendations

 A core job of late-game staff is not just optimizing healthy businesses but identifying weak ones before they become
 permanent sinkholes. An auditor or portfolio agent should be able to recommend soft turnaround, management
 replacement, aggressive re-stock, controlled wind- down, sale to another owner, or full closure. These
 recommendations should be grounded in observed conditions and local evidence rather than raw abstract ratings. A
 weak business in a rising district might deserve patience; an overbuilt service in a stagnant pocket might be better sold
 before more capital is wasted.

 19.5 Office roles beyond auditor

 Other executive roles can emerge over time: portfolio bookkeeper, acquisitions agent, rail superintendent, bank
 manager, mine superintendent, legal or title runner, or utility manager. The design goal is not to create a bureaucratic
 layer for its own sake. The goal is to make late-game delegation legible, grounded, and deeply tied to ownership
 fantasy.

 19.6 Exception management and owner attention

 Late-game scale should create an attention problem without inventing a visible 'attention points' currency. The portfolio
 generates exceptions: a manager requests a large repair, a business misses its cash reserve, a supplier fails, a bank
 exposure breaches policy, a mine superintendent asks for capital, or an acquisition reaches a decision deadline.
 Delegation absorbs routine work when it stays inside policy. The owner becomes involved when something crosses a
 threshold, conflicts with another policy or requires authority that was never delegated. A well-run organization
 therefore feels quieter because it produces fewer unresolved exceptions, not because the game simply hides more
 information.

 19.7 Manager competence, style and organizational memory





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 76

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 313/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 Managers should differ through experience, domain familiarity, judgment and policy preference rather than through
 universal percentage buffs. One manager may be conservative with inventory and cash, another aggressive on sales
 and credit, another unusually good at labor retention. Their choices still operate through the same causal systems.
 Long-serving staff can accumulate valuable knowledge of suppliers, workers, recurring customers, property and local
 seasons. Losing them can therefore create an information and continuity shock even when the replacement has similar
 nominal skill. The player can standardize policy across the portfolio but should still feel that people are administering it.

 19.8 Shared portfolio services and earned synergies

 A large portfolio can centralize work such as bookkeeping, purchasing, legal/title review, acquisitions, treasury,
 maintenance coordination or logistics planning only when the player actually hires the staff and creates the
 relationships needed to do it. Central purchasing can combine recurring demand into stronger supplier terms if orders,
 transport and storage really can be consolidated. A portfolio bookkeeper can improve reporting across several
 businesses because one office is processing the records. A repair department can serve multiple properties if it has
 workers, tools, materials and travel capacity. No 'corporate office' building should grant a generic empire efficiency
 bonus. Synergy is earned through shared capability and scale.

 19.9 Treasury and capital allocation

 The executive layer should make capital allocation one of the central late-game decisions. The owner can retain cash,
 transfer capital between owned businesses where legally and structurally permitted, pay down debt, support a
 distressed but strategic operation, expand a strong business, fund a new corridor, hold liquidity for a downturn, buy a
 rival or distribute/withdraw owner cash. Managers can recommend uses of capital but should not silently move large
 sums across business boundaries without authority. Portfolio performance should therefore be more than the sum of
 individual profit margins: timing and allocation of scarce capital determine which parts of the empire survive and
 compound.

19.9A Talent allocation and portfolio triage

 Capital is not the only scarce late-game resource. A player can have enough money to acquire another business but no
 trustworthy person capable of running it. Senior clerks, foremen, managers, bookkeepers, superintendents and
 specialists can therefore compete for assignment across the portfolio. The principal may promote internally, recruit,
 relocate a manager, supervise personally, delay the acquisition or sell another operation.

 Mature play must also make divestment legitimate. The owner should increasingly ask what not to own. Sale, closure,
 liquidation, lease, restructuring, manager buyout, minority sale, capital withdrawal and strategic abandonment can all
 be rational responses. A portfolio that only grows by accumulating permanent holdings will eventually become the
 same panel multiplied twenty times; capital command requires pruning as well as acquisition.

 19.10 Portfolio policy, local autonomy and escalation

 The player can set portfolio-wide standards - minimum cash reserve, maximum customer-credit exposure, maintenance
 escalation, acquisition return expectations, manager approval limits or preferred internal suppliers - while allowing local
 managers to deviate when authorized. Too much centralization can produce slow or poorly fitted decisions; too much
 autonomy can create hidden risk and inconsistent strategy. Exceptions should explain why local conditions make the
 standard policy awkward. The player can then approve the deviation, change the policy or replace management. This
 creates governance rather than automation.

 19.11 Partners, minority capital and governance conflict

 Where a business or project includes outside investors, silent partners or other meaningful co-owners, the player should
 not behave as if 51 percent economic interest necessarily means unlimited freedom from all agreed obligations.
 Partnership terms can constrain distributions, new borrowing, sale, major expansion or related-party deals where the
 financing structure makes that appropriate. The design does not need a corporate-law simulator, but outside capital
 should preserve the central bargain from 18.3A: sharing risk can also mean sharing control or upside. A partner dispute
 should emerge from a real strategic or financial conflict rather than a random relationship event.

19.11A Economic interest and control rights are separate

 Shared ownership should distinguish economic interest, capital responsibility, ordinary management authority,
 reserved decisions, distributions and exit/buyout rights where the arrangement makes those terms meaningful. A
 forty-percent interest does not automatically grant forty percent of every decision, and a majority economic interest
 does not erase contractual protections given to other investors. This is not an excuse for a corporate-law minigame; it is
 the minimum needed for partnerships, syndicates and minority capital to create real trade-offs rather than functioning
 as free money.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 77

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 314/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE


 19.12 Communication infrastructure and portfolio reach

 The executive transition should have a physical information basis. Telegraph can accelerate written reports and urgent
 instructions; telephone connections can allow rapid conversation between connected businesses, managers, banks,
 depots and industrial sites; improved rail and roads can shorten personal inspection travel. These networks reduce
 delay but do not make remote management omniscient. An unconnected mine or distant property can still produce
 stale reports and require travel or a trusted superintendent. This keeps modernization relevant to how the player
 manages, not only to what the town looks like.

19.12A Information distance and organizational truth

 Remote ownership should distinguish at least four conceptual layers when the distinction matters: World Truth, Local
 Recorded/Observed Truth, Last Reported Owner Knowledge and Management Interpretation/Forecast. The simulation
 can know a remote business's exact current state while the owner possesses yesterday's telegraph summary or last
 week's written report. This should not become an annoyance that hides every owned number. Use information delay
 where it creates a real economic choice, exception or risk. Communication technology changes how quickly authority
 can be exercised; it does not move goods or make local records automatically correct.

19.12B Central offices solve real coordination problems

 A central office, headquarters or portfolio office is justified when it consolidates records, correspondence, treasury,
 specialist review, purchasing support or exception reporting for a geographically distributed organization. It should not
 grant a generic Headquarters +20% Efficiency bonus. Its value comes from reduced duplicated administrative work,
 faster comparison, more reliable reporting and concentrated specialist capability, while also creating salaries, overhead
 and possible single points of failure.

 19.13 Executive failure and key-person risk

 Delegation creates new failure modes. A dishonest or weak manager can conceal problems if records and oversight are
 poor; an overworked portfolio bookkeeper can fall behind; a superintendent can leave for a rival; one acquisitions agent
 can become a bottleneck; a centralized purchasing office can create a single point of failure. The answer should be
 better controls, redundancy, staffing and inspection where justified, not a permanent executive-risk debuff. Small
 portfolios should not need an expensive bureaucracy; large portfolios should feel the value and cost of building one.

 19.14 Executive completeness test

 The executive layer is deep enough when growth changes what the owner does rather than merely reducing clicks.
 Early play is dominated by direct operating choices. Mid-game play adds manager policy and exceptions. Late play
 increasingly asks where capital, authority, specialist attention and information should flow across a portfolio. The player
 should still be able to inspect one store or household in detail, but the primary late-game skill becomes diagnosing and
 governing interconnected assets without receiving magical automation.

PART XII


 Interface & Player Information Design How deep simulation is compressed into readable ownership decisions without
 exposing implementation detail.

  READING RULE This part is the authoritative home for player-facing information hierarchy, management surfaces and
   workflow presentation.

 Technical architecture, persistence, system cadence and Unity implementation live in the separate Technical
 Implementation Bible and do not belong to the design canon except where a technical constraint is explicitly elevated
 into a design decision.

 15.1 Core UI structure

 The UI should read like a clean frontier business ledger, not parchment fantasy clutter. Deep simulation should live
 beneath compact, readable management surfaces. The always-visible HUD should show Liquid Cash, Net Worth, date,
 day of week, season, time speed, and alert strip. Businesses should share one common UI shell with business-specific
 panels layered on top. Household panels should stay lighter and focused on composition, reserves, pressure, and
 settlement state.

 15.2 Tabs and workflows

 Tabs remain overview, browsing, and launch-point surfaces. Loans and acquisitions should break into dedicated
 workflow screens once the player enters a serious multi-step process. Acquisition workflow should support land and
 business purchase under one family with staged process flow and a framed live property preview or photograph-like
 render area. Loan workflow should read like a formal application under review rather than instant cash from a tab
 button.

 15.3 Information priority and readability

 Property and acquisition surfaces should show owner name, owner type, sale status or property state, current use and
 suitability, conversion notes, land scorecard, lead source, confidence, urgency, exclusivity, rival interest, and deadline
 where known. Management readability rules matter. Prefer grouped cards, scrollable content regions where needed,
 and confident player-facing copy over dense internal-sounding dumps. Tooltips should behave intelligently near edges
 and corners. General Store information should remain specific to the store; renting and boarding should have their own
 surface. Government or civic information should remain separate from player holdings where practical. The game
 should proactively surface what the player can act on soon: today's pressure, tomorrow's risk, this week's opportunity,
 and this season's drift. Information surfaces should ideally summarize conditions the world has already begun to imply,
 rather than replacing world readability outright. The notice layer should separate opportunities from active pressures.
 Opportunities can include merchant recruitment, empty prime frontage, boarding shortage, blocked settlement, freight
 bottleneck, underused supply, post- boom vacancy, and town not yet serious enough for outside capital. Pressures can
 include worsening shortages, rival movement, pending closures, time-sensitive deals, transport deterioration, civic
 petitions becoming urgent, or corridor-value shifts tied to outside interest.

15.3A New management surfaces: logistics, supply, and settlement nodes

 The management UI should now surface three additional families of information. First, each business should expose a
 Logistics / Transport section showing owned hauling assets, assigned labor, storage/stabling capacity, active routes,
 and hauling mode. Second, the portfolio should expose a Supply & Trade surface where the player can read and edit
 standing supply agreements, route priorities, reserve rules, and overflow policies. Third, the map and settlement UI
 should expose node-level summaries for population, boarding, business mix, freight burden, service coverage, and
 current growth or decline pressure. These surfaces should follow the same design philosophy as the rest of the project:
 compact, ledger-like, grouped, and player-facing. The goal is not to bury the player in freight microdata. The goal is to
 make the consequences of logistics, regional growth, and inter-business chaining legible enough that the player can
 make deliberate ownership decisions instead of guessing at hidden simulation.

15.3B Business policy, capacity, and delegated-authority surfaces

 Business management UI should distinguish operations from administration. The General Store should be able to show
 Total / Allocated / Occupied capacity by Display, Storage and Bulk/Yard; merchandise-line allocation; stock target and
 reorder state; supplier and landed cost; selling price/markup; turnover and stockout history; cash reserve; seasonal
 policy; operating hours; customer-account exposure; and who currently has authority to change each policy. The
 interface should make fast-selling, dead-stock, overallocated, understocked and cash-constrained conditions legible





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 79

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 316/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



 without prescribing one correct answer. Manager delegation should expose permissions and approval thresholds clearly
 enough that the player understands what the manager may decide and what will escalate.

15.3C Maintenance, records, expertise and housing management surfaces

 Revision XI adds four management-surface families that should remain consistent with the clean ledger presentation.
 Asset/maintenance views should list maintainable assets, readable condition/known defects, maintenance backlog,
 next action, required skill/parts and expected downtime rather than health bars. Bookkeeping views should distinguish
 historical actuals, physical counts/reconciliations, receivable aging and forecast values. Expertise views should show
 professional experience and newly available analysis without presenting unexplained RPG bonuses. Residential
 holdings should summarize tenant, rent, arrears, vacancy, condition, debt and maintenance while allowing
 property-level inspection.

15.3D Forecast presentation standard

 Reports should visually distinguish Actual / Known from Forecast / Estimated. Historical sales, purchase costs, invoices,
 cash counts and confirmed balances are exact. Future sales, demand, market value, repair cost before quotation, cash
 at month end, employee retention and other uncertain outcomes can use central estimate, likely range and confidence.
 Where useful, the player can inspect the drivers behind the forecast so expertise assists judgment rather than replacing
 it.

REFERENCE APPENDICES

 The main body remains authoritative; appendices compress design locks, research and routing.

APPENDIX A


 Canon Lock Register

  • Spring 1880 is the authoritative opening; do not revert to 1892.

  • The authored historical horizon is 1905. Open Frontier normally begins in spring 1880 and has no mandatory victory by
    default; Scenarios may use shorter historical windows.

  • No dialogue checks for deals; use grounded business logic.

  • No modern zoning-style parcel hard locks; use suitability, nuisance, frontage, adjacency, access, legal status and
    conversion cost.

  • Businesses share one shared business model; specialized industries extend it rather than becoming disconnected
   minigames.

  • Owner cash and business cash remain separate authorities. Net Worth includes liabilities; borrowing cash does not
    create Net Worth.

  • Commercial Ruin requires actual exhaustion of viable ownership and recovery capacity; one default, foreclosure or
    bankruptcy is not automatic defeat.

  • Supply, price, fire, disease, weather and other shocks must arise through real footprint, exposure, reserves,
    substitutes, networks and recovery rather than universal percentage penalties.

  • Spring 1880 begins without local common-carrier rail; practical railheads can move closer before local service.
    Industrial, local/interurban and regional rail remain distinct.

  • Telegraph and telephone are parallel networks already regionally plausible at the opening. Information has source and
    age; communication does not move goods.

  • The normal opening town has no electric service, broad piped water/sewer network or normal public telephone
   exchange. Utilities are spatial networks with coverage, capacity, condition and project lifecycles.

  • Mining hierarchy remains gold dominant; lead-silver/polymetallic secondary; tin speculative; coal strategic but often
    regional/conditional; iron niche. Mining progression is functional bottlenecks and metallurgy, not mine levels.

  • 1880 agriculture is already partly mechanized by horses. Machinery changes seasonal work capacity, not biological
    yield. Barbed wire and pumping windmills are opening-era technologies; tractors are not normal core progression by
    1905.

  • Dakota Territory already has codified property, mortgage, exemption, banking, corporate and municipal law.
    Statehood in 1889 preserves existing obligations; the 1898 Bankruptcy Act adds a late federal distress route.

  • Restricted Indigenous/reservation/trust land never enters ordinary Make Offer or normal collateral merely because it is
     visible. Current title, transfer status and historical provenance are separate authorities.

  • Allotment is a process, not an 1887/1890 global conversion. The specific Sioux reorganization becomes operative
    February 10, 1890. The player never drives federal dispossession.

  • No generic hostile-Native raids, Indigenous hostility meter, Civilization score or Wounded Knee profit/combat event.

  • Automobiles may appear rarely by 1905 as background/cutting-edge machines; motor freight, tractor farming and
    automobile-road modernization remain outside the normal campaign.

  • Historical availability never overrides production priority. Late systems protect the destination and do not become
   immediate VP scope.

  • If the implemented game already has a stronger, clearer, more grounded or more production-ready mechanic, update
   canon upward rather than downgrading the game.

  • Every mechanic is judged through historical accuracy, maximum plausible player freedom and premium systemic
    readability. Prefer consequences over arbitrary prohibitions.

  • The player is one actual owner/investor, not an omnipotent municipal authority. Direct commands require a legitimate
    ownership, employment, contractual, financial, management or legal basis.

  • Physical Truth is canonical: locally significant purchases, work, deliveries and services resolve only when required
    people/assets actually reach and satisfy the physical interaction; off-map abstraction changes resolution, not reality.

  • The current managing authority - player owner, NPC owner or hired manager - controls administrative business policy.
    Ordinary workers execute tasks; they do not silently redesign the business.

  • Player and NPC businesses use the same meaningful operating levers. NPCs may succeed or fail through their own
    allocation, pricing, credit, staffing, sourcing and cash-management decisions rather than hidden handicaps.

  • General Store inventory uses dedicated physical capacity. Every item consumes space; reserved-but-empty
   merchandise allocation is not automatically available to unrelated goods until administratively reassigned.





                                                                                                    CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE 81

==================== CAN-XXXI ORIGINAL PDF PAGE 318/346 ====================

LAND & LEDGERS / REVISION XIV / CANONICAL PROJECT BIBLE



  • Routine replenishment can be automatic under standing targets and supplier policy, but cash-reserve protection can
    force manual approval. Seasonal merchandise and target profiles are valid owner/manager controls.

  • Labor is ultimately workload- and occupation-dependent rather than one rigid employee-per-task or universal workday
    model. Continuous 24-hour time and seasonally changing daylight are canonical inputs.

  • Customer credit is a shared commercial capability where historically appropriate, with real receivables and liquidity
     risk; ordinary store tabs do not automatically bear interest.

  • Households are the primary domestic economic unit; individual people remain the actual workers, shoppers, travelers,
    health actors and life-cycle participants.

  • Canonical revisions should not decrease in total page count or word count from the immediately previous numbered
    revision. Replace obsolete material when necessary, but preserve useful detail and add meaningful depth rather than
    shrinking the master reference.

  • Known facts remain exact when legitimately possessed. Expertise may improve interpretation and forecasting but
   must not blur confirmed purchase costs, invoices, counted cash, recorded balances or other known values into
     artificial uncertainty.

  • Experience/Expertise, Commercial Standing and world Modernization are separate progression authorities. Expertise
    cannot research future technology into existence; Standing cannot substitute for skill; skill cannot create unexplained
    discounts or physical bonuses.

  • Asset maintenance is causal. Use/load/exposure/age/defects create deterioration; service and repair require real labor,
    parts, facilities and downtime. Deferred maintenance is allowed and produces asset-specific consequences rather than
   a universal penalty.

  • Repair work is a real service market generated by actual assets. Blacksmithing, horseshoeing, wagon/wheel work,
    harness work and later machine repair are capabilities that may combine or specialize according to people, facilities
   and demand.

  • Residential renting is a major historically supported tenure state, not an edge case. Opening independent nonfarm
    renter share should provisionally calibrate around 35-45% rather than a token percentage, with boarders/lodgers
    tracked separately.

  • The player can set aggressive or irrational rents, maintenance policies, business hours, prices and other
    lawful/physically possible policies. The simulation should answer through vacancy, demand, deterioration, labor,
    competition and other consequences rather than arbitrary designer prohibition.

  • Mining is an economic ecosystem. The player may profit from prospecting/claims, finance, assay, treatment, mineral
    trade, supply, contracting, camp property and redevelopment without owning a producing mine.

  • Agriculture is a seasonal land-and-capital economy. Machinery changes work capacity rather than biological yield;
    livestock remain biological capital; weather acts through the physical crop, forage, water, animal or work process
    actually affected.

APPENDIX B


 Feature Status & Production Priority Core Identity - Ownership-led growth, real households, flexible parcel use, shared
 business shell, realism-first simulation and visible world evidence. VP Core - General Store deep slice, deal-flow
 acquisition, household shopping, notices, Net Worth, staffing continuity and doctor node. Active VP Expansion -
 Boarding/settlement growth, recurring orders, survey/terrain groundwork, workflow UI, node logic, early logistics
 visibility and adversity proof. Post-VP - Broader business pool, richer property markets, stronger manager policies, rural
 production chains and remote-node maturation. Rail Era - Moving railheads, depot/bypass competition, feeder-freight
 transition, corridor projects and rail-linked communications. Late Capital Era - Banks, mines, railway companies, utility
 acquisitions, executive staff, investment workflow and mature regional communications. Long-Term - Deep utility
 operations, municipal infrastructure ownership, mature electric power, toll/rural telephone, richer weather/street
 systems and formal freight contracts. Parked - Specialized reservation trading, deeper commercial-credit/legal edge
 cases, richer gossip, tenant operators, scheduled wagon rounds and other valuable layers not in active production.
 Visual / Background at 1905 edge - Occasional automobile, extremely rare gasoline tractor, cutting-edge mechanical
 refrigeration or other period-valid technology that should not replace the horse/wagon economy. Outside normal
 1880-1905 campaign - Widespread motor freight, ordinary tractor farming, automobile-oriented road systems, universal
 rural electricity, modern zoning and universal professional municipal services. Replaced - Dialogue checks for deals,
 parcel hard-typing, owner-presence- heavy business logic and teleport-heavy supply assumptions.
