APPENDIX D


 Play Modes, Scenario Campaign & Optional Victory Reference

  MODE | RULE

  Scenarios | Authored, difficulty-ranked commercial challenges. Fixed premise, variable economic detail where useful. Same
  underlying simulation rules as Open Frontier.

  Scenario Campaign | The formal campaign is completion across the scenario catalogue rather than one continuous protagonist/save.
  Scenarios can be grouped by era or commercial theme and need not be strictly linear.

  Open Frontier | Flagship procedural sandbox. Recommended opening spring 1880, seed-generated regional economy, no mandatory
  victory by default and full historical simulation through the 1905 horizon.

  Open Frontier + Optional Victory | Sandbox may enable Capital, Selected Legacy, Capital + Legacy or supported custom conditions
  without changing the underlying economy.

  Continuation | After the authored horizon, preferred labels are Continuation Year 1, Continuation Year 2, etc.; existing supported
  capabilities can diffuse but no new post-1905 technology family is implied.

  Commercial Ruin | Separate economic defeat state. It is not the same as failing a scenario objective and need not be enabled in
  every sandbox configuration.

 SCENARIO DESIGN LOCKS

  • Objectives should describe economic outcomes or transitions, not arbitrary object counts.

  • Optional Distinctions reward mastery without becoming required checklist clutter.

  • Difficulty comes from starting conditions, commitments, scarcity, information, time and intertwined pressures - never
    hidden NPC production/revenue buffs.

  • Scenario deadlines should have a world, historical or scenario-scope reason.

  • Scenario completion records the actual economic result, not only one score.

  • Scenario randomization should preserve the premise while varying enough detail to prevent memorized opening
    scripts.

 OPEN FRONTIER REPLAYABILITY LOCKS

  • World generation is a headline feature, not merely objective-free play.

  • The historical skeleton is stable; commercial history is variable.

  • Seed variation can alter geography, ownership, households, businesses, suppliers, labor, condition, resources, rivals,
    debts, migration, settlement potential and infrastructure proposals.

  • Opening information should be commercially plausible but should not reveal hidden truth or an optimal strategy.

  • The sandbox must remain worth playing even after every scenario is completed.

 OPTIONAL LEGACY VICTORIES

  Merchant Prince | Major retail/service network with meaningful household and business service.

   Industrialist | Substantial production/industrial control with real operating chains.

  Financier | Major lending/deposit/regional-capital position.

  Railroad Baron | Meaningful railway control plus sustained traffic/destination importance.

  Land Baron | Major valuable and strategically useful land/property portfolio.

  Regional Power | Meaningful economic presence across multiple settlement nodes.

  Settlement Builder | Durable development of a weak/emerging node through real jobs, services, housing and freight.

  Grand Empire | REWORK REQUIRED; do not implement as simple multi-badge collection.

APPENDIX E


 Commercial Ruin & Distress Reference LOSS RULE: zero cash, negative Net Worth, missed payment, default,
 foreclosure on one asset or a late-campaign bankruptcy filing are not automatic defeat. Commercial Ruin occurs only
 after viable ownership and recovery capacity are effectively exhausted. Financial failure remains playable: strain -> due
 payment -> delinquency -> workout/restructuring -> default -> applicable enforcement -> voluntary or forced sale /
 foreclosure -> possible redemption, deficiency or recovery -> Commercial Ruin only if viable economic capacity is
 exhausted. Opening law is Dakota Territorial, not informal frontier practice. Mortgages and chattel security are
 asset-specific; exemptions and separate property can preserve a recovery foothold. Statehood November 2, 1889
 preserves existing obligations. The federal Bankruptcy Act becomes available to qualifying debtors July 1, 1898 but is
 not a modern universal reset. Recovery tools can include owner cash injection, inter-business cash movement,
 refinancing/revised schedules, additional collateral, investor capital, inventory liquidation, project delay, cost reduction,
 turnaround, voluntary sale and closure of weaker holdings.

APPENDIX J


 Remote Industry, Mining, Logging & Sawmill Reference Mine staging - district information/prospect -> claim control ->
 representative assay/feasibility -> financing/investor structure -> initial works -> production -> expansion. Deposit
 identities - gold dominant; lead-silver/polymetallic secondary; tin speculative; coal strategic but often
 external/conditional; iron niche. Ore authority - grade plus metallurgical character, treatment compatibility and
 confidence. Geological mineralization is not automatically economic ore. Functional mine capacities - development,
 drilling/blasting, ground support, internal haulage, hoisting, water control, crushing, treatment, power, freight and
 skilled labor. Improvement moves bottlenecks rather than granting a mine level. Treatment chronology -
 stamp/amalgamation opening-era for suitable gold; chlorination important by 1889; specialized smelting around 1890;
 early intermittent cyanide 1892; successful cyanidation expands late 1890s/early 1900s. Mechanical chronology -
 serious steam/hoisting opening-era; hand drilling remains credible into early 1890s; compressed-air drilling expands in
 the 1890s; electric lighting appears before broad electric motive power. Industrial rail - private mine/mill/timber
 narrow-gauge can precede common-carrier rail when freight concentration justifies it. Mine as business - preserve
 common cash/income/ownership shell plus local claim, workings, ore, treatment, labor, timber, power, haulage and
 condition state. Mine camps - can become settlement nodes, stall, decline, ghost or convert as underlying economics
 change. Timber extraction - stand/worksite logic with terrain, road, haul distance and quality. Sawmills feed building,
 mine support, rail, farms and repairs; mining can materially raise timber demand.

APPENDIX K


 Finance, Banking & Legal Chronology Reference Bankability - banking exists regionally before 1880; the opening town
 may still be too small or weak for a local bank. Bankability depends on deposits, payroll, business volume, land value,
 debt demand, rail/industrial seriousness and confidence rather than a population unlock. Loan review - purpose,
 repayment source, collateral quality, existing debt, reputation, market outlook, strategic value and portfolio risk.
 Workouts - revised schedules, partial payment, extra collateral, refinance and negotiated asset transfer can precede
 enforcement. Collateral - secured and unsecured creditors differ; mortgages/chattel security remain asset-specific;
 protected property and separate ownership can remain outside creditor reach. Interest chronology - opening Dakota
 general framework: 7% legal/default, up to 12% written contract; covered Black Hills written-contract freedom 1881
 through June 30, 1887; general ceiling returns July 1, 1887. Municipal finance - federal territorial act July 30, 1886: 4%
 general local debt cap and strong limits on public credit/subscription aid to private corporations. South Dakota
 statehood: 5% general constitutional local debt cap subject to later infrastructure provisions. Statehood - November 2,
 1889 changes institutions but preserves existing contracts, rights, corporations, litigation, bonds and debts. Bankruptcy
 - no federal bankruptcy system from 1878 until the Bankruptcy Act of 1898 takes effect July 1, 1898. Late bankruptcy is
 a qualifying distress route, not a universal reset. Credit climate - deposits, liquidity, loan quality, sector exposure,
 outside capital and confidence remain underlying states; a climate label summarizes rather than imposes a global
 modifier.

APPENDIX L


 Rail, Communications, Utilities & 1905 Boundary Reference Rail - no local common-carrier rail at the normal 1880 start.
 Practical railheads move closer over time; industrial rail can precede public regional service; local service depends on
 company strategy, route economics, land and traffic rather than a tier. Regional rail chronology - outside Black Hills
 penetration 1885, Rapid City 1886, Whitewood 1887, substantial late-1880s/1890-91 expansion, multi-company
 network by 1900, major east-west South Dakota connection work still underway in 1905. Telegraph - already unevenly
 regional in 1880; access progresses from mail/traveler and courier-to-wire toward nearby node, local office and mature
 rail-integrated service. Information has source and age. Telephone - regionally present exceptionally early; private line
 -> exchange -> expanded subscriber network -> toll/inter-town -> regional/rural mutual. Property connection matters;
 networks can compete and fail to interconnect. Electricity - normal opening town has none. Lighting-first adoption
 expands during 1880s-1900s according to load, capital, generation and distribution economics;
 steam/water/mechanical power persists. By 1905 strong nodes can have meaningful electric systems without rural
 universality. Water/sewer - young nodes use wells/pumps/privies/drainage; formal
 source/storage/mains/hydrants/sewer districts/property connections expand spatially. Partial coverage can persist for
 decades. Fire service - ad hoc/buckets -> volunteer hook-ladder/hose -> hydrant-supported volunteer service ->
 mature volunteer department; paid/professional service only where unusually large/complex late nodes justify it. 1905
 boundary - rail, telephone, electric light, waterworks, cyanide-era industry and sophisticated finance can coexist with
 horse/wagon rural life. Automobiles are rare background, not a new core transport regime.

APPENDIX N


 Anti-Bloat & Non-Goals

  • Do not turn the game into a full railroad-dispatch simulator.

  • Do not require a fully simulated region of mapped towns before off-map rail expansion is allowed.

  • Do not make banking a constant paperwork chore once the portfolio is large enough for thresholds and staff.

  • Do not treat electricity as a universal modernity switch that erases frontier texture.

  • Do not let stocks, bonds, or luxury goods arrive so early that they undermine the ownership-first climb.

 DESIGN DERIVATION QUESTIONS

  • What frontier reality is this modeling?

  • What tension makes it interesting?

  • What physical, behavioral, and social signals reveal it?

  • What threshold changes it from background to consequence?

  • What ownership response does it ask for?

  • What structure does it strengthen?

  • When in the game timeline does it matter most?

  • What place or district logic changes its meaning?

  • Does it create readable town consequence?

  • Does it fit the prestige-frontier tone?

  • Who has legitimate authority to make this decision?

  • What person, asset, location or physical movement must actually exist before the action can resolve?

  • Can the player be allowed to make a bad or unusual choice and learn through consequence instead of prohibition?

  • What does the ordinary employee execute, what does a manager administer, and what remains an owner-level capital
    decision?

  • Have we understood the real process deeply enough before choosing the abstraction?

 SECONDARY NODES IN 1905 Secondary towns, mine camps, ranch hamlets and farm-service clusters can remain far
 less modern than the strongest center. Some may have rail but no electricity; telephone but no sewer; a mine
 generator but privies; a bank but dirt streets; or neither rail nor piped utilities. Network inequality is canonical.
 TECHNOLOGY BOUNDARY Core by 1905 where economics justify it: rail, telegraph, subscriber telephone, compact
 electricity, water/hydrants/partial sewer, advanced hard-rock mining, horse-powered agricultural machinery,
 fencing/windmills, ice/cold-chain access, office equipment and mail-order competition. Rare/cutting-edge: automobiles,
 gasoline tractors, broad mechanical refrigeration, extensive electric motive power outside major industry. Outside
 normal campaign: motor trucks replacing wagon freight, ordinary tractor agriculture, widespread automobiles,
 automobile-oriented roads, universal rural electricity, universal sewer/paving/professional fire service and modern
 zoning.

APPENDIX Q


 Maintenance, Records & Information Authority Reference

Q1 Maintenance chain

 Use / environment / age / operating practice -> condition and specific defects -> observation/inspection ->
 maintenance or deferred work -> parts/labor/facility/downtime -> repaired condition, continued deterioration or failure.
 Player-facing reports should emphasize readable state and known defects.

Q2 Record chain

 Actual simulation event -> properly recorded transaction or missing/incorrect record -> reconciliation/stocktake/audit
 -> discrepancy explanation/correction -> improved historical information. A known transaction stays exact;
 bookkeeping quality affects completeness and interpretation rather than inventing fake price uncertainty.

Q3 Forecast chain

 Available historical evidence + current state + relevant owner/manager/specialist expertise + information quality ->
 forecast central estimate / range / confidence. Future shock and genuine unknowns remain capable of producing
 outcomes outside the expected range.

Q4 Common maintenance owner decisions

  • Automatic routine-service spending threshold and cash-reserve protection.

  • Inspection cadence and which defects trigger shutdown/owner review.

  • Repair now, temporary repair, defer, overhaul or replace.

  • Stock spare parts or rely on outside sourcing.

  • Own reserve capacity or accept interruption risk.

  • Schedule maintenance during low-demand windows versus continued production.

APPENDIX R


 Experience, Expertise & Commercial Standing Reference

R1 Progression doctrine

 Expertise grows from relevant lived commercial experience; Commercial Standing grows from actual wealth, scale and
 track record; modernization grows from the historical world. None should substitute for the others. Expertise primarily
 reveals, estimates, compares, diagnoses, warns and recognizes patterns. Any real cost/output improvement must be
 explainable through a changed contract, route, allocation, staffing decision, equipment choice, maintenance action or
 other causal process.

R2 Oversized candidate pool

  • 1. Bookkeeping & Commercial Analysis - reports, reconciliation, cost attribution, trend recognition and financial
    interpretation.

  • 2. Merchandising - assortment, turnover, stockout, seasonal and display-space interpretation.

  • 3. Purchasing & Supply - supplier comparison, landed-cost interpretation, procurement timing and concentration risk.

  • 4. Freight & Logistics - route, load, travel-time, utilization and transport-bottleneck analysis.

  • 5. Property & Valuation - land/building value, redevelopment potential, repair burden and comparable-market
    interpretation.

  • 6. Negotiation & Dealcraft - counterparty motive, urgency, deal structure and likely room for movement.

  • 7. Employment & Management - staffing, retention, supervision, delegation and organizational diagnosis.

  • 8. Credit & Collections - customer repayment capacity, receivables, delinquency and collection posture.

  • 9. Finance & Capital - debt capacity, financing structure, investment comparison and capital allocation.

  • 10. Risk & Resilience - concentration, reserve sufficiency, single points of failure and contingency recognition.

  • 11. Retail Trade - industry familiarity with customer traffic, merchandise cycles and store operations.

  • 12. Lodging & Hospitality - occupancy, room/board economics, meal demand and transient-customer patterns.

  • 13. Agriculture - field work, seasonal windows, machinery use and crop-production constraints.

  • 14. Livestock & Ranching - forage, water, herd composition, winter preparation and sale timing.

  • 15. Industrial Operations - machinery, power, throughput, process bottlenecks and heavy-operation reporting.

  • 16. Lumber & Sawmilling - log supply, mill throughput, drying/storage and lumber-chain constraints.

  • 18. Banking - loan portfolios, deposits, liquidity, credit quality and concentration.

  • 23. Inventory Control - days-of-supply, target stock, excess inventory, stockout and reorder analysis.

  • 26. Commercial Contracts - commitments, fulfillment exposure, renewal risk and unfavorable-term recognition.

APPENDIX S


 Residential Property & Tenancy Reference

S1 Tenure calibration

 1890 South Dakota nonfarm housing provides the nearest direct census anchor: about 45% rented overall and about
 44% rented outside cities of 8,000 or more. 1900 known-tenure nonfarm homes remain around 40% rented. Because
 the opening game is 1880 and the census did not yet collect the same tenure table, use approximately 35-45% renter
 households as a provisional opening calibration for independent nonfarm households; boarders/lodgers remain
 additional.

S2 Core entities

  • Property/building owner.

  • Residential unit.

  • Occupant household/person.

  • Tenure arrangement.

  • Rent/arrears/payment history.

  • Condition/maintenance.

  • Debt/encumbrance.

  • Housing suitability and service connections.

S3 Landlord strategy without classes

 Stable landlord, high-rent operator, cheap/crowded housing investor, premium landlord, speculative builder, employer
 landlord, mixed-use owner, distress buyer and land assembler are emergent strategies. The game should not require
 the player to select a landlord archetype or Slumlord perk.

S4 Open historical questions

  • 1880s Dakota/Black Hills rent cadence, written versus oral tenancy and deposit practice.

  • Notice/removal/eviction procedure and tenant treatment through foreclosure.

  • Typical division of repair, fuel and furnishing responsibilities.

  • Distribution of landlord types and portfolio sizes in Black Hills settlements.

APPENDIX T


 Repair, Fabrication & Technical Services Reference

T1 Capability families

 Opening-era: smithing, horseshoeing, wagon/wheel work, harness/tack and general repair. Growth-era: larger
 implement/industrial work, manufacturer parts and internal mine/mill maintenance. Late campaign: machine-shop and
 railway/utility specialized work where capital and industrial demand justify it.

T2 Work-order chain

 Asset/customer need -> reported problem -> physical arrival or on-site service -> diagnosis -> quote/terms ->
 queue/prioritization -> materials/parts -> skilled labor -> completion -> payment/account -> asset returns to service ->
 repair history updated.

T3 Key business tensions

  • Routine work versus rush interruption.

  • Walk-in customers versus recurring contracts/reserved capacity.

  • Fabricate locally versus order a manufactured replacement.

  • Stock slow-moving parts versus preserve cash/storage.

  • Train/retain skilled workers versus risk losing them to competitors.

  • Repair customer assets versus buy/refurbish/salvage used equipment.

APPENDIX U


 Mining & Rural Production Square Matrices

U1 Mining width x depth

 Width lanes: Prospecting/Claims; Mine Operation; Investment; Assay/Technical Services; Custom Treatment; Mineral
 Commerce; Mining Supply; Contract Services; Mine-Camp Property; Reprocessing/Failed-Mine Redevelopment. Depth
 dimensions: Information; Physical Capacity; Labor/Skill; Inputs/Logistics; Customers/Contracts; Cash/Finance;
 Condition/Reliability; Time/Lifecycle; Authority/Delegation; Regional Consequence.

U2 Rural width x depth

 Width lanes: Crop Farming; Hay/Forage; Cattle; Sheep where distinct; Local Produce; Custom Agricultural Work;
 Livestock Commerce; Agricultural Supply; Processing/Storage; Rural Property/Infrastructure. Depth dimensions:
 Land/Resource; Biological State; Seasonal Timing; Labor; Draft/Machinery; Inputs; Storage; Maintenance;
 Market/Logistics; Capital/Authority.

U3 Square rule

 The square matrices are completeness tests. If one lane has only a name and no answers to the depth dimensions, it is
 decorative width and needs design work or removal. If one central activity accumulates many more detailed mechanics
 than the surrounding economic ecosystem, it is excessive depth and the design should widen before adding more
 microscopic detail. The goal is balanced causal richness, not equal UI complexity for every lane.

APPENDIX V


 Household, Accommodation, Kinship & Demographic Lifecycle Reference Status: Revision XII canonical reference
 appendix. This appendix compresses Section 12.6 for routing, balance and future balancing. It does not override the
 body.

 V1. Relationship authority map

 Entity / relationship Answers Key rule Person Who is the individual? Persists through household, work and
 accommodation changes. Family / Kinship Who is related to whom? Explicit parent/child/spouse graph; does not require
 co-residence. Household Who shares a domestic economy? One adult or larger group; size is lifecycle output, not
 building capacity. Residential Occupancy Who is staying where and on what terms? Relationship object; can represent
 rent, boarding, employer lodging, kin hosting or temporary shelter. Accommodation Space What physical shelter is
 usable? Capabilities and condition; can be room, dwelling, bunk space, rough shelter or tent/camp element. Building
 What physical structure contains functions? Can contain commercial, storage and multiple accommodation spaces.
 Parcel What land/legal geography underlies it? Ownership/transfer authority remains separate from occupancy.

 V2. Accommodation arrangement matrix

 Arrangement Typical authority/terms Simulation implication Owner occupied Household/owner controls occupancy
 subject to debt/legal rights. Security depends on finances, condition and legal exposure, not ownership label alone.
 Independent rental Lease/tenancy relationship. Longer-term household settlement; rent, maintenance and removal
 rules apply. Room / partial building Household rents only part of mixed-use or multi-unit property. Supports dense Main
 Street and family/single-person options without one-building-one-household assumption. Boarding / lodging Bed/room
 and often meals/services. Crucial for single workers, transients and early migration; distinct households may share one
 house. Employer lodging Employment-linked bunk, cottage or board arrangement. Recruitment value and
 job-dependence emerge causally. Kin hosted / doubled-up Host household or shared occupancy. Emergency/low-cost
 capacity; households may remain financially separate. Temporary shelter / camp Tent or rough shelter with real
 location/capability. Allows booms ahead of permanent stock; exposes weather, fire, sanitation and crowding pressure.
 No stable shelter No reliable current arrangement. Triggers search/migration pressure; not a passive permanent status.

 V3. Dependent-minor resolution matrix

 Trigger: a dependent minor loses the last locally responsible adult. Resolve care through a dedicated dependency
 process rather than directly assigning the child to a household. Priority Search lane Rule 1 Existing lawful responsibility
 Surviving parent or existing guardian/caretaker relationship where valid. 2 Suitable close kin Adult sibling, grandparent,
 aunt/uncle or other meaningful kin, evaluated for actual suitability. 3 Established non-kin Known
 household/associate/neighbor with strong social connection and ability to care. 4 Suitable local placement Other willing
 household when no stronger relationship resolves the case. 5 Off-map/public/charitable path Distant kin,
 county/public/charitable or institutional route where historically appropriate. Non-negotiable: placement priority is a
 game decision architecture, not a claim that 1880 Dakota law imposed this exact order. Siblings are preferentially kept
 together. Care/guardianship does not transfer inherited property. Exact legal procedure remains a research hold.

 scale. High design confidence; intentionally compressed vs real Rapid City.

 plausibility, not hard validation. Revision XII supersedes hard-band interpretation. U.S. TFR 1880 ~4.24; 1890 ~3.87;

 1880 ~2.96; 1900 ~2.78 to age 10 Prevents births = surviving children. Broad national series. First marriage 1890

  • Across repeated 25-year campaign simulations, compare births per woman and surviving-child distributions against
   broad historical envelopes.

  • Track age at first marriage, widowhood/remarriage, household splitting/merging and adult children remaining/leaving.

  • Check whether family-sized households are disproportionately blocked when a node has beds but the wrong type of
   accommodation.

  • Measure orphan/dependency cases, sibling separation frequency, local versus off-map resolution and
    estate/guardianship continuity.

  • Check whether boom nodes can grow temporarily through boarding/camps without permanent housing, then either
   harden into durable settlement or contract when jobs disappear.

  • Avoid calibration that requires hidden household-size caps, fertility buffs/debuffs or teleporting placement. Fix the
    causal parameters instead.

 V6. Research holds carried forward

 Demography: Black Hills/Dakota parity and childlessness distribution; birth spacing; age-specific fertility and remarriage
 by settlement type; maternal, infant and childhood mortality by place/subgroup; prevalence of multi-generation and
 fostered/kin-care households. Children and legal status: territorial/state majority and contracting authority;
 school-attendance chronology; occupation-specific child-work restrictions; apprenticeship practice and transition to
 independent wage work. Guardianship and dependency: exact spring-1880 guardian appointment law and procedure;
 county poor-relief/charitable practice; property administration for minors; local versus off-map care patterns;
 terminology appropriate to Dakota courts and counties. Accommodation: Black Hills boarding/lodging composition,
 tenancy cadence, oral versus written arrangements, furnished/unfurnished room practice, eviction/removal chronology,
 fuel/repair responsibilities and how period census definitions should map into the game's relationship ontology. These
 holds do not block the relationship architecture. They block only false precision. Future balancing should preserve
 configurable calibration data so validated historical values can replace placeholders without changing the entity model.

 V7. Source anchors

 U.S. Census Bureau: 1880 Census Instructions to Enumerators; Compendium of the Eleventh Census: 1890 - Progress of
 the Nation; 1900 Census, Volume 2: Population, Part II; historical Median Age at First Marriage: 1890 to Present series.
 Social Security Administration: historical U.S. fertility series with survival-to-age-ten adjustment. Dakota Territory: The
 Compiled Laws of the Territory of Dakota, A.D. 1887, Chapter 13, Guardian and Ward. These sources are used as
 architecture/calibration evidence, not as a claim that every national statistic directly describes the fictional opening
 node.

APPENDIX W


 Revision XIV Depth-Balance Audit & Research Anchors

W1 Systems deliberately deepened in Revision XIV

  • Butcher - expanded from a short business identity into sourcing, carcass balance, preservation, capacity, accounts,
    byproducts and continuity.

  • Boarding House / Hotel - expanded into accommodation products, board/meal capacity, customer mix, labor, project
   demand and safety/continuity.

  • Doctor - expanded into time/travel capacity, triage, fees/accounts, practice continuity, reputation/referral and
    illness-wave load.

  • Markets / Competition - expanded into category markets, substitution, rival strategy, price/service competition,
    advertising, entry/exit and memory.

  • Banking - expanded into balance-sheet liquidity, loan concentration, deposits/confidence, correspondent stress,
    acquired assets and governance.

  • Railway ownership - expanded from corridor development into tariffs, traffic, service, depot handling, competition,
    regulation and maintenance.

  • Executive / Portfolio - expanded into exception management, manager differences, shared services, treasury,
    governance, talent allocation and communication reach.

  • Acquisition / Dealcraft - expanded into deal structure, exchanged concessions, time pressure and question-based
    diligence.

  • Expertise - consolidated from an oversized reference pool toward broad owner families plus industry familiarity and
    specialist knowledge.

W2 Systems reviewed but not expanded materially

 Shared maintenance and records, household/kinship/housing, rural production and mining already carry strong causal
 depth relative to their width. Telegraph, telephone, electricity and civic networks also already contain sufficient
 adoption, geography, ownership and reliability logic for the current Canon stage. Further additions to those systems
 should answer a specific design problem rather than increase detail for its own sake.

W3 Verified research anchors used for the Revision XIV pass

  • U.S. Census Bureau, 1880 Instructions to Enumerators: hotels and boarding-style shared-roof/shared-table
    arrangements, boarders, hotel cooks/waiters and nonstandard dwellings are explicitly recognized in contemporary
   enumeration practice.

  • U.S. National Park Service, Lucretia Marshbanks: direct Black Hills evidence for a woman serving as cook and manager
    at the DeSmet mine establishment and later purchasing a boarding house in Sawpit Gulch in 1883, renamed Rustic
    Hotel.

  • Library of Congress, Custer Chronicle overview (1880-1890): opening-era Black Hills newspaper advertising included
    hotels, blacksmiths, banks, a surgeon, groceries, restaurants and other local businesses, supporting advertising as a
    real information channel rather than a modern marketing abstraction.

  • 'A Doctor in the House: The Architecture of Home-offices for Physicians in Toronto, 1885-1930' (PMC): North American
    physician practice retained a strong home-visiting model; travel burden and later transport/telephone access helped
   make office practice more efficient. The Canon uses this as structural evidence, not as a Black Hills fee or staffing
    calibration.

  • FDIC historical timeline, 1850-1899, and Federal Reserve History, Banking Panics of the Gilded Age:
    nineteenth-century banking depended on deposits, reserves, loan quality and interbank relationships; panics could
   produce withdrawals, bank suspensions and transmission between interior and money-center banks. Statutory
    national-bank reserve rules are not applied automatically to every possible player bank form.

  • Smithsonian Libraries / National Museum of American History, 1877 freight tariff and classification and Sinclair's 1869
    Freight Computer: freight charges were explicitly calculated from weight/rates and railroads used freight
    classifications and tariffs well before the game's opening.

  • U.S. National Archives, Interstate Commerce Act (1887): interstate common carriers faced requirements for
    just/reasonable and published rates plus restrictions on rebates, undue preferences and long/short-haul discrimination
   under the new Interstate Commerce Commission regime.

W4 Ongoing depth discipline

 When future design work identifies a broad new business or institution, first compare it against the depth dimensions in
 7.5A and the square-matrix doctrine in Appendix U. If it adds a new name but no new causal relationship, keep it
 parked. If it adds a relationship the existing economy cannot express, research the real process deeply enough to
 understand its inputs, decisions, failure, lifecycle and cross-system consequences before promoting it to active scope.

APPENDIX X


 Revision XIV Commercial-Consequence & Play-Mode Synthesis

X1 Canon-ready systemic doctrines added in this revision

  • Persistent Economic Consequence: important decisions alter later possibilities and the world retains economically
    meaningful history.

  • Ownership-as-Responsibility: ownership converts outside dependency into controlled internal scarcity, obligations and
   maintenance rather than solving the problem.

  • Commercial Commitment Authority: agreements reserve real future resources/capacity and remain distinct from
    physical execution.

  • Credible Alternatives: bargaining power and resilience derive from feasible alternatives rather than Influence,
   Monopoly or Capacity meters.

  • Bounded Awareness: actors reconsider through Trigger -> Awareness -> Feasibility -> Shortlist -> Choice rather than
    omniscient optimization.

  • Advertising-as-Information: advertising changes awareness of a real offer; it does not create demand by modifier.

  • Organizational Coverage: execution, decision, information, administrative and specialist coverage remain distinct
    causal problems.

  • Owner Attention Without Action Points: travel, authority and communication determine what the principal can
    personally resolve.

  • Information Distance: remote organization can know local reality before the principal receives or interprets it.

  • Capital and Talent Allocation: mature play increasingly allocates scarce money, managers and specialist attention
   between competing uses.

  • Partial Ownership and Control Rights: economic interest, governance, capital responsibility and exit rights need not be
    identical.

  • Internal Opportunity Cost: wholly owned businesses do not fake-negotiate, but internal use preserves real physical and
    forgone-market cost.

  • Distress as Option Loss: failure becomes dangerous as credible responses disappear; entity failure need not equal
    player-career failure.

  • Recombination: failed firms release workers, assets, property, customers and knowledge into the wider economy.

  • Commercial Succession: legal ownership, operating capability and financial continuity are resolved separately when
   key people leave or die.

  • Selective Economic Memory: persist identity-changing events; summarize routine execution.

  • Economic Geography: the player changes practical relationships across the map rather than conquering territory.

X2 Play-mode authority added in this revision

 Scenarios are the formal authored campaign layer. They are ranked by difficulty, built around specific commercial
 situations and judged through primary objectives plus optional distinctions. The same simulation rules apply as
 everywhere else. Scenario randomness is encouraged when it preserves the premise.

 Open Frontier is the flagship procedural sandbox. It should be aggressively replayable, generating a different 1880
 regional economy from seed while preserving the same historical capability envelope. It has no mandatory victory
 condition by default. Optional Capital/Legacy goals can be enabled, but they do not define the mode.

 The two modes solve different player desires. Scenarios ask: can you solve this particular commercial problem? Open
 Frontier asks: what kind of economic history will emerge from this world? Neither is a lesser version of the other.

X3 Scenario-family concept pool - design direction, not locked production
 order

 Possible families include Foundations (merchant, property, freight, settlement growth), Industrial Frontier (timber,
 ranch/winter, mine boom, custom processing), Network Era (railhead, bypassed town, telegraph/telephone, electric
 light), Capital & Crisis (Panic of 1893, banking, distressed empire, railroad promotion) and Capital Command (regional
 power, succession, late-portfolio restructuring). Exact scenario names, count, objectives, prerequisites and difficulty
 ratings remain future design work.

X4 Active research/design holds

  • Regional commercial geography, overlapping market areas and whether routes need persistent economic identity.

  • Wholesale/branch-business structure, central purchasing, local books/managers and internal freight.

  • Rail-depot drayage/transshipment and the transformation of long-haul wagon businesses after rail arrival.

  • Exact ordinary B2B agreement conventions where stronger Black Hills evidence is still needed.

  • Probate, partnership death, inheritance and married-property legal details not yet validated.

  • Employee-to-partner/owner pathways and period-specific compensation/ownership arrangements.

  • Exact Legacy qualifications and Grand Empire replacement.

  • Final Open Frontier setup parameters, procedural ranges and scenario campaign catalogue/progression.

X5 Production filter

 Future additions should usually deepen the network of consequences connecting systems the player already manages.
 A new business or institution earns active scope when it introduces a genuinely new economic verb, asset, relationship
 or risk that cannot be expressed cleanly by existing systems. The game does not need to simulate everything about
 frontier life. It should simulate the economic consequences of the things it chooses to represent unusually well.
